en: Oṃ, homage to the Triple Gem.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
In the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered the great city of Śrāvastī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Śrāvastī and finished his meal, the Venerable Ānanda approached a certain well.
At that time, a Mātaṅga girl named Prakṛti was drawing water from that well.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti:
"Sister, give me some water; I shall drink."
When this had been said, the maiden Prakṛti addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"I am the Mātaṅga maiden, Reverend Ānanda.
"Sister, I do not ask you about your family or your birth."
"However, if that water has been discarded, give it to me; I shall drink.
Then the maiden Prakṛti gave water to the venerable Ānanda.
Having drunk the water, the venerable Ānanda departed.

Then Prakṛti, the daughter of the Mātaṅga, having carefully and thoroughly observed the signs in the body, face, and voice of the venerable Ānanda, became possessed by right mental attention and gave rise to a mind of passion, thinking:
"The noble Ānanda has come to be my husband."
"And my mother is a great Vidyādharī; she will be able to bring the noble Ānanda here.
Then Prakṛti, the Mātaṅga girl, taking a water-jar, approached the Caṇḍāla house, set the water-jar aside in a corner, and said this to her mother:
"O Mother, you should know that there is a monk named Ānanda, an attendant and disciple of the Great Śramaṇa Gautama; him I desire as my husband."
"Mother, will you be able to bring him?
She said to her,
"Daughter, I am able to bring Ānanda."
Except for one who is dead or one who is free from passion;
moreover, King Prasenajit of Kośala serves, honors, and attends upon the ascetic Gautama excessively.
If he were to find out, he would act to the detriment of this Caṇḍāla family.
"It is heard that the ascetic Gautama is free from passion;
furthermore, the mantras of one who is free from passion overcome all other mantras.
Having been addressed thus, Prakṛti, the daughter of Mātaṅga, spoke this to her mother.
"Mother, if the ascetic Gautama is free from passion, and if I do not obtain the ascetic Ānanda from his presence, I shall give up my life; but if I obtain him, I shall live.
"Do not give up your life, daughter! I will bring the ascetic Ānanda.
Then, in the middle of the courtyard of her house, the mother of the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti smeared the ground with cow dung.
Having prepared an altar, smeared it with [unguents], strewn it with *darbha* grass, and kindled a fire, she took one hundred and eight *arka* flowers and,
while reciting the mantras, consecrated each *arka* flower individually with incantations and cast them into the fire.
In this regard, the following spell (*vidyā*) is used:
"O Amale, Vimale, Kuṅkume, Sumane!
By whom you have been bound as lightning,
by whose will the god rains, flashes, and thunders— to increase the wonder of the Great King, the gods Śikhigraha and Viśikhigraha [have acted] toward the gods, humans, and gandharvas."
"O gods, for the arrival, the meeting, the treading upon, and the grasping of Ānanda, I offer this oblation; svāhā!
(p. 3.2). Then the mind of the venerable Ānanda was seized; he went out from the monastery and approached the dwelling of a caṇḍāla.
The Caṇḍālī saw the Venerable Ānanda coming from afar;
having seen him, she said this to her daughter Prakṛti:
"Daughter, here comes that ascetic Ānanda; prepare a bed."
Then Prakṛti, the daughter of the Mātaṅga, joyful, satisfied, and delighted in mind, prepared a bed for the venerable Ānanda.
Then the venerable Ānanda approached the house of the Caṇḍāla; having approached, he stood leaning against the sacrificial altar.
Standing to one side, the venerable Ānanda wept; shedding tears, he spoke thus:
"I am fallen into calamity, yet the Blessed One does not take heed of me."
Then the Blessed One directed his attention toward the Venerable Ānanda.
Having so directed his attention, he countered the Caṇḍāla mantras with the mantras of the Perfectly Awakened One.
In this regard, the following is the vidyā:
Stability is non-falling away; it is right conduct.
May there be well-being for all living beings!
The lake is serene, faultless, tranquil, and free from fear on all sides.
Wherever calamities are stilled and fears are dispelled,
there indeed the gods, all the *siddhas*, and the *yogins* pay homage.
By this word of truth, may there be well-being and bliss for the mendicant.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, his Caṇḍāla incantations having been frustrated, departed from the Caṇḍāla’s house and set out for his own monastery. Prakṛti, the Mātaṅga girl, saw the Venerable Ānanda returning; seeing him, she spoke thus to her mother:
"Mother, here goes that ascetic Ānanda.
His mother said to her,
"Daughter, he must surely have been taken into the care of the ascetic Gautama."
"Therefore, my mantras will be thwarted.
Prakṛti said,
"But mother, why is it that the mantras of the ascetic Gautama are more powerful, and not ours?"
Her mother said to her:
"The spells of the ascetic Gautama are more powerful than ours.
Daughter, whatever spells prevail over the entire world, the ascetic Gautama, if he so desires, can counteract them."

"Furthermore, the world is not able to counteract the mantras of the śramaṇa Gautama; thus, the mantras of the śramaṇa Gautama are exceedingly powerful. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
As the venerable Ānanda was standing to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Ānanda, take up this six-syllable vidyā; preserve it, recite it, and master it."

For one’s own benefit and happiness, and for the benefit and happiness of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen— this, Ānanda, is the six-syllable vidyā, spoken by the six perfectly awakened Buddhas, by the four Great Kings, by Śakra, the lord of the gods, by Brahmā Sahāmpati, and by me now.
It was spoken by the perfectly awakened Śākyamuni. Now, Ānanda, you too should uphold, recite, and master it; namely, as follows:
O Aṇḍara, Pāṇḍara, Kāraṇḍa, Keyūra, Arcihasta, Kharagrīva, Bandhumat, Cīramat, Dharavidha, Cilimila! Stir up the poisons in the world!
O Poison, move, move!
O Golamati, Gaṇḍavila, Cilimila, Sātinimna, and you who are as well-distributed as Golamati, to Gaṇḍavilā, Svāhā!
"Ānanda, whoever should provide protection and auspicious security through this six-syllable vidyā—if he should be deserving of death, he is released from punishment;

one deserving of punishment is released by a blow; one deserving of a blow is released by a verbal reprimand; one deserving of a reprimand is released by a hair-raising [spell]; and one deserving of a hair-raising [spell] is likewise released.
Ānanda, I do not see anyone in the world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, nor among the generation of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas..."

Among all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras, whoever is able to overcome one for whom this sixfold protective knowledge has been performed, for whom the protective cord has been bound upon the arm, and for whom the rite of well-being has been established— excepting only the ripening of past karma.

Then, at the end of that very night, Prakṛti Mātaṅgadārikā, having bathed her head and dressed in unwashed fine cloth, adorned with pearl garlands and ornaments, proceeded toward the city of Śrāvastī; having arrived there, she stood leaning against the base of the gate-panel at the city entrance.
They were waiting for the Venerable Ānanda, thinking, "The monk Ānanda will surely come along this path.
Then, in the forenoon, the Venerable Ānanda dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms.
Prakṛti saw the venerable Ānanda, the daughter of a Mātaṅga;
having seen him from afar, she followed the venerable Ānanda closely behind as he went, and stood still when he stood.
Whatever family he entered for alms, she would stand silently at its very door, [watching] the venerable one.
Addressing Ānanda, the Venerable Ānanda saw Prakṛti, the daughter of the Mātaṅga,
following closely behind him; and seeing her, appearing ashamed, lacking confidence, distressed, and dejected, he quickly departed from Śrāvastī.
He approached the Jeta Grove;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Lord, this Mātaṅga girl of mine follows closely behind me as I walk, and stays by my side when I stand."
"Whatever family I enter for alms, at its very door she stands in silence, crying out:
'Save me, Blessed One! Save me, Sugata!
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda."
"Do not fear, do not fear!
Then the Blessed One said this to the girl Prakṛti Mātaṅgī:
"Prakṛti Mātaṅgī, what do you have to do with the monk Ānanda?"
Prakṛti said,
"I desire the venerable master Ānanda.
The Blessed One said:
(7) "Have you been permitted by your parents, Ānanda?
"I have been permitted, Blessed One; I have been permitted, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "In that case..."
"Having obtained my permission in person," [she said].

Then the maiden Prakṛti, having given her word to the Blessed One, bowed her head at the Blessed One’s feet, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed from the Blessed One's presence for where her own mother and father were.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of his parents, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, he said this to his own mother and father:
"Mother and father, in my presence, entrust Ānanda to the ascetic Gautama."
Then the parents of Prakṛti, the Mātaṅga girl, took Prakṛti with them and approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Then Prakṛti, the Mātaṅga girl, bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, she said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, those two, her mother and father, have arrived.
Then the Blessed One spoke thus to the parents of the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti.
"May the maiden Ānandā, the daughter of the Mātaṅga, be permitted by you two to become a lay follower.
They both replied, "She is permitted, Blessed One; she is permitted, Sugata."
"Therefore, leave Prakṛti behind and go to your own home.
Then the parents of Prakṛti, the Mātaṅga girl, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Then, knowing that the parents of Prakṛti, the Mātaṅga girl, had recently departed, the Blessed One said this to Prakṛti, the Mātaṅga girl:
"Are you in need of Prakṛti, Ānanda, the monk?
Prakṛti replied, "I am in need of her, Blessed One; I am in need of her, Sugata."
"Therefore, you must maintain that manifestation of bliss which exists in the present context.
She said, "I shall maintain it, Blessed One; I shall maintain it, Sugata."
"May the Sugata let me go forth; may the Blessed One let me go forth.
Then the Blessed One said this to the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti:
"Come, bhikṣuṇī; practice the holy life.
When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti was shaven and clothed in saffron robes by the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having ordained the Mātaṅga girl Prakṛti with the address "Come, bhikṣuṇī," instructed her with a discourse on the Dharma.
He exhorted them, inspired them, and gladdened them.
This discourse, which for a long time has been disagreeable to hear for those immersed in saṃsāra,
is as follows: the discourse on giving, the discourse on ethical conduct, the discourse on heaven, and [the discourse] regarding sensual pleasures.

The Blessed One fully revealed those factors conducive to awakening— namely, the disadvantage, the escape, the danger, and affliction and purification— to the nun Prakṛti. Then, the nun Prakṛti, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with this discourse on the Dharma,
became joyful in heart, virtuous in heart, delighted in heart, free from hindrances in heart, and upright in heart.
All their minds were capable of understanding the teaching of the Dharma.

And when the Blessed One knew that the nun Prakṛti was joyful in mind, virtuous in mind, glad in mind, free from hindrances in mind, and capable and competent to understand the exalted teaching of the Dharma, then— this which...
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have a preeminent teaching of the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths—
namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—
and the Blessed One proclaimed this in detail to the nun Prakṛti.
Then the nun Prakṛti, seated on that very same seat, directly realized the four noble truths:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean, blackless woolen cloth, free from stains, when thrown into dye-water, would perfectly take on the color,
even so the nun Prakṛti, while seated on that very seat, realized the four noble truths, namely: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Now, a bhikṣuṇī who is of natural disposition—one who has ploughed through the Dharma, attained the Dharma, understood the Dharma, become unshakable in the Dharma, and reached the culmination of the Dharma; one who has realized the attainment of the goal, crossed over doubt and perplexity, become free from hesitation, attained self-confidence, is independent of others and not led by another, who practices in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction, and is a well-bred person— p.9.3 / Now, a bhikṣuṇī who is of natural disposition—one who has ploughed through the Dharma, attained the Dharma, understood the Dharma, become unshakable in the Dharma, and reached the culmination of the Dharma; one who has realized the attainment of the goal, crossed over doubt and perplexity, become free from hesitation, attained self-confidence, is independent of others and not led by another, who practices in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction, and is a well-bred person—
Having prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One regarding these matters, he said this to the Blessed One:
"I have transgressed, O Blessed One; I have transgressed, O Sugata!
Just as one who is foolish, deluded, unrefined, unskilled, and of a nature lacking wisdom, so was I when I addressed the monk Ānanda with the address 'sir'."
"Venerable sir, I see that transgression as a transgression;
having seen the transgression as a transgression, I confess it;
I reveal the transgression as a transgression."
I undertake restraint for the future.
Therefore, O Blessed One, may you recognize this transgression of mine as a transgression and accept it, out of compassion.
The Blessed One said:
"Having established yourself in restraint for the future, you acknowledge your transgression as a transgression before the community.
Ānanda, you have addressed the monk Bhikṣu Ānanda with the title 'Master,' like one who is childish, deluded, unrefined, unskilled, and of a nature lacking wisdom."
"You do not act thus.
Since you recognize your transgression in what has occurred, see the transgression, and undertake restraint for the future, I too accept your transgression as a transgression. This is growth.
In this way, you may expect no decline in your wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*).
Then the nun Prakṛti, having been gladdened and instructed by the Blessed One, dwelt alone in seclusion, diligent, ardent, mindful, clearly comprehending, and with her senses withdrawn, living apart—
just as daughters of noble family do when they shave off their hair, don saffron robes, and out of right faith depart from the home life.

They went forth into the homeless life; having realized for themselves through direct higher knowledge in this very life that which is the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, they attained it and declared: [it is finished].
"Exhausted is birth for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done; I know no further state of existence beyond this.
The Brahmins and householders of Śrāvastī heard that the Blessed One had indeed ordained the Caṇḍāla girl. Having heard this, they spoke disparagingly.
"How indeed can a Caṇḍāla girl practice the right conduct of monks?
How can she practice the right conduct of nuns, laymen, or laywomen?
How indeed can a Caṇḍāla girl enter the families of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, householders, or great landowners?"
King Prasenajit of Kosala heard that the Blessed One had ordained a Caṇḍāla girl. Upon hearing this, he spoke with contempt:
"How indeed can a Caṇḍāla girl practice the right conduct of the monks?"

He will practice the right conduct of the bhikṣuṇīs, the upāsakas, and the upāsikās. How, then, will he enter the families of brahmins, kṣatriyas, and wealthy householders? Having reflected on this, he had a fine carriage harnessed, mounted that fine carriage, and was surrounded and escorted by a great many brahmin householders of Śrāvastī.
He departed from Śrāvastī and proceeded toward the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Having traveled by carriage as far as the ground was passable for a vehicle, he alighted from the carriage; then, surrounded and preceded by a body of foot-soldiers, he entered the grove on foot.
Having entered, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Those many brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and householders from Śrāvastī also bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Some, having exchanged various friendly and pleasant greetings with the Blessed One face-to-face,
sat down to one side; others, having announced their respective names and clans— both maternal and paternal— before the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Some, having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, sat down to one side;
others sat down to one side in silence.
Then the Blessed One, concerning King Prasenajit of Kosala and those many [others]—
Having known with his own mind the thoughts of the brahmins, kṣatriyas, and householders of Śrāvastī, he addressed the monks concerning the former lives of the nun Prakṛti:
"Monks, do you wish to hear a discourse on the Dharma concerning the former lives of the nun Prakṛti, in the presence of the Tathāgata?"
The monks said to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, this is the time; Sugata, this is the occasion for the Blessed One to deliver a discourse on the Dharma concerning the former lives of the nun Prakṛti.
(12) Thus [they spoke] to the Blessed One.
"Having heard it, the monks will retain it.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, monks, listen well and attend closely; I shall speak."
"Very well, Blessed One," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this to them:

"Once upon a time, monks, in the past, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, in a region thick with groves of *atimuktaka*, plantain, *pāṭalaka*, and *āmalakī* trees, there lived a king of the Mātaṅgas named Triśaṅku."
He lived there together with many thousands of Mātaṅgas.

Furthermore, monks, that king of the Mātaṅgas, Triśaṅku, recollected the Vedas studied in his previous births, along with their auxiliary sciences (aṅga) and further branches (upāṅga), the secret doctrines (rahasya), the glossaries (nighaṇṭu) and the Kaiṭabha texts, and the distinctions between phonemes.
There were also other sciences, with the Itihāsas as the fifth.

A master of words, a grammarian, proficient in Lokāyata, sacrificial mantras, and the marks of a Great Man, free from doubt, he spoke the commentary according to the Dharma, and recited the Vedic vows and the traditional texts as they had been heard.
To that king of the Mātaṅgas, Triśaṅku, a prince named Śārdūlakarṇa was born.

Endowed with excellence in form, lineage, conduct, and virtues, and possessed of all qualities, he was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with a supreme abundance of radiant complexion.
Then Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas,
taught the prince Śārdūlakarṇa the Vedas studied in his previous birth.

Namely, the Vedas with their limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), together with the secret doctrines (*rahasya*), the glossaries (*nighaṇṭu*), the *Kaiṭabha* texts, the analysis of phonemes (*akṣara-prabheda*), the histories (*itihāsa*) as the fifth, and other treatises (*śāstra*) and commentaries (*bhāṣya*), as well as the stages of Vedic vows according to the Dharma.
Then, this thought occurred to Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas:
"This son of mine, the prince named Śārdūlakarṇa..."
He was endowed with excellence in form, lineage, moral conduct, and virtues;
possessed of all good qualities, he was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with the highest abundance of complexion.

"Having fulfilled his vows, mastered the mantras, and reached the further shore of the Vedas, this is the agreement: that I shall perform the marriage rite for him. Therefore, how might I obtain for my son Śārdūlakarṇa a wife who is virtuous, endowed with good qualities, beautiful, suitable, and capable of bearing offspring?"

At that time, a brahmin named Puṣkarasārin was enjoying the district of Droṇamukha called Utkūṭa, which had been granted by King Agnidatta as a royal gift (brahmadeya), complete with its seven excellences and provided with grass, timber, water, and grain.

Furthermore, the brahmin Puṣkarasārin was pure on both his mother’s and father’s side; he was unblemished in his wife regarding accusations concerning birth or lineage, extending back through seven generations of maternal and paternal ancestors.

At that time, there was a preceptor and teacher, a master of mantras who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas, along with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and sub-auxiliaries (*upāṅga*), their secret doctrines (*rahasya*),
their glossaries (*nighaṇṭu*) and *kaiṭabha* lexicons, and the distinctions of phonemes; he was an expounder of the five types of traditional lore (*itihāsa*) as the fifth,
a reciter of word-divisions (*padaka*), and a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*).
He had mastered the Lokāyata system, sacrifices, mantras, and the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa). He governed the prosperous district called Utkūṭa, a *droṇamukha* [administrative center].
A daughter named Prakṛti was born to the Brahmin Puṣkarasārin as a young girl.
She was endowed with beauty, noble birth, virtuous conduct, and excellent qualities;
she possessed every virtue, was handsome, lovely, and pleasing to behold, being endowed with the highest excellence of complexion; she was virtuous and possessed of good qualities.
Then, this thought occurred to Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas:
To the northeast there is a market town named Utkūṭa;
there dwells a brahmin named Puṣkarasāra,
who is well-born on both his mother’s and father’s side.

All this was explained in detail in that very Vedic scripture. And he enjoyed that highland plateau and the port-city, together with its seven outlying regions, its grass, wood, and water, along with the enjoyment of grain— all of which had been granted as a *brahmadeya* by King Agnidatta.
That Brahmin Puṣkarasārin had a daughter, a young woman named Prakṛti, who was endowed with beauty,
noble birth, and virtuous conduct; she possessed every excellence, was handsome, lovely to behold, pleasing, and was endowed with the highest abundance of complexion.
"She is virtuous and endowed with good qualities; she will be a suitable wife for my son Śārdūlakarṇa.

Having reflected and deliberated extensively upon this very matter during the night, Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, at the time of dawn when that same night had passed, mounted a chariot drawn by mares that were entirely white.
Surrounded by a great multitude of outcastes and a retinue of ministers, Triśaṅku departed from the city of the Caṇḍāla clan and proceeded northward toward Utkūṭa Droṇamukha.
Then, Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, [reached] the park named Sumanaska to the northeast of Utkūṭa.

He approached that place, which was covered with various trees, blooming with various flowers, and resounded with the warbling of various birds, like the Nandana grove of the gods. Having arrived, he stood waiting for the brahmin Puṣkarasārin, thinking,
"The brahmin Puṣkarasārin will come here to have the young students recite the mantras."
Then, at the end of that very night, the brahmin Puṣkarasārin mounted an all-white chariot drawn by mares and, surrounded by a host of disciples and preceded by about five hundred young brahmins,
set out from Utkūṭa in order to recite the brahminical mantras.
Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, beheld the brahmin Puṣkarasārin, blazing with splendor like the rising sun,
like the sacrificial fire flaming with its heat, surrounded by brahmins like a sacrifice; surrounded by hosts of gods like Śakra,
like the Himavat with its medicinal herbs, like the ocean with its jewels, like the moon with its constellations, and like Vaiśravaṇa.
Seeing him approaching from afar, resplendent like Brahmā surrounded by hosts of Yakṣas or like a celestial sage surrounded by hosts of divine seers,
he went out to meet him and, having performed the customary rites according to the Dharma, spoke as follows:
"O Puṣkarasārin, welcome! Come here; I shall tell you what must be done, so listen to it.
When this was said, the brahmin Puṣkarasārin spoke thus to Triśaṅku, the king of the Maṭaṅgas:
"Indeed, O Triśaṅku, it is not possible for one to make a wager with a Brahmin.
O Puṣkarasārin, I am able to make a wager;
whatever I am able to do, that you are certainly not able to do."
Moreover, O Puṣkarasārin, there are four undertakings of action for a person that have been previously initiated:
namely, for one's own sake, or for the sake of others, or for the sake of one's own possessions, or for the sake of gathering all living beings.
And in this matter, there is a more important task which I shall explain to you; listen to it. Give your daughter Prakṛti as a wife for my son Śārdūlakarṇa.
Whatever you consider to be the family dowry, I shall give that much.

Furthermore, having heard these words of Triśaṅku, the Mātaṅga king, the brahmin Puṣkarasārin became intensely resentful, angry, fierce, and displeased; and on that account, giving rise to wrath, malice, and hatred, he knit his brows into a three-pronged frown upon his forehead, gnashed his teeth, and rolled his eyes.
Turning his gaze away from the tawny-eyed mongoose and fixing it upon Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, he said this:
"Fie on the vulgar realm! O Caṇḍāla!"
This speech of yours, O dog-cooker, is not fitting; for you, being born of a lowly Caṇḍāla womb, desire to insult a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
O evil-minded one!
"You do not know your own nature, yet you imagine yourself to be [something else].
Do not, O fool, place a mustard seed upon the tip of a blade of grass!"
Affliction is the source [of suffering]. (p.16.4ab) Do not long for that which is not to be longed for; do not try to bind the wind with a noose.
(p.17.1ab) For gold, O fool, can never become ashes.
In light or in total darkness, is no distinction perceived?
"You are indeed born from the womb of a caṇḍāla, while I am a twice-born man.
Being inferior, O fool, how can you seek a connection with one who is superior?"
"You have been born from the womb of a caṇḍāla, while I am born of the twice-born;
for one who is superior does not wish to form a connection with one who is base."
In this world, the twice-born form alliances with those who are superior;
for those who are endowed with learning and are perfectly pure in their conduct are indeed the most excellent.
By birth they were not disparaged, and through mantras they attained the highest state;
they were teachers who held the mantras and had mastered the three Vedas.
O Brahmin, those twice-born ones who study the Vedas, including the *Nighaṇṭu* and *Kaṭhas*,
form such associations here with those very people.
For one who is superior does not desire to form a connection with one who is inferior; you seek to bind the wind, which is beyond being bound, with a noose.
"Since you desire to form a connection here with us—
who are despised by the whole world, wretched, and the lowest of men— go away quickly, you outcaste! Why do you insult us?"
Cāṇḍālas form alliances with Cāṇḍālas, and Pukkasas with Pukkasas; in this very world, caste indeed forms connections with its own kind.
Brahmins together with Brahmins, Kshatriyas with Kshatriyas, Vaishyas likewise with Vaishyas, and Shudras likewise with Shudras.
Those who are similar associate with those who are similar;
indeed, Caṇḍālas do not form alliances with Brāhmaṇas.
"You are devoid of all caste and despised by all social classes;
how can you, being so lowly, desire to form a connection with one who is most excellent?"
Having heard these words again from the brahmin Puṣkarasārin, Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, said this:
"Just as a distinction is perceived in gold when it has been reduced to ashes..."
Whether it be a Brahmin or one of another caste, there is indeed no distinction between them in that regard.
Just as a distinction is perceived between light and darkness,
so indeed there is no distinction whatsoever between one born of a Brāhmaṇa and one born of another caste.
"O Brāhmaṇa, the Jātavedas (Fire) has not arisen from the sky nor from the winds,
nor was it born by splitting the earth, as it is born from the fire-drill."
Brahmins are born from a womb, and Caṇḍālas are also born from a womb;
what cause do you see for their superiority or their status as outcasts?
Even a Brāhmaṇa who has been cast off after death is said to be loathsome and impure; so it is with others of the [other] castes as well—what then is the distinction in that regard?
Whatever evil action there may be, whether it be sin or strife,
that which leads to the injury of living beings was proclaimed by the Brahmins.
Thus have these rituals been proclaimed by the Brahmins;
yet, even through these cruel rites, the twice-born declare, "I am meritorious."
"But for Brāhmaṇas desiring to eat meat, goats and sheep,
when consecrated with mantras, go to heaven once they have been prepared."
If this path leads to one's own welfare, why is it that these brahmins do not sprinkle themselves or their kinsmen with mantras?
These twice-born ones do not sprinkle their mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, or wife with water.
Whether they be friends, kinsmen, companions, or even those who dwell in the same realm—
if they are sprinkled with the consecrated waters while reciting the mantras, they all shall go to a happy destination.
p.19.7ab. All those invoked with sacrifices shall go to the destination of the virtuous. p.19.7cd. O sir, what is the use of sacrificing animals? Why do you not sacrifice yourself?
Neither by sprinkling with water nor by mantras do goats and sheep go to heaven;
for this is not the path to heaven—this is called a false sprinkling.
This method was indeed devised by Brahmins of cruel intent;
for those desiring to eat meat, the sprinkling of the animal was contrived.
Furthermore, I shall declare what has been formulated by the Brahmins:
indeed, four kinds of sins are proclaimed among the Brahmins.
The theft of gold, the drinking of liquor, violating the teacher’s wife,
and the killing of a Brahmin— these four are the mortal sins (*pātaka*) among Brahmins.
The theft of gold must be avoided; no other theft exists [as grave as this].
That brahmin who steals gold thereby ceases to be a brahmin.
Wine must not be drunk; other drinks may be consumed as one pleases.
However, that Brahmin who drinks wine thereby ceases to be a Brahmin.
One must not approach the wife of one's guru; as for the wives of others, one may approach them as one pleases.
However, he who approaches the wife of his guru thereby ceases to be a Brahmin.
One should not kill even a single Brāhmaṇa, for by killing one, one might kill many others.
Indeed, he who would seize a Brāhmaṇa becomes, by that act, a non-Brāhmaṇa.
Thus, these four kinds of mortal sins (pātaka) have been declared regarding Brāhmaṇas;
because [those who commit them] cease to be Brāhmaṇas, others are remembered as non-mortal sins (apātaka).
Having committed even one of these four [sins], he becomes a non-Brāhmaṇa;
he does not attain the proper conduct due in the assembly of Brāhmaṇas,
nor does he deserve a seat, water, or a formal salutation.
The Brahmins have seen an escape even for one who has fallen;
indeed, by undertaking a vow, he may once again attain the status of a Brahmin.
Having worn a donkey skin for twelve years,
he raised up a skull-topped staff and took his food from the heads of the dead.
Having undertaken this vow with firm resolve and without interruption,
when the twelfth year is complete, he shall again attain the status of a Brahmin.
Thus was liberation perceived by those brahmins who practiced austerities,
yet they were deluded, treading upon a false path, and failed to see true deliverance.
Therefore, O Brahmin, I tell you this:
what is called "Brahmin," or "Kṣatriya," or "Vaiśya," or "Śūdra" is merely a designation for the world.
Knowing that all this is indeed one, give your daughter Māṇavikā as a wife to my son Śārdūlakarṇa.
"I shall bestow upon you whatever bride-price you deem appropriate.

Now, having heard these words from Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, the brahmin Puṣkarasārin became resentful, angry, fierce, and displeased; giving rise to wrath and hatred based on that cause, he knit his brows into a three-pronged frown upon his forehead.
Having rubbed his eyes, rolled back his eyelids, and produced a glance tawny like that of a mongoose, he spoke thus to Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas:
"Indeed, this recognition was made by you without due reflection;
for in this world there is but one single birth, common to all, and not of diverse kinds."
"How is it that you, born of the Śvapāka caste and originating from a low womb, desire here to assail a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas?"
"Vṛṣala, kings indeed are knowers of distinctions—

whether regarding the laws of regions, the laws of cities, the laws of villages, the laws of market towns, the laws of tolls, the laws of marriage by capture, the laws of formal marriage, or regarding prior legal actions. Vṛṣala, there are these four castes."
Namely: the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra. Regarding their laws of marriage, a Brahmin may have four wives;
namely, a Brahmin woman, a Kṣatriya woman, [a Vaiśya woman, and a Śūdra woman].
A Vaiśya woman and a Śūdra woman—
these three are the wives of a Kṣatriya:
a Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, and a Śūdra woman.
A Vaiśya has two wives:
a Vaiśya woman and a Śūdra woman.
A Śūdra has only one wife: a Śūdra woman alone.
In this way, O Vṛṣala, a Brāhmaṇa has four sons:
namely, a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra.
A Kṣatriya has three sons.
[The sons are] a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra.
Of the Vaiśya there are two sons: a Vaiśya and a Śūdra. But of the Śūdra there is only one son, namely, a Śūdra himself.
O Vṛṣala, those Brāhmaṇas are again the sons of Brahmā; they are the legitimate sons born from his mouth. From his chest were born the Kṣatriyas.
From his navel, the Vaiśyas;
from his feet, the Śūdras. O Vṛṣala, this world and all living beings were indeed created by Brahman.
"We are his eldest sons, the Kṣatriyas immediately following him; the Vaiśyas are the third caste, and the fourth is known by the name Śūdra. Thus it is said.
"O outcaste, you are not even to be seen among the fourth caste;
yet I belong to the foremost caste, the best caste, the supreme caste, the preeminent caste.
And you, O outcaste, desire a union with me for the sake of the ultimate truth—you shall quickly perish!"
"And do not despise us.
Having heard these words again from the brahmin Puṣkarasārin, Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, said this:
"O brahmin, listen here to what I say."
"This world was created by Brahmā; all beings were fashioned by him. We are his eldest sons, the Kṣatriyas, who follow immediately after him."
The Vaiśyas are the third caste, and the fourth is that which bears the name Śūdra. Thus [it is said].
Men have shanks complete with their lower parts, along with nails, flesh, and both sides of the ribs and the back;
since there is no distinction even in a single part, the four castes do not exist on this basis.
"Furthermore, if there is some distinction or superiority [among them], tell me what that is and how it is approved by you.
Or, if indeed no such superior distinction exists, then these four castes do not exist apart from this [human race]."
Just as children playing on a great highway,
having gathered heaps of dust, create for themselves names for them.
"This is milk, this is curd;
this is meat, this is ghee.
Yet, merely because of a child's words, dust does not become food.
The four castes are exactly as you describe them, O Brāhmaṇa;
this so-called "heap of dust" has no connection whatsoever with them.
Not by the hair, not by the two ears, not by the head, not by the eyes;
not by the mouth, not by the nose, not by the neck, nor by the arm.
Nor with his flanks, nor with his back or belly;
nor with his thighs, nor with his shanks, nor with the nails of his hands and feet.
Neither by voice, nor by complexion, nor by all physical traits, nor by sexual characteristics,
do any distinctions exist among all human beings.
"Just as in other classes of beings the gender and the womb are each distinct,
what do you consider to be the common cause there among those classes?"
Furthermore, [if one were to claim that the four castes are distinct], then men would possess heads, be joined with human bones, have skin, and possess sense organs and internal cavities;
since there is no distinction in these respects, it is not logical to designate four castes.

24.9ab. Now, if there exists some preeminent distinction, then state it, and how it is approved by you. 24.9cd. Or, if no such preeminent distinction exists here, then the four castes are not logically fit to be designated.
Indeed, this fault would exist here which you have stated regarding the diagnosis;
but having heard it from me, O gentle one, and having understood it, listen as I explain what I consider to be the correct response.
"O father, being appointed to this task, I shall declare to you whatever is appropriate here—

whether it be difficult or easy— and indeed, whatever fault may arise from what is improper, I shall explain to you further and further. Having heard from me, O gentle one, and having understood that human beings arise through the power of their own actions, proceed accordingly."
Furthermore, O Brahmin, if inference is also a valid means of knowledge for you,
then as for what you say— that Brahmā is one— it follows that all creatures must also be of a single birth;
we too are of a single birth.
And as for what you say, that this world and all beings were created by Brahmā— if this, O Brāhmaṇa, is your authority,
then it is inconsistent with that, O Brāhmaṇa, that you say there are four castes: Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
"Moreover, O Brahmin, my words would be false if, through a comparison with humans, a distinction were perceived in the human species—
whether by way of the head, the face, the ears, the nose, the eyebrows,
the form, the configuration, the color, the shape, the birth, the food, or the appearance."

"Furthermore, O Puṣkarasārin, just as various distinctions are recognized among cows, donkeys, camels, deer, birds, goats, and sheep— whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by spontaneous generation; that is to say,
distinctions are recognized by their feet, by their mouths, by their color, by their shape, by their food, and by their mode of birth— yet no such distinction is recognized among these four castes."

Therefore, all this is one. Furthermore, O Brahmin, a distinction is perceived among these various fruit-bearing trees, such as the āmrātaka, jambu, kharjūra, panasa, dāla, vanata, tinduka, mṛdvīkā, bījapūraka, kapittha, akṣoḍa, nārikela, tiniśa, karañja, and so forth.
That is to say, a distinction is perceived in terms of roots, trunks, bark, heartwood, leaves, flowers, and fruits;
yet no such distinction is perceived among the four castes.

For example, [there is a distinction] among these land-growing trees, such as the *sāra*, *tamāla*, *naktamāla*, *karṇikāra*, *saptaparṇa*, *śirīṣa*, *kovidāra*, *syandana*, *candana*, *śiṃśapā*, *eraṇḍa*, *khadira*, and so forth.
A distinction is perceived;
that is to say, a difference is observed in terms of the root, the trunk, the bark, the shoots, the heartwood, the leaves, the flowers, and the fruit.
Yet, no such distinction is perceived among the four castes.
"Thus it is, O Puṣkarasārin: among these milk-exuding trees—such as the udumbara, plakṣa, aśvattha, nyagrodha, valguka, and so forth—a distinction is perceived;
that is to say, a distinction is perceived in their roots, trunks, bark, heartwood, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Yet, no such distinction is perceived among the four castes."
For example, Puṣkarasārin, even among these medicinal fruit trees such as the *āmalakī*, *harītakī*, *vibhītakī*, and *pharasaka*,
as well as various other medicinal plants— whether growing in villages or on mountains, whether grasses or forest trees— their distinct characteristics are known.
That is to say, a distinction is perceived in terms of roots, trunks, branches, pith, leaves, flowers, and fruits;
but such is not the case for the four castes.
A distinction is perceived.
For example, among land-growing flowering trees—such as the *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *pāṭala*, *sumanā*, *vārṣikā*, *dhanaṣkārikā*, and so forth—a distinction is perceived;
that is to say, a distinction is perceived by way of form, color, fragrance, and shape.
However, no distinction whatsoever is perceived among the four castes.
It is just as, for example, a distinction is perceived among various water-born flowers—such as the lotus, the blue lotus, the fragrant lily, the soft-scented lily, and so forth;
that is to say, a distinction is perceived by way of their form, their scent, their shape, and their color.
Indeed, no distinction between castes is perceived; for example, Puṣkarasārin, [one does not perceive] "these are Brāhmaṇas," "these are Kṣatriyas," "these are Vaiśyas," or "these are Śūdras.
Therefore, all this is indeed one.
I shall also tell you another [view] as it has been devised by the Brahmins:
the sky together with the stars is the head, and the atmosphere is the belly.
The two thighs are the mountains, the feet are the surface of the earth,
the sun and moon are the eyes, and the grasses and forest trees are the body hair.
Brahmā Prajāpati declared that tears are the rain of this [world], and urine is the rivers; even the oceans are indeed impure. Thus spoke Brahmā Prajāpati.
Examine for yourself the specific characteristic of Brahman.

Since the Brāhmaṇas were born from Brahman, therefore the Kṣatriyas, the Vaiśyas, and the Śūdras were also born. If such an origin were indeed real, then there would certainly be a distinction based on caste.

If the Brāhmaṇas were to go to the world of Brahmā while the other three castes did not go to heaven, then there would be a distinction based on caste; but if that were not so, then there would not be four castes.
Since it is the fourth caste alone that thus ascends to heaven by its own performed action,
and since austerity and the way of the seers (ārṣa) are praised here [only for them], therefore there can be no distinction [of status] for one who is not twice-born.
If there were only one Brāhmaṇa here who possessed two tongues and likewise four ears,
four tusks, many feet, and two heads— only then would there be a distinction based on caste.
Passion, the slaying of others, and likewise various forms of harassment,
as well as the destruction of a being's merit— these are the unwholesome deeds committed by the Brahmins.

War, dispute, and constant strife, as well as the ritual sprinkling of cattle contemplated by the Brahmins, and the act of terrifying through Atharvan rites— these are the rituals performed by the learned priests with mantras.
Evil desire, the deceiving of many people, as well as guile and deceit— having thus reflected upon the harm done to others, when will they ever depart from here to heaven?
Those Brahmins who possess fierce asceticism, who are disciplined and always endowed with vows and virtuous conduct,
who are non-violent and delight in self-restraint and control— those Brahmins go to the city of Brahmā.
Possessing bones, flesh, nails, and skin, [the body] consists of nothing but suffering, pleasure, urine, and excrement.
Since there is no distinction made by the five sense faculties, this fourfold system of castes does not exist at all.
It is just as if, O Brahmin, a certain man had four sons, and he were to give them names such as Nandaka, or Jīvaka, or Aśoka, or Śatāyus; furthermore,
these sons of that man were beloved by him.
In that regard, he who is Nandaka should rejoice; he who is Jīvaka should live;
he who is Aśoka should not grieve.
He who has a lifespan of a hundred years shall live for a hundred years.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, their distinction is known by name, not by birth.
For what reason?
Furthermore, O Brahmin, here indeed a son is born from the father;
therefore, regarding this, there is this traditional explanation:
"The mother is a leather bag; the son belongs to the father, for he is the very same as the one by whom he was begotten."
"If you understand it thus, O sir, then your sons have never been anyone else's."
"Examine this thoroughly, O Brahmin: who here is a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra?
All are one-eyed and hunchbacked, or even all are afflicted with epilepsy;
some have leprosy and others skin-disease, and they are individually fair or dark."

“O Brahmin, since these beings are established with equal marrow, nails, skin, flanks, bellies, and faces by virtue of their own karma, when this is the case, there can be no distinction at all. What distinction, then, could be produced by birth?”
"Because there is no distinguishing characteristic of birth, therefore there is indeed no such thing as the fourfold caste system.
Therefore, O Brāhmaṇa, I tell you: this which is called a 'Brāhmaṇa,' or a 'Kṣatriya,' or a 'Vaiśya,' or a 'Śūdra,' or a 'Caṇḍāla'—this is merely a designation of the world.
All this is one; this is one."
"Give your daughter Prakṛti to my son Śārdūlakarṇa as his wife; I shall give you whatever family dowry you deem appropriate.
Having heard these words of Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, the brahmin Puṣkarasārin said this to him:
"Have you, moreover, studied the Ṛgveda?"
The Yajurveda has been studied;
the Sāmaveda has been studied;
the Atharvaveda has been studied.
You have studied Āyurveda, as well as the section on ritual procedures (kalpādhyāya).
You have also studied metaphysics (adhyātma), whether it be the cycle of animals, the host of constellations, or the sequence of lunar dates.
Or perhaps you have mastered the wheel of karma.
Or have you studied the science of limbs, or the science of garments, or the science of jackals, or the science of omens?
Or have you studied the movements of Rāhu, or the movements of Venus, or the movements of the planets?
"Or perhaps you have studied the Lokāyata, the exposition of the Bhāṣya, the Pakṣādhyāya, or the Nyāya?
When this was said, Triśaṅku, the king of the Mātaṅgas, spoke thus to the brahmin Puṣkarasārin:
"O brahmin, all this has been studied by me, and even more besides."
Furthermore, O Brahmin, if you should think, "I have reached the further shore of the mantras," then,
O Brahmin, I shall state an inference in accordance with the Dharma regarding that matter:
indeed, O Brahmin, this did not occur to the beings of the first eon.
Namely, whether as a brahmin, or a kshatriya, or a vaishya, or a shudra—
this entire world is one; this whole is one.
p.32.2. Then, O Brāhmaṇa, among beings who were dissimilar and yet similar in both respects, other beings began to tend, protect, and sow fields of *śāli* rice; they were designated as "Kṣatriyas.
Then, O Brāhmaṇa, it occurred to certain other beings there:
“Possession is a disease; possession is an abscess; possession is a thorn.

What if we were to abandon our own possessions, go to a forest retreat, gather grass, wood, branches, leaves, and foliage, and having constructed either a grass hut or a leaf hut, enter it and practice meditation?”

Then those beings, having abandoned their own possessions and gone to a forest retreat, constructed either grass huts or leaf huts from grass, wood, branches, leaves, foliage, and twigs; entering right there, they practiced meditation.
For the sake of a seat in the evening and for the sake of a morning meal, they would enter the outskirts of the groves and the village for alms.
Then, this thought occurred to those beings living in the village:

"Alas, these beings are indeed performers of difficult deeds who, having abandoned their own possessions, have gone out from the villages, towns, and settlements; they are called 'Brahmins' because their minds are directed toward the outside.
Furthermore, those beings living in the village paid them the highest honor.
And they thought that these [teachings] should be given to them.
Then, among those very beings, certain beings, unable to realize those meditative absorptions (dhyāna), descended into the villages and recited the words of mantras.
The village-dwellers said to them: "These beings are not merely reciters; they are teachers."
The designation "their teachers" arose in the world.
This was the cause, this was the condition for the appearance of the brahmins in the world.
Then, at a time of seclusion, certain beings engaged in various types of activities associated with worldly gain.
The designation "vaiśya" arose for them. Then, among other beings, those who made their living by means of lowly work were designated as "śūdra."
Long ago, O Brahmin, a certain being, having taken his bride, mounted a chariot and went to a certain forest region.
There the chariot broke down;
from that circumstance, the designation "mātaṅga" (do not go) arose.
The designation "plowmen" (karṣaka) arose for those who cultivate the field;
and because he delighted the assembly with his discourse on the Dharma through the correct practice of moral conduct and vows,
the designation "king" (rājan) came to be for him.
Then other beings made their living by means of trade; for them, the designation "merchants" (*vaṇija*) arose.
Furthermore, other beings went forth into the religious life (*pravrajanti*).
Having gone forth, they conquered others and conquered the afflictions (*kleśa*); thus, the designation "those who have gone forth" (*pravrajita*) arose in the world for them.
"Moreover, Brahmin, there arose in the world a single designation;
I shall declare it to you.
In this world, Brahmā causes these Vedas to be recited."
Brahmā, the supreme ascetic among the gods,
used to teach the Vedas to Indra Kauśika;
Indra Kauśika, in turn, taught the Vedas to Araṇemi Gautama.
Araṇemi Gautama had Śvetaketu recite the Vedas;
Śvetaketu had the learned Śuka recite the Vedas;
and the learned Śuka used to analyze the Vedas.
For example: the Puṣya [sacrifice] belongs to the Bahvṛcas; the Paṅkti to the Chanters (Chandogas); the twenty-one-fold [stoma] to the Adhvaryus;
and the Kratu to the Arthavaṇikas.
These are the Brāhmaṇas of the Bahvṛcas.
All of these are explained:
Puṣya, being one, became divided into twenty-five parts,
namely, the Śuklas, the Valkalas, and the Māṇḍavyas.
Among them, there are ten Śuklas,
eight Valkalas,
and seven Māṇḍavyas.
Thus, O Brahmin, this is the branch of the Bahvṛcas;
having been one, Puṣya became divided into twenty-five parts.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, inference is also a means of valid cognition for the Chandogas.
All these Brāhmaṇas are Chāndogas.
This *paṅkti* [lineage], having become one, is divided into eighty-one thousand branches.
They are as follows: the Śīlavalkas, Araṇemikas, Laukākṣas, Kauthumas, Brahma-samas, Mahā-samas, Mahā-yāgikas, Satyam-ugras, and Samanta-vedas.
Therein, there are twenty Śīlavalkā [dice], twenty Araṇemikā [dice],
and forty Laukākṣa [dice].
There were one hundred Kauthumas,
one hundred Brahmāsamānas,
and five hundred Mahāsamānas.
A hundred Mahāyāgikas,
a hundred Ugras who speak the truth,
and a hundred Samantavedas.
Thus, O Brahmin, this is the branch of the Chāndogas;
what was originally a single *paṅkti* has become divided into eighty thousand branches.
Furthermore, inference (*anumāna*) is also a means of valid cognition for the Adhvaryus.
These Brahmins, having been twenty-one Adhvaryus, became divided into one hundred and one branches, as follows:
the Kaṭhas, the Kāṇvas, the Vājasaneyins, the Jātukarṇas, the Proṣṭhapadas, and the Ṛṣis.
Among them, there are ten Kaṭhas, ten Kāṇvas, and eleven Vājasaneyins.
There are thirteen Jātukarṇas,
sixteen Proṣṭhapadas,
and forty-one Ṛṣis.
Thus, this is the branch of the Brāhmaṇa-Adhvaryus;
having originally been twenty-one Adhvaryus, they became divided into one hundred and one schools.
"O Brahmin, inference (*anumāna*) is also a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the followers of the Atharvaveda.
All these mantras belong to the Atharvavedins.
The single *kratu* became divided into two."
Having become two-fold, it split into four;
having become four-fold, it split into eight;
having become eight-fold, it split into nine and ten.
Thus, this is the branch of the Brāhmaṇas who follow the Atharvaveda.
The single *kratu* is divided into one hundred and sixteen parts.

Furthermore, O Brāhmaṇa, inference (*anumāna*) is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), based upon which these twelve hundred and sixteen divisions were correctly perceived by the ancient Brāhmaṇas.
Whether in Vedic literature, in grammar, in Lokāyata, or in the investigation of words (*padamīmāṃsā*), no reasoning or refutation is discernible among them;
that is to say, having understood that they are merely of a single kind, one ought to be their kinsman.
Therefore, O Brahmin, I tell you this: that which is called "Brahmin," or "Kshatriya," or "Vaishya," or "Shudra" is merely a designation for the world.
This entire universe is one; this [all] is one.
"Give your daughter Prakṛti to my son Śārdūlakarṇa as a wife; I shall bestow upon you whatever family dowry you deem appropriate.

The Rohiṇī constellation consists of five stars, is shaped like a cart, has a conjunction lasting forty-five muhūrtas, has Prajāpati as its deity, and belongs to the Bhāradvāja lineage; its food is the flesh of deer. The Mṛgaśiras constellation consists of three stars, is shaped like a deer's head, has a conjunction lasting thirty muhūrtas, has Soma as its deity, and belongs to the Mṛgāyaṇīya lineage; its food is fruits and roots.

The Ārdrā constellation has one star, is shaped like a sectarian mark (tilaka), has a conjunction lasting fifteen muhūrtas, has clarified butter as its food, has the Sun as its deity, and belongs to the Hārītītāyanīya lineage by gotra. The Punarvasu constellation has two stars, is shaped like a footstep, has a conjunction lasting forty-five muhūrtas, has boiled rice as its food, has Aditi as its deity, and belongs to the Vāsiṣṭha lineage by gotra.

The Puṣya constellation has three stars, a shape like a *vardhamāna*, a conjunction lasting thirty *muhūrtas*, honey-scented food as its sustenance, Bṛhaspati as its presiding deity, and the Aupamanyava lineage as its clan. The Aśleṣā constellation has one star, a shape like a sectarian mark (*tilaka*), a conjunction lasting fifteen *muhūrtas*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as its food, the serpent (*sarpa*) as its presiding deity, and the Maitrāyaṇīya lineage as its clan.
Thus, O Puṣkarasārin, these are the seven constellations that have the eastern gate.

The constellation Maghā has five stars, is shaped like a river-crook, has a conjunction lasting thirty muhūrtas, has sesame and kṛsara as its food, has the ancestors as its deity, and belongs to the Piṅgalāyanīya lineage by clan.
The constellation Pūrvaphalgunī has two stars, is shaped like a footstep, has a conjunction with thirty muhūrtas, has the bilva fruit as its food, Bhava as its deity, and Gautama as its lineage.
The constellation Uttaraphalgunī has two stars,
is shaped like a footstep, has a conjunction with forty-five muhūrtas, has wheat and fish as its food, Aryaman as its deity, and Kauśika as its lineage.
The constellation Hasta has five stars, is shaped like a hand, is conjoined with thirty muhūrtas, has śyāmāka grain as its food, Sūrya as its deity, and the Kāśyapa as its lineage.

The constellation Citrā has one star, is shaped like a sectarian mark (tilaka), is conjoined with thirty muhūrtas, has an offering of mung-bean porridge, ghee-cakes, and clarified butter as its food, Tvaṣṭṛ as its deity, and the Kātyāyanīya as its lineage.

The constellation Svātī has one star, is shaped like a sectarian mark, is conjoined with fifteen muhūrtas, has an offering of mung-bean porridge and fruit as its food, Vāyu as its deity, and the Kātyāyanīya as its lineage.

The constellation Viśākhā has two stars, is shaped like a pair of horns, has a conjunction lasting forty-five muhūrtas, has sesame flowers as its food, has Indra and Agni as its deities, and belongs to the Śāṅkhāyanīya lineage by clan.
Thus, O Puṣkarasārin, these are the seven constellations whose gates face south.

The constellation Anurādhā has four stars, is shaped like a row of jewels, has a conjunction lasting thirty muhūrtas, has liquor and meat as its food, has Mitra as its deity, and belongs to the Ālaṃbāyanīya lineage by clan.

The constellation Jyeṣṭhā consists of three stars, has the shape of a barley grain in the middle, is conjoined with fifteen muhūrtas, its food is rice and barley gruel, its presiding deity is Indra, and its lineage is Kātyāyanīya of the long [tradition]. The constellation Mūla consists of seven stars, has the shape of a scorpion, is conjoined with thirty muhūrtas, its food is roots and fruits, its presiding deity is Nairṛti, and its lineage is Kātyāyanīya.

The constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā consists of four stars, has the shape of a cow’s stride, is conjoined with thirty muhūrtas, has the Nyagrodha tree as its food, and has the waters as its deity; it belongs to the Darbha lineage and the Kātyāyanīya gotra. The constellation Uttarāṣāḍhā consists of four stars, has the shape of an elephant’s stride, is conjoined with forty-five muhūrtas, has honey and parched grain as its food, and has Viśva as its deity; it belongs to the Maudgalāyanīya gotra. The constellation Abhijit consists of three stars, has the shape of a cow’s head, and is conjoined with six muhūrtas.

The deity of [this asterism] is Ahirbudhnya; its lineage is Jātūkarṇya.

The nakṣatra Uttarabhādrapadā has two stars, a rectangular configuration, a conjunction lasting forty-five muhūrtas, meat as its food, and Aryaman as its deity; its school is the Dhyāna-Drāhyāyaṇīya, and its lineage is [the same].

The Aśvinī asterism has two stars, is shaped like the head of a horse, has a conjunction lasting thirty muhūrtas, its food is honey and milk-rice (pāyasa), its presiding deity is the Gandharvas, and it belongs to the Maitrāyaṇīya lineage by gotra.

The *bharaṇī* constellation consists of three stars, has the shape of the vulva (*bhaga*), is conjoined with thirty *muhūrtas*, has sesame and rice as its food, has Yama as its deity, and belongs to the Bhārgava lineage by clan.

By this sequential connection, one night and day (*rātridivasa*) is inferred as consisting of thirty *muhūrtas*.

When the sun rises with a shadow of ninety-six *pauruṣas*, the muhūrta named Caturoja occurs;

when the shadow is five *pauruṣas* long, there is the muhūrta named Atisamṛddha;
and when the shadow is four *pauruṣas* long, there is the muhūrta named Udgata.
When the shadow measures three puruṣas, there is the muhūrta named Sumukha;
when midday has arrived, there is the muhūrta named Vajraka;
and when midday has passed and the shadow measures three puruṣas, there is the muhūrta named Rohita.
When the shadow is four *pauruṣas* long, the *muhūrta* is named Bala; when the shadow is five *pauruṣas* long, the *muhūrta* is named Vijaya;
when the shadow is six *pauruṣas* long, the *muhūrta* is named Sarvarasa.
When the shadow is twelve *puruṣas* long, the muhūrta is named Vasu;
when the shadow is sixty *puruṣas* long, the muhūrta is named Sundara;
and as the sun descends, when the shadow is ninety-six *puruṣas* long, the muhūrta is named Parabhaya.
p.55.3/.Thus are these the muhūrtas of the day.
p.55.4/.Now then, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the muhūrtas of the night:
when the sun has set, there is the muhūrta named Raudra.
Then there is the muhūrta named Tārāvacara,
the muhūrta named Saṃyama,
and the muhūrta named Sāṃpraiyaka. (56)
The moment named Ananta;
the moment named Gardabha;
the moment named Rākṣasa.
When midnight has arrived, there is the muhūrta named Avayava;
when midnight has passed, there is the muhūrta named Brahmā; the muhūrta named Diti; and the muhūrta named Ātapāgni.
The moment named Abhijit—
these are the names of the moments of the night. Thus,
O Puṣkarasārin, these are the thirty moments by which the day and night are known.
A *kṣaṇa*, a *kṣaṇa*, a *lava*, and a *muhūrta*:
therein, a *lava* is the thirtieth part of a *muhūrta*;
a *kṣaṇa* is the sixtieth part of a *lava*.
One hundred and twenty parts of a moment (kṣaṇa) constitute a tatkṣaṇa.
For example, it is like the pull of a thread by a woman spinning who is neither too tall nor too short;
such is the length of a tatkṣaṇa.
One hundred and twenty moments constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*;
sixty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*;
thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta*.
By this sequential calculation, thirty muhūrtas constitute one day and night;
thirty days and nights constitute one month.
Twelve months constitute a year:
Caturojas, Śveta, Samṛddha, Śarapatha, Atisamṛddha, Udgata, Sumukha, Vajraka, Rohita, Bala, Vijaya, Sarvarasa, Vasu, Sundara, and Parabhaya. (57)

Raudra, Tārāvacara, Saṃyama, Sāṃpraiyaka, Ananta, Gardabha, Rākṣasa, Avayava, Brahmā, Diti, Arka, Vidhamana, Āgneya, Ātapāgni, and Abhijit—these are the names of the muhūrtas. [This concludes] the origin of time (kālotpatti). 57.1–2.
O Brahmin, I shall also tell you of the arising of time; listen. As for what the measure of time is, that is now being stated: two winks of the eye constitute one *lava*.
Eight *lava*s make one *kāṣṭhā*;
sixteen *kāṣṭhā*s make one *kalā*;
thirty *kalā*s make one *nāḍikā*.
In that context, two *nāḍikās* constitute one *muhūrta*. Furthermore, what is the measure of a *nāḍikā*? That is stated:
it is one *droṇa* of water.
From holding that [water], it amounts to two hundred palas.
What is the measurement of the hole in the nālikā?
It is the size of a suvarṇa.
Above [the opening], a golden rod four finger-breadths long should be made;
it should be circular and round, square at both ends, and elongated.
When that water in the jar has thus leaked away, that constitutes one *nāḍikā*.
By this measure of the *nālikā*, two *nāḍikās* divided [in this way] constitute one *muhūrta*. By this, O Brahmin, thirty *muhūrtas* [constitute] those by which nights and days are inferred.
Then, sixteen *nimeṣas* constitute one *kāṣṭhā*;
sixteen *kāṣṭhās* constitute one *kalā*;
sixty *kalās* constitute one *muhūrta*.
Thirty muhūrtas constitute one day and night;
thirty days and nights constitute one month;
twelve months constitute one year.
Listen, O Brahmin, to the origin of the krośa and the yojana:
seven atoms (paramāṇu) constitute one minute particle (aṇu);
seven such particles constitute that which is perceived as the most subtle of all visible things.
Seven of those window-dust particles make one rabbit-hair dust particle. Seven rabbit-hair dust particles make one [particle of] hare-hair dust.
Seven rabbit-hairs make one sheep’s hair;
seven sheep’s hairs make one cow’s hair;
and seven cow’s hairs make one louse.
Seven *yūkās* make one *likṣā*;
seven *likṣās* make one *yava*;
seven *yavas* make one *aṅguli*.
Twelve finger-breadths make one span;
two spans make one cubit;
four cubits make one bow-length.
One thousand bows make one *krośa*;
four *krośas* make one *māgadha-yojana*.
This is the measurement of a *yojana* when calculated as a total mass.
Five hundred and twenty-four thousand, twenty-nine million, and twelve hundred thousand atoms—
thus is a *yojana* measured.
Listen, O Brahmin, to the derivation of the measurement of gold.
Therefore, may your honor explain it:
twelve barley grains make one *māṣaka*;
sixteen *māṣakas* make one *karṣa*.
"The measure of gold,
when aggregated, is two crores, twenty-five thousand, five hundred, and eight atoms.
Thus, O Brahmin, is the origin of the measurement of gold established."
Listen, O Brahmin, to the measure of a *pala*:
sixty-four *māṣakas* constitute a *pala* according to the Magadhan standard;
this is the total measure of a *pala* according to the Magadhan scale.
"Eighty-eight million, four hundred and seventy-seven thousand, two hundred and eighty atoms— O Brahmin, such is the measured quantity of a *pala*.
Listen now, O Brahmin, to the origin of the measurement of liquids."
Twenty-four palas make a Māgadha-prastha;
that is the measure for liquids.
The total measure of *prastha*s, when weighed by the Magadhan scale,
amounts to two hundred and three *koṭis*, twenty-nine hundred thousand, seventy-four thousand, seven hundred and twenty atoms (*paramāṇu*s).
Thus, O Brahmin, has the origin of the measure of liquids been explained.
Now listen, O Brahmin, to the origin of the measure of grain:
twenty-nine palas minus one karṣa constitute a Magadhan prastha.
The measurement of grain was determined;
the quantity of a *prastha* was calculated using the Magadhan scale as follows:
one hundred and fifty-eight crores, eighty-two lakhs, sixty-one thousand, five hundred and thirty atoms (*paramāṇu*).
"Thus, O Brahmin, has the measure of grain been measured.
"Recite, O Triśaṅku, the chapter named 'The Exposition of the Constellations' (Nakṣatravyākaraṇa)."
"Now then, O Brahmin, I shall explain the chapter called 'The Exposition of the Constellations.
Listen to that;
may your honor speak."
A man born under Kṛttikā becomes illustrious;
one born under Rohiṇī becomes fortunate and possessed of enjoyments;
one born under Mṛgaśiras becomes a seeker of battle.
One born under Ārdrā becomes a source of food and drink;
one born under Punarvasu becomes a farmer and a cattle-herder;
one born under Puṣya becomes virtuous.
One born under Āśleṣā becomes lustful;
one born under Maghā is wise and possesses a great soul.
One born under Pūrvaphalgunī has a short lifespan;
one born under Uttaraphalgunī is inclined toward fasting and is destined for heaven.
One born under Hastā becomes a thief;
one born under Citrā becomes skilled in dance and song,
and is knowledgeable in the methods of fashioning ornaments.
One born under Svāti becomes an astrologer or a high-ranking official of the royal court;
one born under Viśākhā becomes a royal soldier.
One born under Anurādhā becomes a merchant or a caravan leader.
One born under Jyeṣṭhā has a short lifespan and possesses little wealth. One born under Mūla—
One becomes possessed of sons and renowned.
One born under Pūrvāṣāḍhā becomes a practitioner of yoga (yogācāra). One born under Uttarāṣāḍhā becomes a lord of food and of noble birth.
A person born under Abhijit becomes renowned;
one born under Śravaṇa is honored by kings.
One born under Dhaniṣṭhā becomes wealthy;
one born under Śatabhiṣā becomes a root-herbalist;
and one born under Pūrvabhādrapadā becomes a commander of thieves.
One born under Uttarabhādrapadā becomes a perfumer and a *gandharva*;
one born under Revatī becomes a mariner.
One born under Aśvinī becomes a horse-dealer;
one born under Bharaṇī becomes an executioner.
This, O Puṣkarasārin, is called the Exposition of the Lunar Mansions (nakṣatra-vyākaraṇa).

62.1. Recite, O Triśaṅku, the chapter named "Instruction on the Lunar Mansions.
Now, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter named "Instruction on the Lunar Mansions"; let it be heard.
"May your lordship speak:
A city situated under the Kṛttikās indeed blazes with splendor;
one should designate that city as radiant with abundant jewels."
One should designate that city as being situated in Rohiṇī;
there the people shall be righteous and possess abundant stores of wealth,
and they shall be endowed with the nature of learning and devoted to their own wives.
When [the moon] is situated in Mṛgaśīrṣa, the city is crowded with women, cattle, and wealth,
as well as garlands and enjoyments, and is graced by wonders.
Under Ārdrā, there will be fish and meats, as well as various kinds of food and wealth;
however, the men in the city will be cruel and of a foolish disposition.
When the moon is situated in Punarvasu, the city shines with prosperity;
having become abundant in wealth and grain, it may even perish.
When the illustrious Puṣya is established, the wicked subjects become placid;
they are endowed with prosperity, most righteous, and likewise long-lived.
They will be radiant, long-lived, and endowed with wealth, grain, and flavors;
likewise, the lord of the forest (the tree) will quickly flourish there again and again.
When [the moon] is situated in Aśleṣā, the lowest of men dwell there— unfortunate, fond of quarreling, ill-behaved, and partakers of suffering.
When the moon is situated in Maghā, mortals are born who are learned, possess great wealth,
delight in their own wives, and are endowed with excellent prowess.
When Phalgunī is situated over the city, women will obtain auspicious garlands, food, clothing, and fragrant, blessed items.
When the moon is situated in Uttaraphalgunī, there will be abundance of grain and wealth;
however, foolish people will be overcome by women within the city.
When [the moon] is situated in Hastā, those possessed of knowledge and great wealth will exist,
and there shall be mutual affection for beds within the city.
When the moon is situated in Citrā, all men are overcome by women;
one should predict that the city will be prosperous, beautiful, and radiant.
When the asterism Svāti is situated in the city, there will be abundant accumulations of wealth;
however, those who are greedy, cruel, and foolish shall be numerous in the city.
A city established under Viśākhā blazes with splendor;
one should predict that it will be crowded with people devoted to sacrifice and will end in weapons.
When the moon is situated in Anurādhā, people are virtuous in character and have conquered their senses;
they are devoted to their own wives, meritorious, and dedicated to the practice of recitation and fire-offerings.
But when [the moon] is situated in Jyeṣṭhā, the city is filled with beings endowed with many jewels and wealth who are knowers of the Vedas, and it increases perpetually.
A city established at the root [of the asterism] is endowed with grain and wealth,
yet it perishes through being crowded with people of immoral character and by means of dust.
A city situated under Pūrvāṣāḍhā shall possess wealth and grain;
however, the lowest of men—greedy, cruel, and foolish—dwell there.
When [the moon] is situated in Uttarā, there is an accumulation of wealth and grain; moreover, the people are endowed with learning and natural excellence, yet they are fond of quarreling.
When the city was settled under the asterism Abhijit, all the people there rejoiced;
they were always delighted and possessed mutual affection for one another.
When [the moon] is situated in Śravaṇā, one should predict that the city will be endowed with grain and wealth, and filled with a great many people free from disease.
When [the moon] is situated in Dhaniṣṭhā, one should predict that the city will be conquered by women;
it will abound in garments and garlands, yet be devoid of sensual enjoyments.
When the moon is joined with Śatabhiṣaj at dawn, women who are fond of fools and deceit,
who are addicted to women and drinking, perish by water.
When the Pūrvaproṣṭhapadā constellation presides, the people there are fond of pleasure;
they are harmful to others, foolish, and devoid of pride and desire.
When the moon is situated in Uttarā, there is constant and unsurpassed prosperity;
one should declare that [the person] will be filled with wealth and grain and enriched with jewels.
When the moon is situated in Raivata (Revatī), the populace will be handsome;
there will be abundance of donkeys, camels, and cattle, as well as great wealth and grain.
One should declare that a city established under Aśvinī will be auspicious,
filled with people free from disease, and crowded with handsome folk.
When [the moon] is situated in Bharaṇī, the lowest of men dwell there— unfortunate, fond of quarreling,
ill-behaved, and partakers of suffering.
Having carefully observed the conjunctions of the lunar mansions, the wise man should establish cities, kingdoms, and likewise houses;
for this was obtained by me in a previous birth as something desired and praiseworthy.
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter called 'The Exposition of the Lunar Mansions' (*nakṣatra-nirdeśa*).
[This is] the exposition of the positions of the lunar mansions.
Now then, O Puṣkarasārin, regarding the twenty-eight [mansions]..."
I shall proclaim the chapter entitled "The Description of the Positions of the Constellations.
Let this be heard!
"May the Blessed One speak! [he requested].
"O Puṣkarasārin, the lunar mansion Kṛttikā belongs to the Kaliṅgas and Magadhas;
Rohiṇī belongs to all subjects;
and Mṛgaśiras belongs to the Videhas and those who serve kings."
Likewise, Ārdrā belongs to the Kṣatriyas and the Brāhmaṇas;
Punarvasu to the Sauparṇas;
and the Puṣya constellation to all those clad in pure white garments.
And Aśleṣā is for those who serve kings and for the Nāgas of the Himalayas;
Maghā is for the Gauḍikas.
Pūrvaphalgunī belongs to the thieves;
Uttaraphalgunī to the people of Avanti; and Hastā to the inhabitants of Saurāṣṭra.
Citrā is for birds;
Svātī is for all who have entered the religious life;
Viśākhā is for aquatic creatures.
Anurādhā is for merchants and carters;
Jyeṣṭhā is for gatekeepers;
Mūlā is for travelers.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā belongs to the Vāhlīkas; Uttarāṣāḍhā to the Kāmbojas;
and Abhijit to all those of the southern region and the Tāmraparṇikas.
Śravaṇā belongs to the singers and thieves;
Dhaniṣṭhā belongs to the Kurus and Pañcālas;
Śatabhiṣā belongs to the Mūlikas and the merchants.
Pūrvabhādrapadā belongs to the perfumers and to the Yavanas and Kambojas;
Uttarabhādrapadā belongs to the Gandharvas;
and Revatī belongs to the mariners.
Aśvinī is for horse-dealers and for the Bhadrapadakarmans and the Bhadrakāyakas. O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter titled "The Exposition on the Designation of the Positions of the Lunar Mansions."
"O Triśaṅku, recite the chapter named 'Ṛtuvarṣa.
I shall speak it; let it be heard."
"May the Blessed One speak:
if the god rains here during the last month of summer under the asterism Kṛttikā, he rains sixty-four āḍhakas;
the rain lasts for ten nights."
If the Agnīdhra priest is appointed on the day of the Śravaṇā or Proṣṭhapadā nakṣatras, there will be rain during the monsoon nights;
he brings forth rain later on.
In both winter and summer, there will be three [rainy days] here. (69)
There will be fears of being seized;
there will be fear of fire, fear of weapons, and fear of water.
Thus it has been said regarding the Kṛttikās.
If the god rains during the last month of summer under Rohiṇī, he rains twenty-one āḍhakas. In that case, cultivation should be carried out on low-lying ground,
while high ground should be avoided.
And this rainy season, though obstructed by calamities, brings about a successful harvest;
yet two diseases prevail here:
diseases of the stomach and diseases of the eyes.
And in these directions, there will be an abundance of thieves.
It is also said regarding Rohiṇī:
"If it rains here during the last month of summer in the asterism Mṛgaśiras, it rains sixty-four āḍhakas."
The rainy season is characterized by the obstruction of the upward flow;
subsequently, it produces rain.
And in this [season], weapons are laid down.
The kings become secure and well-governed; the quarters of the world become peaceful,
and the districts therein become joyful.
It has been stated regarding Mṛgaśiras.
Regarding Ārdrā: if it rains here during the last month of summer, the god rains eighteen āḍhakas.
In that case, agriculture should be carried out on low-lying lands.
One must avoid certain places, treasures must be guarded,
and the directions in this region abound with many thieves.
Kings will lay down their weapons,
and three diseases will become prevalent therein:
fever, asthma, and throat-obstruction.
The death of children and young girls occurs;
thus it is said regarding Ārdrā.
Furthermore, if the rain-god pours down rain here during Punarvasu, in the last month of summer:
It rains ninety āḍhakas;
it produces great clouds,
and when the month of Āṣāḍha has entered, it rains gently.
And immediately thereafter, it rains incessantly;
moreover, kings lay down their weapons.
Thus it was said regarding Punarvasu.
If the god rains here during the last month of summer under the asterism Puṣya, he rains thirty-two āḍhakas. In this case, agriculture should be carried out on low-lying ground,
while high ground should be avoided.
It is evident that there will be a great rain from the clouds, and the crops will flourish;
however, a conflict will arise between the Brāhmaṇas and the Kṣatriyas.
And here, powerful fanged creatures abound;
therein three diseases arise: swellings, pustules, and scabies. Thus it has been said.
In the month of Puṣya,
during the last month of summer, if it rains there, the deity pours down twenty-one āḍhakas;
in that case, agriculture should be carried out in low-lying areas.
The regions should be avoided;
moreover, turbulent winds blow there,
and wise kings become agitated.
This rain brings all crops to fruition,
yet it causes discord between husband and wife, as well as between kings and their ministers.
This has been stated regarding Āśleṣā.
If the god rains here during the last month of summer under the asterism Maghā, he rains sixty-four āḍhakas;
this rain brings all the crops to fruition.
"In this [constellation], the embryos of wild animals, birds, cattle, and humans perish;
and there will be death among the people. Thus it was said regarding Maghā.
If the god rains during the last month of summer under the asterism Pūrvaphalgunī, he rains sixty-four āḍhakas.
This rain brings all crops to fruition;
yet, although it has produced that grain, people oppressed by the armies of enemy kings do not enjoy it with ease.
The embryos of both animals and humans become comfortable during this time;
this was stated regarding Pūrvaphalgunī.
Regarding Uttaraphalgunī: if it rains here during the last month of summer, the god rains eighty āḍhakas.
This rain brings all crops to fruition;
moreover, the kings in this region lay down their weapons,
yet there arises conflict between the Brahmins and the Kṣatriyas.
And the subjects, being free from calamities, will perish quickly.
It is also said regarding Uttaraphalgunī:
