"If it rains here during the last month of summer under the asterism Hasta, there will be forty-nine āḍhakas. (73)
The rain falls, and the god rains in such a way that he encircles it;
and the crops that have fallen are without the excellence of flavor for people, lacking vigor, possessing little essence, and containing little moisture.
And there will be famine here. It is said regarding the Hasta [nakṣatra]:
if it rains here during the last month of summer under Citrā, it rains sixty-four āḍhakas.
Thereafter, the obstruction of the Sāra constellation produces rain;
kings lay down their weapons,
and the districts there become joyful.
It has been stated regarding Citrā.
On the twenty-first day of the last month of summer, if it rains there, the deity pours down twenty-one āḍhakas;
and kings lay down their weapons.
And in this case, thieves become more powerful. It has been said regarding Svāti:
"If it rains here during the last month of summer in Viśākhā, [there will be] eighty āḍhakas. (74)
It rains;
this rain brings all crops to fruition,
yet during this time kings become susceptible to vulnerabilities.
In this [constellation], fires and conflagrations become powerful;
and here, even strong fanged creatures meet their destruction.
Thus it has been said regarding Viśākhā.
If the god rains during the last month of summer under the asterism Anurādhā, he rains sixty āḍhakas;
this rain brings the crops to fruition,
and friendships become firm in that year.
It has been stated regarding Anurādhā.
Regarding Jyeṣṭhā: if it rains here during the last month of summer, the deity pours down sixteen āḍhakas of rain;
in that case, those engaged in agricultural work should withdraw [their efforts].
The yoke-pins must be removed;
one's own grain must be gathered in;
and the sacred fires must be maintained.
The ploughs must be withdrawn;
this country will inevitably be ruined,
or it will be oppressed by a foreign army.
It has been stated regarding Jyeṣṭhā:
if the god rains here during the last month of summer in Mūla, he rains sixty-four āḍhakas.
This year brings about a bountiful harvest;
however, the regions will abound with thieves,
and three diseases will prevail there with great force.
There will be wind-swelling of the cheeks, pain in the sides, and diseases of the eyes;
however, flowers and fruits will flourish there, and kings will lay down their weapons. This was stated in the *Mūla*.
If it rains during the last month of summer under the constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā, the god pours down sixty āḍhakas of rain; however, there will be two obstacles to this:
either under Proṣṭhapadā or under Aśvayuj in the fortnight.
This year brings all crops to full maturity;
however, two diseases prevail here:
abdominal disease and eye disease.
It has been stated regarding Pūrvāṣāḍhā.
Regarding Uttarāṣāḍhā: if it rains here during the last month of summer, the deity pours down a full hundred āḍhakas.
In that case, high ground should be prepared for cultivation.
One should avoid low-lying places;
for great currents flow there,
and the rains there consist of acid water.
It brings all crops to fruition;
however, three diseases become prevalent there:
goiters, skin diseases, and throat ailments.
It has been stated regarding Uttarāṣāḍhā.
If it rains during the month of Abhijit, the last month of summer, it will rain sixty-four āḍhakas;
and the god will send down rain in a circular pattern.
Subsequently, the rain produces crops,
and there is an outpouring of aquatic beings;
this was stated regarding Abhijit.
If, however, during the last month of the summer season in the month of Śrāvaṇa, the god rains here, he rains sixty-four āḍhakas;
and the god rains in circular patches.
Subsequently, the rain brings the crops to fruition.
There will be a release of aquatic beings,
men will be afflicted by many diseases,
and kings will become severe in their punishments.
It has been stated regarding Śravaṇā:
if it rains here during the last month of the summer season under Dhaniṣṭhā, the deity pours down fifty-one āḍhakas;
and in this case, the rains are distributed [evenly].
In that case, low-lying areas should be made fit for cultivation, while high ground should be avoided; furthermore,
the rain will fall at night with a harsh sound.
It brings the crops to fruition;
however, there will be one disease here:
a disorder of the glands.
And kings become those who take up weapons.
It has been said regarding Dhaniṣṭhā:
"If it rains here during the sixteenth [day] of the last month of summer under Śatabhiṣā, [there will be] sixteen āḍhakas. (77)
It rains there;
therefore, agriculture should be carried out in the low-lying areas,
while the high ground should be avoided.
This rain brings all crops to maturity;
the countryside becomes filled with wheeling carriages;
and men, along with their sons and daughters, travel to other lands carrying them upon their shoulders.
It has been stated regarding Śatabhiṣaj:
if it rains here during the last month of the summer season under Pūrvabhādrapadā, it rains sixty-four āḍhakas;
and at the beginning of the rainy season, there will be a drought lasting nineteen nights.
It destroys the flower crops,
and these rains are accompanied by many thieves;
furthermore, two great diseases arise therein.
First there arises a fever from the heat of bile;
afterwards, a powerful and great planetary seizure (mahāgraha) occurs for mortals and women.
And death occurs.
As was stated regarding Pūrvabhādrapadā:
"If it rains here during the last month of summer under Uttarabhādrapadā, it rains a full hundred āḍhakas."
Great currents flow;
villages, cities, and market towns are swept away by the currents;
and here, four diseases become powerful.
Namely: abdominal disease, eye disease, cough, and fever;
thus there occurs the death of young boys and girls.
In this place, the high ground should be cultivated; the low ground should be avoided.
And these rains bring about flowers and fruits.
It has been stated regarding Uttarabhādrapadā.
Regarding Revatī: if the god rains here during the last month of summer, he rains sixty-one āḍhakas.
In that case, agriculture should be carried out on low-lying lands.
Those places should be avoided where they consume [meat];
moreover, kings there have laid down their weapons and staffs.
The districts become free from agitation,
yet the donors become agitated;
and the districts become afflicted by gods and constellations.
The friendships become united. It is said regarding Revatī:
"If the god rains here during the last month of summer in Aśvinī, he rains forty-eight āḍhakas."
And whatever falls during the middle of the rainy season, in that regard, low-lying areas should be prepared for cultivation,
while high ground should be avoided.
This rainy season brings all crops to fruition;
however, the inhabited regions there become beset by fear,
and thieves become powerful.
It has been stated regarding Aśvinī.
Regarding Bharaṇī: if the god rains here during the last month of summer, he rains a full hundred āḍhakas;
in that case, dry lands should be cultivated.
Low-lying places should be avoided;
for there, famine occurs,
and for the people there is aging and death.
And in this [constellation], kings become mutual slayers of one another,
and there is strife between sons and grandsons. Thus it was said regarding Bharaṇī.
p.79.2/.This, Ghoṣa Puṣkarasārin, is the chapter on the constellations, seasons, and rains.
The ripening of results during an eclipse by the planet Rāhu, p.
79.3: "O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the ripening of results for these twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) during an eclipse by the planet Rāhu.
O Puṣkarasārin, if there is an eclipse of the moon in the *Kṛttikā* mansion, there will be affliction for the Kaliṅgas and Magadhas."

If there is a lunar eclipse in Rohiṇī, there will be affliction for the subjects. If there is a lunar eclipse in Mṛgaśiras, there will be affliction for the Videha country and for those who serve the king.
The same should be stated for Ārdrā, Punarvasu, and Puṣya.
If there is a lunar eclipse in Aśleṣā, there will be suffering for the Nāgas and those from the Himalayas.
If there is a lunar eclipse during the Maghā constellation, there will be affliction for the people of Gauḍa.
If the Moon is eclipsed during Pūrvaphalgunī, there will be affliction for thieves.
If the Moon is eclipsed during Uttaraphalgunī, there will be affliction for the people of Avanti.
If the Soma is drawn under Hasta, there will be affliction for the people of Saurāṣṭra.
If the Soma is drawn under Citrā, there will be affliction for birds and bipeds.
If the Soma is drawn under Svāti—
There is affliction for all who have entered the religious life.
If the moon is seized during Anurādhā, there is affliction for merchants and cart-drivers.
If the moon is seized during Jyeṣṭhā, there is suffering for gatekeepers.
If the moon is seized at Mūla, there will be suffering for travelers;
if the moon is seized in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, there will be suffering for the people of Avanti;
if the moon is seized in Uttarāṣāḍhā, there will be suffering for the Kāmbojas.
And for the Bāhlīkas. If the Soma is drawn in Abhijit, there will be suffering for those of the southern region and for the inhabitants of Tāmraparṇa.
If Soma is drawn during the Śravaṇā constellation, there will be affliction for thieves and assassins.
If Soma is drawn during Dhaniṣṭhā, there will be affliction for the Kurus and Pañcālas.
If Soma is drawn during Śatabhiṣaj, there will be affliction for root-diggers and practitioners of the Atharvaveda.
If the moon is seized in Pūrvabhādrapadā, there will be affliction for perfumers and for the Yavanas and Kambojas. If the moon is seized in Uttarabhādrapadā,
there will be affliction for the Gandharvas.

If the Soma is drawn under Revatī, there will be suffering for the sailors; if under Aśvinī, there will be suffering for the merchants. If the Soma is drawn under Bharaṇī, there will be suffering for the people of Bharukaccha.
"Thus, O Puṣkarasārin, when there is a lunar eclipse in a particular constellation, there will be suffering for that specific region.
Thus ends the chapter on the ripening of the results of Rāhu’s eclipses.
[This concludes] the Instruction on the Activities of the Constellations.
Listen to the ritual acts as they are prescribed in the *Pratinakṣatravaṃśaśāstra*,
O Brahmin, just as these words of the seers (*ṛṣi*) are being spoken.

One should know that Kṛttikā consists of six stars; one should cause [the performance of] a rite to take place under them. The establishment of the sacred fire (agnyādhāna), the domestic cooked sacrifice (pākayajña), and whatever brings about prosperity and progeny [should be performed then].
One should churn clarified butter there and construct a cowshed;
goats and sheep should be purchased, and a bull should be released for the cows.
In this case, one should have all vessels made of iron;
furthermore, one should employ the work of goldsmiths and provide training in archery and weaponry.
A maternal uncle should measure out here a small hut and a place for fire;
furthermore, one should cause the seeds of yellow and red flowers to be sown here.
In this [year], one should have a house measured out and likewise construct a dwelling;
one should cover oneself with new clothing, but one should not engage in buying or selling here.
Cruel deeds—such as war, siege, and imprisonment—are accomplished [under these conditions];
however, even in this case, the wise man should not intentionally inflict suffering upon others.
In this [month], one should have all weapons and razor-shaving implements prepared;
one should also have lustrous vessels made or purchased.
Bathing the head confers long life and serves as a means of subduing women;
however, if there is excessive rain from the god [Indra], the enmity therein is not pacified.

One born under Kṛttikā is irascible, joyful, brave, radiant, and fond of daring deeds; he is long-lived, renowned, and devoted to sacrifice. Under Rohiṇī, one should employ all agricultural activities and labors.
One should cause fields, land, monasteries, and a new dwelling to be constructed.
One should employ wheel-turners, servants, and even domestic animals;
one should sow all kinds of seeds and certainly have garments woven.
One should not pay a debt in that case, for enmity will increase therein;
one should avoid both battle and the consumption of liquor.
The rain of the god [Indra] and his birth are praised here.
One born under Rohiṇī is compassionate, endowed with patience, fond of women, and greedy for food; he is long-lived, possesses cattle, is fortunate, and becomes one of great wealth. Under Rohiṇī.
One should know that Mṛgaśiras is gentle and consists of three straight stars;
one should perform all those actions which are soft (mṛdu) under this asterism. One should also perform all those actions which are prescribed for Rohiṇī.
One should cause trees that yield milk and seeds that produce milky sap to be planted;
one should also cause royal palaces, turrets, and parasols to be constructed.
One may engage in discourse on all manner of activities, but one should not cause [others] to dwell in the practice;
one may even break in camels and oxen for the purpose of plowing.
One should clothe [the image] in new garments and provide it with ornaments;
furthermore, one should have all the rites for the twice-born performed here.
One should predict abundant rainfall and excellent showers from the god during this time;
likewise, such a person becomes inclined toward sleep, fearful, yet endowed with intelligence.
In Mṛgaśiras.
Under Ārdrā, one should seek wealth and perform auspicious deeds;
however, the wise man should avoid those cruel actions that are accomplished under this asterism.
One should have wells, moats, and tanks constructed there;
one should sell the first rainwater, but not a cow.
Likewise, one should establish oil-pressing operations and taverns for liquor-sellers.
One should press the stalks of sugarcane or sow the seeds of sugarcane;
one should know that there will be a downpour from the god [Indra] with abundant flow.
One who is irascible, fond of hunting, and desirous of meat is born here under Ārdrā.
When the moon is conjoined with Punarvasu, one should indeed undertake the observance of vows;
the gift of a cow and the initiation ceremony—all these are successfully accomplished therein.
Having taken a woman who is giving birth, one should bring her home;
if one so desires, one may have her perform ritual acts there again and again.
One should not perform medical treatment if one desires to avoid misfortune;
moreover, the raining of the god [Indra] and birth are praised during this time.
In this [constellation], a man is born who is playful, yet also fickle toward women;
he is said to be of diverse character, with his mind not fixed upon any one thing.
In Punarvasu.
One should always perform auspicious acts that bring wealth, fame, and long life under the asterism Puṣya;
and one should cause all the rites of the twice-born to be performed under it.
One should employ oneself as a minister to the king and practice service and discipline;
one should consecrate the king and adorn one's own body.
One should perform the work of shaving, as well as the clipping of hair and nails;
one should appoint a domestic priest and cause a banner-top to be raised.
When there is heavy rain from the god, one should predict moderate rainfall;
there will be neither disease nor thieves, and there shall always be security in this region.
One who is constantly engaged under the asterism Puṣya should accomplish all undertakings.
One should avoid those people who are hostile or afflicted with abscesses during this time.
Under Puṣya, one is born long-lived, illustrious, and possessed of great wealth. [Puṣya]
A fierce rite is accomplished; one should perform it under the asterism Aśleṣā.
One should fashion ornaments here and construct a rampart.
Under Aśleṣā, one should have buildings constructed, dams built across rivers, and perform acts of reconciliation.
There will be a year with many gadflies and mosquitoes, and it rains only sparingly.
One born under this asterism is prone to anger, given to sleep, and deceitful.
Under the asterism Maghā, one should sow all kinds of grain and also gather them in;
one should perform acts of assembly and carry out auspicious ceremonies therein.
One should construct storehouses and deposit the harvest there;
and one should always perform the *śrāddha* ceremony for the ancestors and the gods here as well.
If the rain-god pours down here, there will be an abundance of crops;
a person born under this [asterism] becomes a friend, a gatekeeper, and one who desires flavorful tastes.
He is long-lived, has many sons, is fond of women, and is greedy for food.
In that [battle], if one engages first, one is defeated;
therefore, a wise man should avoid those terrible deeds under the asterism Maghā.
Under the *pūrvaphalgunī* asterisms, one should perform rites for the sake of good fortune;
specifically, one should employ fruits such as the *āmalaka* and others.
One should have auspicious rites for the maiden performed, as well as ceremonial baths;
and one should also have a monastery constructed for the purpose of conveying the girl [to her husband].
One should have houses built there; one should employ a Vaiśya for this purpose. One should also employ those who subsist on shares for their work.
One with indistinct hair or no hair at all is born fortunate in this world;
one should predict abundant rain and excellent showers from the god.
One should declare that whatever has been lost, pierced, or done no longer exists.
Under Pūrvaphalgunī.
Under Uttaraphalgunī, however, one should perform all rites;
under this asterism, one is born intelligent, handsome, and illustrious.
Then, in this case, one should declare that everything lost or burnt is recovered;
and one should know that there will be rain from the god and unsurpassed prosperity.
Under Uttaraphalgunī.
With his hand, he should perform all light tasks;
and he should cause all the various duties for all members of the twice-born classes to be carried out.
One should have an elephant-rider, a high official, and a lotus pond constructed;
however, theft is successful there, and therefore the wise man should avoid it.
When there is a heavy downpour from the god and the rains are proclaimed as abundant,
one should know that a person born at this time will be a hero, a thief, or a wise man,
skilled in all branches of knowledge.
May he be free from disease and long-lived. //Haste//
Under Citrā, one should have new cloth woven and ornaments fashioned;
one should look upon a king adorned with finery and observe the array of an army.
One should cause gold, silver, wealth, and cities to be measured out;
likewise, one should adorn oneself with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
He should train the mathematicians in their science, as well as in instrumental music, dancing, and singing;
he should instruct the former image-makers and chariot-makers;
and he should have painters, scribes, and those skilled in book-making perform their respective tasks.
One should predict that the rain from the god will be variegated;
[the person born under this influence] will be intelligent, handsome, have variegated eyes, and be greedy for food.
One born under Citrā is gentle in character, timid, fickle-minded, and curious; such a person is long-lived, fortunate, and yet prone to lust for women. (p.89.2)
Under Svāti, one should employ warriors, horses, mules, and donkeys;
as well as those who must travel quickly, foodstuffs, acrobats, and those who measure the road.
One should cause kettledrums, clay drums, small drums, and large drums to be sounded;
and one should perform invitations, weddings, and acts of friendship therein.
There is the banishment of enemies, yet one does not depart from home of one's own accord;
there is the raining of the deity, and frequent winds and rain.
One born under Svāti becomes intelligent, but is subject to much disease and has a fickle mind.
Under Viśākhā, one should employ plows and engage in plowing;
however, one should avoid all work related to barley and wheat, as well as leguminous grains.

One should plant rice, sesame, and beans, as well as trees with beautiful branches, under Viśākhā; one should also undertake the construction of houses. One should perform head-baths and generally carry out purificatory rites.
One should know that the raining of the deity signifies the overflowing of a *kalpa*.
One born under Viśākhā is high-minded, handsome, and intelligent; however, he is prone to anger, has few children, is unfortunate, and is greedy for food. In Viśākhā.
Under Anurādhā, one should cultivate association with friends and virtuous people;
all gentle activities and acts of sweetness should be performed at this time.
On this day, one should have a haircut performed and undergo surgical procedures. One should also constantly employ diplomatic stratagems involving alliances and conclude treaties.
Furthermore, one should predict that what has been lost or consumed by heat will be recovered with very little effort.
In this [constellation], one is born with friends and kinsmen, and as one whose nature is established in righteousness;
one should predict that the rain-god will pour forth a bountiful and well-timed rain.
Under Anurādhā.

Under Jyeṣṭhā, one should be a pioneer; one should consecrate a king, and one may measure out or begin the construction of a city, a market town, or a village. One should cause all the affairs of kṣatriyas and kings to be carried out.
Among brothers, he who is born of the eldest wife becomes the eldest;
he is long-lived, renowned, and takes delight in the learned.
In this case, one should ascend a palace, as well as an elephant, a horse, or a chariot;
one should establish the forces of the guild-leaders within the villages, towns, and kingdoms.
One should declare that what is lost or scorched by affliction (*kleśa*) alone will be recovered;
one should avoid those [omens] that indicate cruel things will succeed here, though the wise man should recognize them.
Furthermore, one should predict good rain from the falling of rain from the sky.
In Jyeṣṭhā.
At the root [of the tree], one should employ all those things produced from roots— such as radishes, tubers, and lotus roots— as well as all types of bulbs and seeds.
If there should be an old debt and wealth stands before one,
then everything, including the most excellent limb, should be undertaken for the sake of securing the root [of that wealth].
Whatever medical treatments there are here for women, for boys, and for girls— one should employ them all at the root of the tree, as well as bathing in the rivers.
In this [period], fierce rites are accomplished; one should perform auspicious ceremonies, but one should not prepare fermenting agents or preparations for liquor in association with enemies.
One born under Mūla becomes wealthy, possesses many sons, and is endowed with roots [or foundations].
Furthermore, one should declare that whatever is lost or burnt here does not truly exist [is irretrievably gone].
One should also predict abundant rainfall and excellent showers from the god. (Mūla)
In the first half of Āṣāḍhā, one should cause rivers and lakes,
as well as ponds, wells, water-stations, and tanks to be constructed.
One should cultivate flowers as well as roots and fruits; one should establish pleasure groves and employ those who subsist on alms.
Furthermore, those fierce rites that are to be accomplished succeed here.
One should declare that what is lost or afflicted does not exist;
there, one is born long-lived, virtuous in conduct, and handsome.
In Pūrvāṣāḍhā.
Under the *uttarāṣāḍhā* constellation, one should not engage in hostilities;
one may cause all clothes to be woven, but one should not put on new ones.
One should neither demolish nor cause division; otherwise, the work concerning the site will not succeed.

Likewise, regarding the construction of halls for cattle and other such animals, as well as for the village headman in the village, the king should establish a guild and ensure that an agreement is made therein.

One who is born under this [asterism] is bold, possesses the character suited for assemblies, and is accomplished; he is diligent in the service of friends and is discerning in the discussion of counsel.
Whether something is lost or afflicted with distress,
one should declare it to exist;
and regarding the rain of the god, one should predict a well-timed, bountiful shower.
In Uttarāṣāḍhā.
One should not perform the worship of Brahmā-deva during the asterism Abhijit; indeed, one should not do so during Abhijit.
One should not perform any martial activities under the asterism Śravaṇā;
likewise, the study of vocal training and song will indeed be mastered without delay.
One should perform the piercing of the ears and consecrate a king;
furthermore, one should cause all the duties of the twice-born to be undertaken.
One should perform offerings of oblations and display one's powers as well;
for one born under this [asterism] becomes intelligent, free from disease, strong, and devoted to sacrifice.
When the moon is situated in Śravaṇā, one should predict abundant rainfall from the god;
furthermore, what is lost is recovered there when the moon is in Śravaṇā.
Dhaniṣṭhā is a light lunar mansion, honored for all undertakings;
having studied, a Brāhmaṇa should perform his ceremonial bath, and one may consecrate a king under it.
He should cause all members of the twice-born castes to perform all their respective duties;
he should appoint a merchant-leader (śreṣṭhin) in the city and a head of the guild (gaṇādhyakṣa) among the guilds.
He shall be intelligent, renowned, possessed of great enjoyments, and very wealthy.
One born under this [asterism] becomes possessed of many offspring, gentle, self-controlled, and high-souled;
one should also know that there will be abundant rain from the god and excellent showers here.
Under Dhaniṣṭhā.
One should always administer medicines during the conjunction with Śatabhiṣaj;
one should also perform acts for renown, and the rites of the Atharvaveda will succeed.
One should display various goods for sale and employ a vintner;
one should have curdless milk drunk there and cause sesame and mung beans to be sown.
One should employ sea-borne merchandise and ships;
one should take what is to be taken from them and must not incur any expenditure therein.
He should employ boundary guards, gatekeepers, and scribes;
he should also perform medical treatments and collect medicines.
One should have a treasure-trove dug there, or one may deposit a treasure there;
one should invest wealth in this place and also train in the art of medicine.
Furthermore, if one searches for something lost here, it will be found even after a long time.
In this [constellation], one is born healthy yet prone to anger and inclined toward sleep. One should predict that there will be rain from the god, resulting in a bountiful harvest.
Under Śatabhiṣā.
In conjunction with Pūrvabhādrapadā, the success of cruel deeds is declared;
however, one should indicate that this does not apply to things that are lost, pierced, or afflicted.
One born under this [asterism] is long-eared, possesses great wealth, and is always dear to his kinsmen; he is very wealthy, performs deeds without cruelty, and is free from envy.
One should predict that the rain-god will send down heavy showers and fierce rains.
In Pūrvabhādrapadā.
One should perform rites for longevity and prosperity in the north;
one should not go toward the south, and in this case, one should cause a city to be established there.
One born under this [asterism] becomes long-lived, famous, and wealthy.
Furthermore, one will find there a threefold gain whether in income or expenditure.
One should predict abundant rainfall from the god and a well-timed rain.
In Uttarabhādrapadā.
Under Revatī, one should employ gems, silver, wealth, and grain;
one should construct storehouses, but one should not prepare fermenting agents (kinva) here.
One should perform the work of distilling liquor, [procure] gold, and [acquire] herds of cattle;
one should establish a herd of cows there and have a cowshed built there.
One should clothe oneself in new clothing and also wear gold.
One born under Revatī becomes a mendicant, charitable in nature, poor, and free from envy;
he is constantly devoted to his kinsmen and is a knower of the Dharma.
Regarding Revatī, one should predict good rain and the loss of profits. Revatī.
The Aśvins should join together a man and a woman, and one should cause a horse stable to be built;
one should employ horses here, and one should employ a chariot here as well.
One should engage in lending on interest and sow seeds there;
one should also employ vehicles, horses, draft animals, and elephants.
In this case, one should administer medicine and have medical treatment performed;
such a person will be intelligent, handsome, and endowed with qualities suitable for royal service.
One who is born under Aśvinī becomes free from disease, strong, brave, and indeed fortunate.
One should predict good rain and the loss of what was acquired when [the moon is] in Aśvinī.
Regarding Aśvinī: p.97.4ab/.One who is healthy, powerful, brave, and indeed blessed is born here; p.97.4cd/.one should indicate good rain and the loss of gains in Aśvinī. Regarding Aśvinī.
One should know that Tritārā is Bharaṇī; one should accomplish cruel deeds under it.
Likewise, one should hire servants and laborers, or cause them to be presented.
In this situation, one should bring about prosperity but not marry a wife;
for from such a marriage is born the *utkaṭaka*, the *vañcataka*, and the false witness.
One born here under Bharaṇī is knowledgeable in ritual procedures, yet of evil conduct and miserly;
one born here is ill-behaved and envious of elders;
he is a tormentor of others, greedy, and intent on the affairs of others. (Bharaṇī)
When the twenty-seven lunar mansions, beginning with Kṛttikā, are present,
one should perform the ritual by assigning these constellations accordingly.
When all their crops, as well as medicinal herbs and forest trees, are afflicted while that planet remains [in a particular position],
everything should be bestowed [as a gift] during the ritual acts prescribed for those constellations.
The chapter entitled "Instruction on the Rites of the Lunar Mansions" has been explained.
"O Puṣkarasārin, there are four constellations that are fixed and half-nights; these are the fixed constellations, and I shall explain them.
Listen to that."
Namely:
the three Uttarās and Rohiṇī;
one should dwell in safety.
(99) One should sow seeds here, establish a settlement here, and consecrate a king here.
And one should perform those other rites which have been prescribed.
Whether [the object] is lost, burnt, pierced, or even stolen,
or if it has been thus specifically pointed out, well-being will swiftly come to pass.
Now, one born here will be fortunate, possessed of knowledge, and renowned;
he will be auspicious, a possessor of great enjoyments, and a great yogin.
"O Puṣkarasārin, there are four constellations that are swift:
namely, Puṣya, Hasta, Abhijit, and Aśvinī.
A wise person should have swift tasks performed under these."
One should employ here the study of the Vedas, the commencement of mantras, departure on a journey, and also cattle and horses;
likewise, sacrificial fires, activities requiring application, the use of medicinal herbs,
and all healing remedies should be applied here.
In that case, one should perform the commencement of a sacrifice and the Cāturmāsya rites;

furthermore, it should be declared: "Whatever has been lost, burnt, or pierced here shall become well. Moreover, one should know that a birth occurring at this time will be auspicious, glorious, and renowned.
And [he sees] the king Mahābhoga, the great yogin, the lord.
"One who possesses great wealth, great enjoyments, and likewise great excellence;
a Kṣatriya who is generous by nature, and a Brāhmaṇa who serves as a domestic priest. Thus it is said.
"Indeed, O Puṣkarasārin, there are five constellations that are cruel, namely:"
Maghā, the three Pūrvas, and Bharaṇī as the fifth—
whatever is burnt, lost, or pierced here shall not come to pass.
Thus it should be said:
there are six [periods] at midnight,
namely:
Ārdrā, Aśleṣā, Svātī, Jyeṣṭhā,
Śatabhiṣā, and Bharaṇī—
these nine lunar mansions have six *grāsa*s and two fields.
Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, and Viśākhā,
as well as the three Uttarās—
these are the asterisms divided into two parts.
There are fifteen fields:
Kṛttikā, Maghā, Mūlā, and the three Pūrvas;
these six belong to the eastern portion.
Mṛgaśirā, Puṣyā, Hastā, Citrā, Anurādhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Revatī, and Aśvinī—
these nine lunar mansions belong to the western quarter; they possess a conjunction of thirty muhūrtas and are [astrological] fields.
Moreover, O Brahmin, there are auspicious moments (muhūrta), there are inauspicious moments,
and there are moments that are both auspicious and inauspicious.
When all the asterisms in conjunction have auspicious muhūrta-entries, they are favorable;
when they have inauspicious muhūrta-entries, they are not favorable;
but when there are both auspicious and inauspicious entries, they are neutral.
Regarding the decrease and increase of nights and days:
now, it is explained how the decrease or increase of nights and days occurs here.
In the first month of the rainy season, the moon reaches the conjunction with the Puṣya constellation on the new moon day.
On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa,
the day consists of eighteen muhūrtas and the night consists of twelve muhūrtas.
At midday, when the shadow of a sixteen-aṅgula stick is half an aṅgula long, the sun turns back;
it leads toward the night of Āṣāḍhā,
and the sun has entered Mṛgaśiras— the beginning of the rainy season.
In the second month, the new moon occurs under Maghā and the full moon under Bhādrapadā;
the day consists of seventeen muhūrtas and the night consists of thirteen muhūrtas.
When the shadow is two finger-breadths long, the sun turns back; the moon in Śravaṇā brings on the night,
and the sun has entered Puṣya.
In the third month of the rainy season, the moon is in the constellation Phalgunī on the new moon day;
it is in Aśvinī on the full moon day.
The day consists of sixteen muhūrtas.
The night consists of fourteen muhūrtas;
when the shadow is four aṅgulas long, the sun turns back.
Pūrvabhādrapadā conducts the night;
the Sun has entered Maghā.
In the fourth month of the rainy season, Citrā occurs on the new moon day, and Kṛttikā on the full moon day.
The day consists of fifteen muhūrtas;
the night consists of fifteen muhūrtas.
When the shadow is six aṅgulas long, the sun changes its course.
The Aśvins lead the night;
on the day of Phālgunī, the Sun has departed.
In the first month of the winter season, Anurādhā coincides with the new moon.
During the full moon of the month of Mṛgaśirā,
the day consists of fourteen muhūrtas and the night consists of sixteen muhūrtas.
When the shadow is eight finger-breadths long, the sun turns back;
it leads the night of Kṛttikā,
and by the time of Citrā, the sun has reached its [southern] limit.
In the second month of the winter season, the new moon coincides with the asterism Jyeṣṭhā;
on the full moon day, it is Puṣya;
the day consists of thirteen muhūrtas.
The night consists of seventeen muhūrtas; when the shadow is ten aṅgulas long, the sun turns back;
Mṛgaśirā brings the night to its end.
The sun enters Viśākhā;
in the third month of winter, the new moon occurs in Pūrvāṣāḍhā,
and the full moon occurs in Maghā.
The day consists of twelve muhūrtas and the night consists of eighteen muhūrtas;
at a shadow length of twelve aṅgulas, the sun revolves.
Puṣya brings on the night;
Āditya has entered Jyeṣṭhā during the fourth month of the winter season.
In that month, the new moon falls on Śravaṇā,
and the full moon on Phalgunī;
the day consists of thirteen muhūrtas.
The night consists of seventeen muhūrtas;
when the shadow is ten aṅgulas long, the sun turns back;
Maghā brings on the night.
The sun has entered Āṣāḍhā. In the first month of summer, the new moon occurs in Uttarabhādrapadā;
on the full moon day, it is in Citrā, and the day consists of fourteen muhūrtas.
The night consists of sixteen muhūrtas.
When the shadow is eight finger-breadths long, the sun turns;
it brings about the night of Phalgunī.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, the sun has moved [to the constellation Śravaṇā]. In the second month of summer, the new moon occurs in Aśvinī,
and the full moon occurs in Viśākhā.
The day consists of fifteen muhūrtas;
the night consists of fifteen muhūrtas.
When the shadow is six aṅgulas long, the sun changes its course.
The Citrā constellation conducts the night;
when the sun has entered Uttarā-bhādrapadā,
it occurs on the new moon day of Kṛttikā in the third month of summer.
On the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha,
the day consists of sixteen muhūrtas and the night consists of fourteen muhūrtas.
When the shadow is four finger-breadths long, the sun turns back;
Viśākhā brings on the night;
the sun has entered Kṛttikā.
It occurs as follows: in the fourth month of summer, on the new moon day, the moon is in Mṛgaśiras;
on the full moon day, it is in Uttarāṣāḍhā;
and the day consists of seventeen muhūrtas.
The night consists of thirteen muhūrtas.
At midday, when the shadow is two finger-breadths long, the sun turns;
it brings about the longest night.
The sun enters the constellation Puṣya.
By searching through the year according to the specific muhūrtas, all these constellations are joined with the new moon and the full moon in their respective portions.
One must calculate both the deficient night and the full night;
in that regard, an additional month is joined in the third year,
for the days and nights of six months are equal.
Therefore, for six months the day increases;
for six months the night increases.
For six months, the day [increases] equally month by month.
It diminishes; night diminishes month by month for six months. After six months, the sun turns and moves toward the northern direction.
For six months [the sun moves] toward the southern direction;
for six months, there occurs a decrease and an increase in the volume of water in the ocean.
The rise of the ocean tides occurs through the movement of the sun and the movement of the moon.
In this regard, one who is mindful of calculation and vigilance—thus is this year explained.
[The planet.]
The moon, the sun, Venus, Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, and Mercury—
these are the planets.
Among these planets, Jupiter is the one who abides for a full year.
In this way, Śanaiścara, Budha, Aṅgāraka, and Śukra are these [planets] that move through the mandalas.
Regarding the circle of constellations (nakṣatramaṇḍala):
Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and Mṛgaśirā constitute the first common mandala.
Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, and Āśleṣā—this is the second common maṇḍala.
Maghā, the two Phalgunīs, Hasta, and Citrā—this is the third common maṇḍala.
Svātī, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā—this is the fourth common maṇḍala.
Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, and the two Āṣāḍhās (105):
here all great dangers arise;
this is the fifth mandala.
Abhijit, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, and both Bhādrapadas—this is the sixth common mandala.
Revatī and Aśvinī—this is the seventh common mandala.
During the year, whichever lunar mansion mandala afflicts [the sky], affliction should be predicted for that specific region or for its inhabitants.
Twelve muhūrtas are fixed during the day and twelve during the night;
six muhūrtas are mobile.
Which are the six?
Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Bharga, Deva, and Raudra—
these six are the wandering [deities].
Now, here in the month of Śrāvaṇa, when the day is eighteen muhūrtas long, at sunrise there occurs the muhūrta named Caturoja.
Between the muhūrta Rohita and the muhūrta Bala, midday occurs.
At the sun's descent, however, the muhūrta named Vicārī occurs.
When the sun has descended into the twelve-muhūrta night, at the sixth muhūrta, the muhūrta named Nayanana occurs.
The *muhūrta* at the end of the night is called Ātāpāgni.
When the month of Bhādrapada is complete, during the seventeenth *muhūrta* of the day at sunrise, the *muhūrta* is called Caturoja.
At midday, there is the muhūrta named Abhijit. At the sun's descent, there is the muhūrta named Raudra.
When the sun has descended during the thirteenth muhūrta of the night, there is the muhūrta named Vicārī.
At midnight, there is a most terrifying moment called Vāyava;
at the end of the night, there is a moment called Ātapāgni.
When the month of Aśvayuja is full, the day consists of sixteen muhūrtas.
At sunrise, there is the muhūrta named Caturojas;
at the interval between the muhūrta Samudgata and Abhijit, it is midday;
and at sunset, there is the muhūrta named Bhargodeva.

When the sun has descended during a night of fourteen muhūrtas, the muhūrta named Raudra occurs. Midnight falls between the muhūrta of Abhijit and the muhūrta of Bhīṣamaṇa. At the conclusion of the night, there is a muhūrta known as Ātapāgni.
In the full month of Kārttika, the day and night are equal;
the day consists of fifteen muhūrtas and the night consists of fifteen muhūrtas.
When the day and night are equal at sunrise, there occurs what is called the "fourfold-born" (caturoja) muhūrta.
The moment called "Face-to-Face" occurs at midday;
the moment called "Continuous" occurs at sunrise.
As soon as the sun has descended at night, there occurs the muhūrta named Bhṛgu;
at midnight, there occurs the muhūrta named Abhijit;
and at the end of the night, there occurs the muhūrta named Ātapāgni.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, when the day consists of fourteen muhūrtas, at sunrise there occurs the muhūrta named Caturoja.
Between the muhūrtas of Virata and Saṃmukha, midday occurs.
At the sun's descent, there occurs the muhūrta named Varuṇa.
When the sun has just descended during a night of sixteen muhūrtas, there occurs the muhūrta named Saṃtāpana-saṃyama.
Midnight falls between the muhūrtas of Rākṣasa and Abhijit. At the end of the night, there occurs the muhūrta named Ātapāgni.
In the month of Pauṣa, when the day is full of thirteen muhūrtas, at sunrise the muhūrta is called Caturoja;
at midday the muhūrta is called Virata;
and at sunset the muhūrta is called Nairṛta.
When the sun has just set during a night of seventeen muhūrtas, the muhūrta is named Varuṇa;
at midnight, the muhūrta is named Rākṣasa;
and at the end of the night, the muhūrta is named Ātapāgni.
In the month of Māgha, when the day consists of twelve muhūrtas, at sunrise there occurs the muhūrta named Caturoja.
Between the muhūrtas of Sāvitra and Virata, midday occurs. At the sun's descent, there occurs the muhūrta named Vijaya.
When the sun has just set during a night consisting of eighteen muhūrtas, there occurs the muhūrta named Nairṛta;
the interval between the muhūrta of Gardabha and that of Rākṣasa constitutes midnight,
marking the end of the night.
The *muhūrta* called Ātapāgni is as it is in the month of Śrāvaṇa, so it is in Māgha;
as it is in Bhādrapada, so it is in Phālguna.
As it is in Āśvayuja, so it is in Caitra; as it is in Kārttika, so it is in Vaiśākha;
as it is in Mārgaśīrṣa, so it is in Jyeṣṭha.
As it is in the month of Pauṣa, so it is in Āṣāḍha.
In this manner, the movement and the course of these constellations and the muhūrtas should be known.
This concludes the first chapter, titled "The Movement of the Constellations."
Just as the midpoint of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) must be adjusted according to the waxing and waning [of the moon] by means of night and day—
whether the day or month is decreasing or increasing, or when a full month, half-month, or fortnight has passed—
the lunar digit (*kalā*) increases during the day within this interval on the second, sixth, ninth, twelfth, and fourteenth days, while the digit decreases during the night.
The Exposition on Earthquakes (Bhūmikampānirdeśa), p.
108.3ab: By whom the four Great Kings sustain the earth: Ativṛddhi, Viśuddha, Vardhamāna, and Pṛthakśravas.
The four great elements cause the earth to tremble;
so too do the waters, Indra, Vāyu, and the Blessed One, Agni.
When three of those [wind-forces] are present on one side, there are six forces within a single month;
this would be an indication of another wheel, wherein the earth trembles incessantly.
Viśākhā lasts for ten nights; Jyeṣṭhā lasts for twelve nights;
Āṣāḍhā lasts for twenty-five; and Śravaṇā lasts for seventy-five.
In Bhādrapada, the sacrifice is remembered as lasting one hundred nights; in Āśvayuja, it is remembered as lasting one hundred and fifty nights.
In Māgha, it is remembered as lasting one hundred and fifty nights;
in the month of Phālguna, it lasts one hundred and fifty nights, while in Caitra, it lasts thirty nights.
The ripening of the forces of the earth-elements thus gives rise to an earthquake.
When the earth trembles constantly throughout all the months,
and likewise when trees shake or if the water quivers, and if a mountain should tremble like a leaf, one should predict fear in that situation.
Then cities, or villages, and those who dwell there in cowherd settlements,
quickly become desolate like forests, becoming the refuge of wild beasts.
Wildernesses will prevail for fifteen years;
one should know that the quarters will be devoid of inhabitants and shaken by earthquakes.
If the earth quakes during the asterism of Kṛttikā, whether in villages or in cities,
fire will break out repeatedly and burn down dwellings along with their inhabitants.
Black fire, the falling of thunderbolts, smiths, and those who have established their hearths— their dwellings are destroyed, like the elements at the time of universal dissolution.
Those who have been born, those who have grown up, and those who reside in that village—
all these suffer calamity when shaken by an earthquake.
When the earth trembles under Rohiṇī, there is the destruction of all seeds;
the grain that has been sown will not sprout, and there will be difficulty in obtaining fruit.
The fetuses of pregnant women will be severely oppressed,
and the population, overcome by the calamity of famine, will remain with only one-third remaining.
Even kings of great soul, illustrious and foremost among men,
meet with calamity when shaken by an earthquake.
If the earth trembles under Mṛgaśīrṣa, there will be the destruction of medicinal herbs;
physicians, Vedic scholars, potters, and those who perform Soma sacrifices [will suffer].
Those Brahmins who have drunk the Soma juice, as well as forest-dwellers and ascetics—
these all encounter calamity when shaken by an earthquake.
When the earth trembles under Ārdrā, milky trees perish;
food and drink are destroyed, and travelers are protected by fanged beasts.
Those who dig wells, those who dig moats, and those who are evildoers and thieves— these meet with calamity when the earth is shaken by an earthquake.
When the earth trembles under Punarvasu, as do the celestial spheres and the water-jars;
there will be distress for those who live by snares, for water-fowls, for wheel-bearers, and for parrots and mainas.
Children, those who cause confusion, butchers, and conch-shell merchants—
these suffer calamity when shaken by an earthquake.
Under Puṣya, the earth shall tremble, as well as the leading Brāhmaṇas,
those who travel to distant lands, merchants, and those men who are caravan leaders.

Kings, those dwelling in the mountains, and whoever are under their dominion— all these shall encounter calamity when shaken by an earthquake. They shall rain down showers of stones, and there will be a great ruin of the crops.
When Aśleṣā moves, all the earth-dwelling serpents, reptiles,
insects, ants, dogs,
and those wild animals that have only one hoof [shall suffer].
Physicians, snake-charmers, and those beings who dwell in mountain caves—
these suffer calamity when the earth is shaken by an earthquake.
When the earth trembles under the asterism Maghā, a great king suffers there;
likewise, those who are faithful cease their assemblies and festivals.
Sacrifices and all rites for the gods are here brought to completion.
Those who have been born, those who have grown up, and others who are the most eminent scholars,
as well as the gandharvas and men of noble lineage— they all meet with calamity when shaken by an earthquake.
When the earth trembles under the asterism Phalgunī, then the season turns;
a crosswind blows, and the eternal *kṛta* age perishes. Travelers suffer distress, as do those who subsist on the cultivation of beans.
Those who delight in the Dharma, those who live by their seats, and those who subsist on tolls—
these all encounter calamity when the earth is shaken by an earthquake.
When *Uttaraphalgunī* wavers, merchants, those who travel to islands,
chair-makers, and those who live by their crafts are affected.
Aṅga, Videha, Magadha, and the Nairṛtas, along with those who have taken wives as their possession—
these suffer calamity when shaken by an earthquake.
The earth trembled with its hand; the potters and physicians, the leaders of the guilds, the high officials, and those men who were commanders of the army [were shaken].
The Nārapaṭas,
the Vipsaras,
and the Kauṭikas; and also—
These [beings] encounter calamity when shaken by an earthquake.
When the earth trembles under Citrā, artisans, preparers of materials,
young maidens, all kinds of gems, and the seeds of crops shall flourish.
The Vaṅgas, Daśārṇas, Kurus, Cedis, and Māhiṣakas—
these likewise encounter calamity when shaken by an earthquake.

When the Svāti asterism is active, the earth trembles; likewise, thieves, those of immoral conduct, those who are harmful, those devoted to such violent deeds, and beggars who are like rats [will prevail].
To the north, ascetics subsisting on air alone [dwell]; p.113.9cd/.these suffer calamity when shaken by an earthquake.
If the earth should tremble under Viśākhā, there would be the destruction of great mountains;
fierce winds blow there, and the people of Aśmaka become ill-fated.
When Anurādhā is affected, the earth shall tremble and there will be great misfortune for bandits;
likewise, those men who are gamblers, those who practice gambling, and those who are pickpockets [shall suffer].
The Andhras, Puṇḍras, and Pulindas remain in a state of fear, having no refuge.
And at that time, powerful dissension among friends arises in the world.
When the constellation Jyeṣṭhā is active, O Great King, the earth trembles and the great king suffers;
likewise, crows, bulls, predatory beasts, and fierce wild animals [are afflicted].
The Kurus, the Śūrasenas, the Mallas, the Bāhlīkas, the Nigrahas,
those who are swift in hostility, and those who are devoted to them— these all encounter calamity when the earth is shaken by an earthquake.
When the earth is shaken by the *mūla* [constellation], those with four legs as well as those with two,
the grahas, the piśācas, and whatever beings dwell in caves—
all these encounter misfortune when moved by the earthquake.
It quickly brings about famine, and grain will become scarce due to lack of water;
at that time, people on earth will flee to mountain caves and the foot of mountains.
When Pūrvāṣāḍhā wavers, the earth trembles, and aquatic creatures—
fishes, oysters, otters, crocodiles, sea-monsters, and tortoises— are disturbed.
Those who are preeminent by birth and lineage, those who are wealthy and wise,
those of noble second birth, and those who possess great learning—
these all meet with calamity when shaken by an earthquake.
If the earth trembles in the north, there will be great misfortune for artisans;
blacksmiths, architects, tin-workers, and carpenters [will suffer].
The poor and even the wealthy, as well as various artisans—
even these meet with calamity when shaken by an earthquake.
It destroys village huts and everything both moving and stationary.
When the earth trembles in the region of Viṣṇu, then that which is undesirable occurs.
Teachers of the Vedas, scholars of the scriptures, poets, masters of mantras, the Yugandharas, and the Śūrasenas [shall suffer].
The Abhirājas are the Paṭaccaras.
The Kuśaṇḍas and the Śaradaṇḍas— those men who are honored by kings— meet with calamity when shaken by an earthquake.
When the earth trembles under Dhaniṣṭhā, there will be great mental distress for the wealthy;
likewise, the Maheśvaras, the great Nāgas, and the merchants [shall suffer].
The Pracaṇḍas, the Svastimantas, the Bhadrakāras, the Yugandharas,
the Pārikūlas, the Bhojas, and others such as the Sannāgaras—
these all encounter calamity when shaken by an earthquake.
When the earth trembles in the western quarter, there will be great disorder among those living by water;
elephants, horses, donkeys, and camels will suffer terrible affliction.
Then he will afflict the Vīrakas, the Madras, the Bāhlīkas, and the Kekayas; he will also oppress the helpless Cakravākas and the inhabitants of Janasthāna.
When the earth trembles with the sound of goats, it likewise strikes down the Rākṣasas who act as slayers,
as well as sheep-butchers, pork-butchers, and the Sauvīras.
He shall destroy the Vaiśyas who live by trade, as well as the Śūdras, the Karītis, the Yavanas, the Mālavas and others, and the pickpockets.
When Ahibudhnya is [conjoined], the earth trembles and there is great misfortune for merchants;
likewise for those perfected ones who delight in dharma and those engaged in the work of pearl-fishers.
He will soon afflict all the Śibis, Vatsas, Vātsyas, and the Kṣatriyas of the Ārjunāyana clan, as well as the Saindhavas, the Rājanyas, and the Dhanuṣpāṇis.
If the earth trembles during the asterism Revatī, there shall be a most terrible battle;
village raids will occur, and indeed, village will attack village.
He shall utterly consume the seafarers who live by the water, the Ramaṭhas, the Bharukacchas, the Sudhanvanas, the Abhisāras, and all the Sarvasenas.
When the earth trembles under Aśvinī, there is great misfortune for horses;
village massacres occur, and brother seeks to kill brother.
And she who conceives a child here, and those who are born here—
these three shall experience uninterrupted suffering from this point forward for three years.
Those who are united, those with variegated offspring, and whatever other women there may be—
the royal Arjunāyanas— these he indeed destroys thoroughly, even three times over.
When the earth trembles under Bharaṇī, there will be great misfortune for thieves;
likewise, libertines, gamblers, and those men who are cut-purses [will suffer].
Mirror-makers, wheel-makers, gamblers, as well as prison guards,
those who dwell at the outskirts, the sinful, and those wicked men who wander about— they too perish there, shaken by the earthquake.
When the earth trembles,
the immediate sign that follows is that within seven days a desired rain will occur there.
For Indra does not send rain there— [the land] which is moist, resembling collyrium, and like unto a great mountain— in accordance with the word of the Great Seer.
[Thus it has been declared, yet no rain falls here from Indra.
[The clouds] resemble the shape of a svastika and are like the banner of Indra’s thunderbolt.
For clouds are seen at twilight after having swallowed both the moon and the sun.
Then clouds resembling pomegranates arise in the sky;
seeing such a sign, one should know them to be shaken by Indra. That is the instruction therein, according to the word of the Great Seer.
In that place, one should plant all kinds of seeds with the utmost confidence; there, merchants may carry out their business without fear. Among all types of earthquakes, this one is auspicious.
They were shaken by Indra.
When the earth trembles, the following form will immediately appear:
within seven days, a cloud shall cover the sky there.
Then clouds resembling silk (*kauśeya*) arise in succession;
moving toward the western quarter, they proceed in a favorable direction.
At twilight, clouds resembling porpoises, water-fowl, fish, and sea-monsters are seen after having swallowed the moon and the sun.
Having observed such characteristics, one should know those [omens] to be caused by water;
that is the instruction there, according to the word of the Great Seer.
In basins, on mountain peaks, in fields, and in groves, seeds are sown; yet at that time, they truly perish in low-lying places.
By mud, by water, or even by dust, these [effects] may perish;
among these earthquakes, those shaken by water are auspicious.
When the earth trembles, an immediate sign will appear:
within seven days, most terrible winds will blow there.
A tawny twilight is seen, and both the moon and the sun are red;
having observed such a sign, one should know that they have been shaken by the wind.
Then follows the instruction, according to the words of the Great Seer:
"A wise man should not dwell there; he should protect himself in this regard."
One should keep it secret and create obstructions; one should dig walls and moats.
Border regions will fall into conflict, and fear will arise among men.
The shaking of the earth for all these [beings] has been proclaimed as their quality;
specifically for humans, it is produced and shaken by the wind.
When the earth has trembled, the form that follows immediately will be that there shall be most terrible falls of meteors within seven days.
When the twilight glows red and both the moon and the sun appear crimson,
having observed such a sign, one should know that the fires are trembling.
Fire burns through wood as well as protected treasures;
columns of smoke are seen rising, and weapons become excessively heated.
Lutes are seen in the sky for nine months when it does not rain;
among these earthquakes, those shaken by fire are the least significant.
On the forenoon, he conquers the Kṣatriyas and the kings;
at midday, the chief horses, elephants, chariots, and ministers;
and in the afternoon, the cowherds, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
At night, the twilight burns the dwellings of endless thieves.
On this night, at the onset of dusk, he indeed slaughters hosts of Mlecchas;
at the midnight watches, he slays endless women and eunuchs; and in the third watch, he destroys those who subsist on agriculture and trade.
It causes distress to the faction of the gods, O Kṛṣṇā, you who perform fierce deeds that bring about the end.
In the fortnight of the moon, it burns the Brahmin and Kshatriya who perform sacrifices;
it cooks those of pure conduct who are preeminent in dharma;
and indeed, he who studies finds gentleness even toward the learned.
That Brahmin, who has beheld the gods, becomes worthy of honor by kings.
The four [years] of Bṛhaspati are equal to auspicious deeds;
the four [years] of Sūrya are equal to the deeds of Śukra;
the four [years] of Soma and the deeds of Brahmā are likewise equal to them.
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter titled 'The Exposition of Earthquakes.
Now, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter titled 'The Arising of Diseases' concerning these twenty-eight lunar mansions."
Listen to that;
may the Blessed One speak:
a disease arising under the asterism Kṛttikā affects either a woman or a man.
The illness shall last for four nights, and after that, one is liberated from it.
For Agni is the deity there; one should offer him an oblation of curd. By this ritual of offering, one is therefore liberated from that disease.
If a disease arises in a woman or a man under Rohiṇī,
that illness shall last for five nights, after which one is liberated from it.
There, one should offer an oblation with pure garlands to the god Prajāpati;
by this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
If an illness occurs under the asterism Mṛgaśiras, whether affecting a woman or a man, that illness shall last for eight nights; after that, one is liberated from it.
For Soma is the deity there; one should offer a bali-oblation with a *maṇḍa*.
By this offering of a bali, one is liberated from that disease.
(124) A disease arising for either a woman or a man under the constellation Ārdrā shall last for ten nights; thereafter, one is liberated from it.
For Rudra is the deity there; one should offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa).
By means of this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
If a woman or a man should fall ill under the asterism Punarvasu, the illness shall last for eight nights; thereafter, they will be liberated from it.
The deity there is Āditya; one should offer an oblation with perfumes and garlands.
By this rite of oblation, one is liberated from that disease.
A disease that arises under the Puṣya asterism, whether in a woman or a man, will be of short duration; he shall be freed from it after five nights.
The deity there is Bṛhaspati; one should offer an oblation with perfumes and garlands.
By means of this ritual of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
Under Āśleṣā, there will be illness for either a woman or a man;
physicians shall not be able to treat it, for the serpent is the presiding deity there.
A disease arising under the asterism Maghā, whether in a woman or a man, shall last for eight nights; thereafter, one is liberated from it.
The ancestors are the deities there; one should offer an oblation of *kṛsara*.
By means of this ritual of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
One born under Pūrvaphālgunī will suffer from illness, whether it be a woman or a man;
the illness shall last for seven nights, and after that, one is released from it.
Āryamā is the deity there; one should offer an oblation with perfumes and garlands. By this ritual of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
If [the moon] is in Uttarā, there will be illness for either a woman or a man;

physicians shall not be able to treat it, for Bhaga is the deity presiding over this [constellation]. If illness arises even when [the moon is] in Hasta, whether for a woman or a man, [it is incurable].
The illness shall last for five nights, and thereafter one is liberated from it.
For the Sun is the deity there; one should offer an oblation with perfumes and flowers.
By this rite of oblation, one is therefore liberated from that disease.
If a disease arises for either a woman or a man under the asterism Citrā, that illness shall last for eight nights; thereafter, one is liberated from it.
For Tvaṣṭṛ is the deity there; one should offer an oblation of ghee with the *udgītha*.
By this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
If a disease arises under Svāti for either a woman or a man, that affliction shall indeed be troublesome for twenty-five nights.
In this case, the deity shall be Vāyu; one should offer an oblation with variegated garlands.
By means of this rite of oblation, one is liberated from that disease.
Under Viśākhā, there may be illness for either a woman or a man;
that illness will be severe and shall last for nineteen days.
(126) There, one should offer an oblation with perfumes and garlands to the deities Indra and Agni.
By means of this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
A disease arising under Anurādhā affects either a woman or a man;
the illness shall last for half a month, after which one is liberated from it.
For Mitra is the deity there; one should offer an oblation of a vessel of clarified butter.
By this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
If a disease arises in one under the asterism Jyeṣṭhā, whether it be for a woman or a man,
that afflictive illness will indeed persist for thirteen days and nights.
For Indra is the deity there; one should offer an oblation with perfumes and garlands.
By means of this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
A disease that has arisen in the root of either a woman or a man shall indeed last for one month; after that, he is liberated from it.
Nairṛti is the deity there; one should offer an oblation of liquor and meat.
By this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
If it occurs under Pūrvāṣāḍhā, there will be illness for either a woman or a man;
this illness will be distressing and will last for eight months, without a doubt.
The waters are indeed the deity there; one should offer an oblation of *kṛsara*.
By this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
If [the moon] is in Uttarā, there will be illness for either a woman or a man;
the illness shall last for seven nights, and after that, one is released from it.
For Viśva is the deity there; one should offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa).
By this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
(127) A disease arising under the asterism Abhijit affects either a woman or a man;
that illness may persist for six months, after which one is liberated from it.
Viṣṇu is the deity there; one should offer curd-whey as the sacrificial oblation (*bali*).
By means of this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
A disease that arises for either a woman or a man upon hearing [this] will indeed be a severe illness lasting for a full twelve months.
For Viṣṇu is the deity there; one should offer an oblation with perfumes and garlands.
By this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
Under Dhaniṣṭhā, there will be illness for either a woman or a man;
indeed, that illness shall be severe for thirteen full months.
The Vasus are the deities there; one should offer an oblation with ghee and garlands.
By this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
A disease arising under Śatabhiṣaj affects either a woman or a man;
it lasts for thirteen days, and thereafter one is liberated from it.
Varuṇa is the deity there; one should offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa).
By means of this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
A disease arising from Pūrvabhādrapadā, whether in a woman or a man, cannot be cured by physicians; Ahirbudhnya is the presiding deity in this case.
If Uttarabhādrapadā is [the asterism], there will be illness for either a woman or a man;
the illness shall last for seven nights, and after that, one is released from it.
Āryamā is the deity there; one should offer an oblation with perfumes and garlands.
By this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
A disease that arises under Revatī, whether in a woman or a man,
will be mild and shall last for twenty-eight nights.
For Pūṣan is the deity there; one should offer an oblation with perfumes and garlands.
By means of this rite of offering, one is liberated from that disease.
A disease that arises under Aśvinī, whether in a woman or a man,
will be a distressing illness lasting for twenty-five nights.
The Gandharva is the deity there; one should offer a bali-oblation with barley gruel. By this performance of the bali-rite, one is liberated from that disease.
A disease that arises under the asterism Bharaṇī, whether in a woman or a man, cannot be cured by physicians; Yama is the presiding deity there.
A wise person should guard their moral conduct, for through that they will go to heaven.
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter called 'The Arising of Disease. [Now follows] the Liberation from Bondage.
Furthermore, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter called 'Liberation from Bondage.'"
Let that be heard;
may the Blessed One speak.

"O Puṣkarasārin, if someone is bound or obstructed under the asterism Kṛttikā, it should be said: 'He will be released within three nights. If bound or obstructed under Rohiṇī, he will be released within three nights.
If bound or obstructed under Mṛgaśiras, he will be released within twenty-one nights."
If one is bound or obstructed under Ārdrā, one will be released within half a month;
if under Punarvasu, within seven nights;
if under Puṣya, within three nights.
In Aśleṣā, [one succeeds] in thirty nights;
in Maghā, in sixteen nights;
in Citrā, in seven nights.
In Svāti, [he is freed] in ten nights;
in Viśākhā, in twenty-six nights;
in Anurādhā, in thirty-one nights.
In Jyeṣṭhā, it is accomplished in eighteen nights;
in Mūla, in thirty-six nights;
and in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, in fourteen nights.
In Uttarāṣāḍhā, it takes fourteen nights;
in Abhijit, six nights;
and in Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā, and Revatī [the same applies].
In fourteen nights;
under Aśvinī, in three nights;
under Bharaṇī, it should be declared that he will suffer affliction, whether bound or imprisoned.
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter entitled 'Liberation from Bondage.
Now, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter on the *tilaka*."
Let that be heard;
may the Blessed One speak.
If she has a fine, smooth mole upon her head that is the color of a lotus, a king shall be her husband in this world; they say there is a reflection above her breasts.

If she has a tiny mole on her forehead, resembling the color of powdered collyrium, her husband shall indeed be a commander-in-chief; moreover, there shall be a reflection [of this mark] between her breasts.
If there is a tilaka-mark between her eyebrows, they say that woman is a woman of ill-conduct;
she shall have exactly five husbands and obtain abundant food and drink.

If a woman has a reflection of a mole (*tilaka*) on the upper part of her cheek near the nose, they say that woman will be a partaker of sorrow; they call such a reflection a "hair-region" (*romapradeśa*).
If there is a mole or curl upon her ear, they say that woman is highly learned;
she is both highly learned and a retainer of what she has heard if there is a reflection [of her face] upon her nape.
If a woman has a mole or a freckle on her upper lip, they say that woman is one whose truth is broken;
she indeed obtains her livelihood only with great difficulty. They say that there is a mole on her thigh as well.
If there is a mole or a curl upon her lower lip, they say that woman is a woman of loose conduct;
she obtains much sweet food and drink, for likewise there is a reflection [of this] in the private parts.
If there should be a mole or a curl on her chin, they say that woman is a woman of loose conduct;
she shall obtain much sweet food and drink, and there should be a second reflection [of the navel] at the secret place.
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter named 'The Chapter on the Tilakas.
Now then, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter named 'The Qualities of Birth under the Lunar Mansions';
let it be heard."
"May your honor speak, Triśaṅku:
A man born under Kṛttikā will be radiant, fond of daring deeds, brave, fierce, and a speaker of pleasant words."
A man born under Rohiṇī is wealthy and likewise righteous;
he is industrious, steadfast, and brave, and his face is always bright.
A man born under Mṛgaśiras is gentle and mild;
he shall be handsome and especially beloved by women.
One born under Ārdrā is violent by nature, fierce, and excessively talkative; he will perform cruel deeds, yet he may become a great lord over hundreds of people.
A man born under Punarvasu who is not fickle and possesses intelligence shall be virtuous in character, yet that person may also be prone to anger.
A man born under Puṣya shall be radiant and become a Brāhmaṇa;
he may also become a Kṣatriya king, or a Vaiśya or Śūdra who is highly honored.
A man born under Aśleṣā is a breath-controller, prone to anger, and cruel; he is a wicked man and fierce—
one should predict all such traits for him here.
A man born under Maghā shall be possessed of great wisdom, be devout, likewise very fortunate, wealthy, abundant in grain, and an enjoyer of pleasures.
Any man who is born under Pūrvaphalgunī will be half-witted, of poor character, and one who violates the wives of his teachers.
One born under Uttaraphalgunī becomes possessed of enjoyments;
such a person shall be endowed with divine knowledge regarding discernment and be fortunate.
Born under Hasta, he is pure-souled, valiant, and moderate in eating;
he holds the office of commander-in-chief and shall be one whose actions are free from theft.
A man born under Citrā will have beautiful eyes, be a storyteller of wonderful tales, handsome, possess many wives, and be of diverse character.
A man born under Svāti is a kinsman, light-handed, and discerning;
he is gentle, fond of drink, a maker of friends, and reflective.
A man born under Viśākhā will be radiant, wealthy, and great;
he shall be heroic, valorous, skillful, and fortunate.
A mortal born under Anurādhā is a man who possesses friends and is a gatherer of people;
he shall be pure, grateful, and righteous in soul.
A man born under Jyeṣṭhā becomes possessed of friends;
he delights in the science of archery and sets his heart upon women.
A man born under the Mūla nakṣatra will be ungrateful and unrighteous;
yet that person will also be steadfast, heroic, and sinful.
If [the moon] is in the former Āṣāḍhās, that man will be envious, have unsteady senses, be fond of fish and meat, and be a killer.
A man born under Viśvadeva is compassionate, generous, devoted to knowledge, and a friend to all people; this is indeed certain.
A man who is a teacher, an author of treatises, trustworthy, and devoted to ritual action,
as well as one born under Śravaṇā, shall be long-lived, illustrious, and prosperous.
A man born under Dhaniṣṭhā will have an unstable mind, be fond of various material objects, and be suspicious of everything.
If a man is born under the lunar mansion of Vāruṇa,
he will be harsh, of a wrathful disposition, and a detractor in every respect.
A man born here under the former Bhādrapadā is endowed with virtuous conduct and qualities, is grateful, and likewise eloquent.
A man born under the asterism Uttarā will be discerning,
intelligent, possessed of many offspring, virtuous in character, and very wealthy.
A man born under Revatī is righteous in nature and a servant to his kinsmen;
though always poor and possessing little wealth, he is a giver and free from envy.
A man born under Aśvinī becomes exceedingly wise;
he is beloved by the great multitude, as well as brave and fortunate.
A man born under Bharaṇī is of wicked conduct and lacking in discernment; he is intent on amorous dalliance and lives off others.
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter called 'The Qualities of Birth under the Constellations.
O Triśaṅku, recite the chapter called 'The Wheel of Portents,' and he shall explain it."
U1. The Exposition on the Wheel of Portents (Utpātacakra-nirdeśa).
U1.1ab. Within the entire circle of constellations, extending to its twenty-eight limits, U1.1cd.
divine portents are observed among the sun, the moon, the planets, and so forth.
If, during the first fortnight of the month of Māgha, there is thunder from a mountain or from the earth, or if there is a rain of smoke while the sun is shining;
If lightning is seen rising at dawn, then one should know that there will be a destruction of people.
If smoke issues forth from the sun while it is in Aśvinī, it shall even obscure [the sky];
one should then know that there will be no rain for twelve full years.
If, in the month of Māgha, the sun is seen yellow while in the asterism Bharaṇī, the kingdom will be besieged on all sides; one should predict famine in its midst.
If, during the month of Phālguna, there is a trench [dug] under the constellation Kṛttikā while the sun is present,
the market towns (karvaṭas) therein will perish if the god does not send rain.
When the sun is seen in its dark phase during the month of Caitra under the Puṣya asterism,
at the time of its recent rising, the protector of the earth is besieged.
If, in the month of Vaiśākha, during the asterism Ārdrā, the sun appears as a reflected sun (pratisūryaka),
one should know that a battle will occur there and both kings will be slain.
If the moon or the sun should be eclipsed during the month of Jyeṣṭha while the moon is in the asterisms of Bharaṇī or Jyeṣṭhā,
the king, along with his ministers, shall be slain, and one should predict famine in the kingdom.
When the sun is in Āṣāḍhā and situated in Pūrvabhādrapadā,
if at evening a wound appears excessively red upon its orb;
Then that kingdom will be oppressed by a foreign army for six months;
and the protector of the earth, along with his ministers, sons, and wives, shall be slain.
If the moon is eclipsed in Āṣāḍha under either Pūrvāṣāḍhā or Uttarāṣāḍhā,
one should know that famine, strife, and diseases will be predicted therein.
Furthermore, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, when the moon and sun do not shine during the Mūla asterism,
and sparks are seen there, one should know that there will be great fear of disease.
In the month of Āśvayuja, when the moon and the sun are eclipsed during the same fortnight,
there shall then be a destruction of thousands of princes.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, the moon is without its characteristic marks and devoid of luster;
both the sun and the moon appear the color of fire in the red-hued sky.
That kingdom shines like the sun, yet it shall perish again and again;
one should know that for slain kings, the earth indeed drinks their blood.
If, in the month of Māgha, a black wind arises under the asterism Bharaṇī and quickly obscures both the moon and the sun, the kingdom will perish.
In the month of Phālguna, if there is a wind accompanied by a rain of dust and lightning,
former kings are slain and others are established in their place.
If at that time any planet moves together with the sun or the moon,
or if the wind blows in an irregular manner, one should know that there will then be the death of the king.
If a thunderbolt or a meteor rises together with the sun during the month of Vaiśākha,
one should predict calamity for the kingdom within six months.
When the sun emerges from its eclipse in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
then all the planets are afflicted by that solar affliction.
If dust falls during the month of Jyeṣṭha and the sun is surrounded by a halo,
it portends that one among thousands of rulers of the earth will perish.
But one is slain.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, winds blow while the moon is situated in Bharaṇī;
the wells dry up and all the crops wither away.
If in the month of Śrāvaṇa the winds are yellow and the expanse of the sky is always black,
one should recognize that danger has arisen from all sides.
If fire rains down during the month of Śrāvaṇa, or during the day of Pūrvabhādrapadā, the clouds will produce a loud noise; one should predict disease and famine.
When the month of Bhādrapada has a sky covered with clouds and thunder,
then a foreign army will seize the accumulation of wealth within the kingdom.
If, in the month of Āśvayuja, a wind and rain come from the northern direction and cause a violent downpour,
the entire kingdom will be struck by calamity and perish.
When the moon is in Sagittarius on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the kingdom perishes on all sides; one should predict famine in its midst.
If meteors fall or thunderbolts strike during the month of Māgha in the region of Aśvinī, the people there will be destroyed by fear of horses.
If, during the month of Phālguna,
there should be a shower of fire from the sky accompanied by a sound in the atmosphere, that kingdom will quickly perish.
If, during the month of Caitra under the asterism Svāti, rain is obstructed or accompanied by wind,
and a rainbow is seen, that city will soon perish.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, if a sound should arise from the north during the asterism Bharaṇī,
the sky will appear yellow in color, and there will be fear of an enemy army.
If, moreover, lightning is seen in the sky during the month of Āṣāḍha under the Puṣya asterism,
the people will be released from [misfortune] by three parts through rains accompanied by grass and water.
