When, during the month of Śrāvaṇa, much rain falls under the asterism Mūla and a rainbow is seen there,
it portends great fear for the Kṣatriyas.
If a thunderbolt falls upon the earth during the month of Bhādrapada,
harsh winds blow and there is then great fear of disease.
In the month of Bhādrapada, when Puṣya is the lunar mansion, if a sound issues from the intermediate directions,
the Kṣatriya will soon become agitated, and the subjects will be oppressed by their enemies.
If a sound occurs above in the asterisms of Bharaṇī or Aśvinī,
and one should cast dust along with grass, there will be great danger for ascetics.
If, however, in the month of Kārttika, when the moon is in Ārdrā, a terrifying sound is heard,
one should predict death there for the four-footed livestock of the farmers.
If, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the sound of musical instruments should arise in the sky during the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā,
then a terrible disease will afflict the kingdom, causing distress from wind.
When a terrifying sound occurs in the month of Pauṣa during the asterism Svāti,
and lightning flashes repeatedly in the sky, there is great danger for the learned.
If a thunderclap occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, the earth will always be pacified;
however, one should know that in the third year, there will be total upheaval throughout the kingdom.
If, in the month of Phālguna, during the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra,
there is a wind agitated by darkness and the earth trembles repeatedly, then there will be danger for those practicing celibacy (brahmacārins).
If, however, during the month of Caitra, the earth should tremble by day under the asterism Pūrvabhādrapadā,
then in that year and in that kingdom there will be great fear from enemy armies.
If the moon remains motionless during the night of the *Pūrvāṣāḍhā* constellation in the month of Caitra,
the king will be slain by swords and the great multitude of people will perish.
If the earth trembles frequently during the dark fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha,
one should predict famine due to drought for six months.
If, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the asterism of Bharaṇī, the earth should tremble by day,
one should know that the ground will drink the blood of thousands of warriors.
When the earth trembles at night during the month of Jyeṣṭha under the asterism Mūla, a frontier king is slain; one should impose a heavy tax upon the kingdom.
If the earth trembles in the month of Āṣāḍha when the moon is situated in the Puṣya constellation,
the crops will perish there and strife and wicked deeds will arise.
When the shrines tremble during the asterisms of Ārdrā or Maghā,
or when they blaze or fall down, then the kingdom will soon perish.
Where the shrines tremble, laugh, and bow down,
there the king, together with his kingdom, shall soon meet with destruction.
If the earth trembles during the month of Śrāvaṇa while the moon is situated in Pūrvabhādrapadā,
the king will be constantly defeated, and thieves will be executed within the kingdom.
If, in the month of Kārttika, a shrine (caitya) collapses due to an earthquake,
or if the gate of a city [collapses], then the population will mostly perish.
If Jupiter should stand at the waning horn of the moon in the north,
those of great enjoyment who are illustrious lords of the earth shall perish.
When the planet Mars ascends the horns of the sun and the moon,
one should predict suffering for the border regions due to the influence of cruel-eyed sorcerers.
When Saturn ascends the peak of the Moon,
then a terrible fear of disease should be known to arise, and one should predict famine in that situation.
When the moon is seized by Rāhu and struck by a meteor,
one should predict misfortune for the king within six months.
Furthermore, on whichever lunar mansion the moon or the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu,
the kings along with their kingdoms shall suffer affliction.
If a comet enters the lunar mansion of the King (Pūrvaphalgunī),
one should predict a conflict with weapons against neighboring kings.
When Venus enters the middle of the moon while the moon is in Phālgunī or Maghā, all grains will wither; at that time, one should predict disease.
When Jupiter, Venus, Mars,
and Saturn draw lines upon the horn of the moon, one should then know that there is great danger.
The highly fortunate Dhūmaketu stands positioned upon Puṣya;
at that time, he shall scour the four quarters and bring about defeat by the enemy armies.
If Mars should remain in Maghā, or Jupiter in Śravaṇā,
for three years, one should know that there will be fear extending across the entire ocean.
If Venus should somehow remain in Rohiṇī during the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one must predict with certainty that there will be great danger for the Kṣatriyas.
When Jupiter and Saturn are situated near Viśākhā,
or when the Moon is together with the Sun [in that asterism], there is then fear of an enemy army.
Crows, hawks, and cranes will dwell together in joy;
they will engage in sexual intercourse even when forbidden, and then there will be conflict with others.
A hawk may repeatedly alight upon the elephant's dwelling,
and there may also be repeated battles with the enemy army.
Where a girl gives birth with four hands and four breasts,
there shall indeed be a most terrible death for the women alone.
Where fetuses in the womb laugh and speak,
one should know that the destruction of that region is at hand.
Where women give birth to children with one foot, three feet, or likewise four limbs,
one should predict misfortune for the king.
In whatever region women give birth to deformed fetuses, to offspring with terrifying features,
there the king perishes.
Where women give birth to those with small hands, heads, and faces who have taken on human bodies,
there the kingdom perishes.
Where asses and buffaloes, as well as other such beasts,
are born with two or three heads, that country perishes.
In whatever land men are born with the forms of jackals, dogs, crocodiles, or horses,
that land quickly perishes.
When both feet of a pregnant Vaiśya woman are born first,
one should predict the destruction of the country through a terrible invasion by a foreign army.
If the embryo of a bird or a serpent is born in the first half [of the month],
the king or the king’s minister, along with the country, perishes.
Where a *kumbhāṇḍa* is born with two faces or four faces,
or even with three eyes or three mouths, one should know that there is great danger in that place.
If a human body is struck by a hog-like curved [meteor],
it will undoubtedly destroy the kingdom and its people in all four directions.
When a human is born with the form of the sun,
the entire kingdom, through delusion, goes to its destruction.
But if a child lying on its back sees an excellent twice-born man in a certain place reciting the Vedas, that place will quickly perish.
When the child, having burst through the womb, emerges from the womb by himself,
making his helpless mother his refuge, that region quickly perishes.
If pigs,
camels, snakes,
and birds are born from the wombs of women, one should predict danger for the region.
If cows give birth to a human, a donkey, or a pig, or to a half-formed creature, one should predict that danger has arrived.
If a woman conceives a fetus while her breasts have not yet appeared,
one should predict the destruction of that region along with its king.
Where one with matted hair, long nails, very black and coarse skin is born together with his kinsmen, that kingdom along with its ruler shall be consumed by fire.
Where children are born without necks but with teeth,
all crops will wither and the people will go to their destruction. Furthermore, where a fetus is born with only one arm or no head at all, [the same calamity follows].
That kingdom will itself become agitated and will undoubtedly perish.
When one sees fruit upon fruit, or flowers resting upon flowers,
women shall suffer miscarriages and the crown prince shall be put to death.
Where trees flower and bear fruit out of season,
or where creepers, shrubs, or climbing vines do so, there will be danger in that region.
If one should see one's own blood flowing from atop a tree,
or if one sees a bird shrieking, then one should know that there is great danger.
The shadows of trees or pavilions do not shift;
there, fear among the four castes and the deeds of the Kali age arise.
Where trees are in bloom with various kinds of flowers,
one should know that there is great danger from the nature of the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*).
When flowers and even fruits are seen that do not turn back [from their stalks],
one should declare the destruction of that region, as well as famine and strife.
If trees are seen anywhere, having shifted from their proper places to improper places,
the king who was previously established will not long remain in his position.
One shall behold a battle between the gods and the asuras of wondrous appearance;
there, weapons will become blunted, and likewise by thieves, as before.
If the Teacher trembles or weeps as he goes, or wherever he is seen,
one should know that from that time on there will be a total defeat by the enemy's army.
In whatever place the deities dance and laugh,
or shed tears, one should then know that there is great danger.
Wherever deities play, or flash, or blink their eyes,
or wherever they might tremble, then another king shall arise.
When the Śiva-liṅga trembles, or is seen in the sky,
or sinks into the earth, there will certainly be the death of the king.
Images will shift, emit smoke, and weep;
they may perspire or run about, for another king shall arise.
The immovable may move from its place, or the moving may become immovable;
in such a case, one should predict that a minister will kill the king and that strife will arise therein.
If maidens vomit blood, or if they bow down toward the ten directions,
or if they move about improperly, there will be great danger for the Kṣatriyas.
Where it rains flowers, or even drops of blood,
or where various living beings appear, one should know that there will then be fear of thieves.
When ancient sacrificial posts, sacred scriptures, temples, shrines,
and cities are enveloped in smoke, the king will soon perish.
If the moon, or a lamp-tree, or a lamp does not shine there,
a prince desiring the kingdom, or even a minor official, shall be agitated.
When honey-bees build a nest within the inner apartments,
or when a weapon or even a house is consumed by fire, one should predict calamity for the king.
If lightning should strike within the inner apartments, or upon a tree in a hermitage,
or upon the shadow of a sacred tree (*caitya*) in the city, it has indeed fallen for the sake of the king.
If a crow builds its nest upon a rampart, in an armory, or at the gateway of a city, the king, along with his ministers, shall perish.
If sound should issue forth spontaneously from drums that have not been struck,
the entire kingdom will be plundered due to the fault of the agitation of one's own wheel.
When rain falls as showers of flesh and blood, or as leaves, flowers, and fruits,
that rain signifies the kingdom will be plundered by the [conquering] wheels.
Honey, molasses, and flowers, or even rains of perfumes,
as well as the burning of the quarters— these shall be seen as the signs of Māra’s famine.
If clouds thunder on all sides and rain down along with lightning,
and if there be blood mixed with hailstones, then one should know that there will be danger from an enemy.
When a terrible lightning bolt strikes and there is a rain of hailstones,
and when one sees a city of the Gandharvas, one should know that there is great danger.
When the moon resembles blood in color, dark in its center,
and discolored at its periphery, one should know that the kingdom will be afflicted by great fear.
When the moon is seen resembling a blazing fire,
then the sky is consumed by flames and the world suffers from fever.
When that which resembles red ochre quickly subsides,
one should know that rain is approaching, provided the wind blows [in the proper manner].
If, during the twilight when it is of a smoky color, both the moon and the sun should be seen separated by the form of Brahmā, one should predict rain there for that year.
He does not sink in water, nor does he burn in fire, and as before, he is not seen.
Yet, a fire will arise there and it will consume his storehouse.
Wherever a crow flaps its wings at the top of a banner, one should quickly fetch water; for there is a very great danger from fire.
If the water itself burns fiercely and a fish consumes it,
one should then predict drought, famine, and great terror.
When a wild forest deer should come of its own accord to the city gate,
one should predict famine in both divisions of the realm and the outbreak of disease within the kingdom.
When a snake with three heads or five heads is seen,
one should know that there will then be no rain and all the crops will perish.
When a granary is seen shaking the earth,
storehouses and other accumulations of wealth shall perish;
and a serpent with its head raised fights together with men.
One should know that from the two wheels and from disease there is great danger in that case.
If many snakes are seen well-concealed together in a single hole,
one should know that there will be death by the sword and great terror for the Kṣatriyas.
When swords, blazing with light, emerge from their scabbards upon focused concentration,
then one shall soon behold battle approaching.
If a crow, a hawk, or a vulture should alight upon someone's head,
within six months the king, along with his domestic priest, shall die.
The palaces, shrines, and houses tremble;
and the protector of the kingdom, though possessing great strength, shall be slain.
When all the directions are torn asunder by thunderbolts during the dark fortnight across the four quarters,
and blood rains down there, the ruler of the earth shall be slain.
When a great meteor falls at the time of sunrise,
the earth shall drink the blood of thousands of princes.
If trees and serpents tremble, or if they shed their skins,
one should know that there will be great danger from enemies throughout the entire kingdom.
If, indeed, during the day a blazing meteor is seen to be discharged,
one should know that there will then be the emergence of blood and a battle of terrifying appearance.
One should see a blazing sword, as well as a lance and a discus; one should know that when weapons appear [in dreams], they portend a battle of terrifying aspect.
If the horse breathes deeply and long, sheds tears,
or quickly drags with its hoof, the death of the king in battle is certain.
If a crow, having climbed onto a house, caws "Alas, my son!",
then the entire region— including its cities, villages, and market towns— will perish.
When smoke arises where there is no fire, or when lotuses grow upon dry land,
one should predict the imminent destruction of that region with certainty.
When clouds and likewise wolves and wild beasts utter terrible cries,
one should know that the destruction of that region is swiftly at hand.
Even rivers whose currents have been cut off may continue to flow for a long time;
likewise, houses may remain dry even when their water supply is exhausted—therein lies the danger.
When rivers flow against their currents without being obstructed,
one should indicate that the inhabited lands will be constantly agitated and that there will be a destruction of the people.
When bows being drawn emit smoke and even burst into flames,
or when another weapon appears [against them], fear arises from one's enemies.
When a halo resembling the neck of a peacock appears around the moon,
one should know that thousands of kings will drink the blood of the earth.
Neither for men nor for women does joy or delight arise;
everywhere there is grief and anxiety, and great fear will prevail there.
If virtuous sages depart from a region, whether by crossing a river or passing through its groves, that land will perish before long. (Uttaragītā 1.141cd)
Where the medicinal herbs have lost their potency and the water dries up, one should know that such a place has been abandoned by the gods, sages, and virtuous men.
Where fish, tortoises, and snakes, as well as wild animals, die,
there the husband’s wealth shall be plundered by his wife’s rivals.
If birds never seen before are seen on land or even in the water,
or if they are seen by an enemy army, a great mass of wealth will be destroyed.
When the great highway becomes a trackless path due to overgrown thickets,
the kingdom, along with its villages and market towns, perishes together with its prince.

one born under Svāti will be greedy, a hater of virtues, and indeed unlearned.

The wise man, a hero who has conquered his enemies, is constantly devoted to happiness;

If a tilaka mark is seen on the forehead of one born under Uttarāṣāḍhā,

Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, as well as life and death—

In that case, sesame seeds that are crushed or scorched are said to be of that [inferior] form; likewise, those with the color and appearance of boils or pustules are recorded as being called "piṭakas."

Indeed, [a mole] on the head brings wealth, grain, beauty, and good fortune.
One should know that injury to the eyebrows occurs [thereby], while the joining of the eyebrows portends the acquisition of a woman.
A boil in the region of the eye makes one pleasing to behold;
in the area of the eyes and eyebrows it leads to grief; on the cheek, the death of a son is certain.

for it is indeed like a flower appearing in a single spot upon the teeth and the nails.
One should know from its appearance in the heart that there will be a meeting with brothers and sons;
from its appearance in the belly, one should predict the giving of wealth, and from its appearance at the navel, the acquisition of a wife.
One should know that misfortune and indeed immorality reside in the hips of a woman;
however, the birth of a son occurs in the testicles, while a beautiful wife resides in the penis.
If there is a pimple at the end of the back, one will experience happiness; if it is on the buttocks, there will be loss of wealth.
Pimples arising on the thighs, however, bestow both wealth and good fortune.
One should know that there is fear of enemies at the knees, and likewise, the loss of wealth; at the joint of the knee and at the penis,
one should recognize victory, the acquisition of knowledge, and the birth of a son.
The gain of a woman occurs at the chest, while another [gain] is useless;
however, at the shanks, there is service to others, and one enjoys [wealth] from a foreign land.

Those that are established, stable, ulcerous, fissured, as well as those recently formed,
and those resembling the "Dharma-stake"— all these are known as *piṭakas*.

Chapter Four: On Dreams.
Regarding the results of dreams that have been declared as auspicious or inauspicious: he who, at the end of a dream, beholds deities, Brahmins, cows, or a blazing fire, his family shall prosper.
But he who, at the end of a dream, sees royal food, an elephant, a horse, gold, or even a bull, his household prospers. [He also sees] cranes, parrots, swans, curlews, and white birds.
But he who sees his own family in a dream, his household indeed prospers; likewise,
he sees crops that are abundant, fresh, and fragrant,
as well as lotus ponds in full bloom and jars filled to the brim.
He who, at the end of a dream, sees clear water and various kinds of flowers, his family prospers.
Whether a blow is dealt with a weapon, a bow, or even with the hand, the foot, or the knee,
the garment of that person against whom it is struck shall increase in size.
He who, at the end of a dream, beholds Tārā and the Moon, the Sun, the lunar mansions, and likewise the planets, his family shall prosper.
He who, at the end of a dream, mounts the back of a horse, the shoulder of an elephant, various vehicles, or couches, shall attain great sovereignty.
One who has fallen may ascend again, and while remaining there, he awakens;
this should be indicated for the sake of attaining sovereignty, wealth, and the recovery of lost gains.
He who, in a dream, mounts a chariot drawn by a yoke of oxen, or a horse,
and while remaining there awakens,
attains sovereign power.
The man who climbs a precipice or even a mountain,
and while remaining there awakens,
attains sovereign power.
Whether it be a seat, a bed, a vehicle, the body, or a house—
destruction follows for those whose ascent is auspicious, yet from their very ascent there is prosperity; for those whose ascent brings faults, from their ascent virtues arise.
If one cuts off the head of a three-headed being, there shall be a reward of three thousand;
if one eats the head, one obtains a kingdom or a hundred thousand.
If one sees a dried-up river or lake, or enters an empty house,
or finds a dried-up well in a dream, one will certainly experience fear.
If one sees a jackal, a naked human, an iguana, a scorpion, a pig,
or a goat in a dream, one should predict suffering from disease.
If one sees a crow, a hawk, an owl, a vulture, or even a quail,
or a peacock, in a dream, one should predict misfortune for that person.
If one sees oneself naked, or indeed covered with dust,
or smeared with mud, one will encounter the affliction of disease.
Furthermore, having seen in a dream eunuchs, women, thieves, gamblers, those of immoral conduct, wandering performers, or rogues, one will certainly experience fear.
A person who voids urine or excrement while wearing a garment,
or who performs anointment with fragrant unguents at the end of sleep, falls ill.
If at the end of a dream one sees a banner, a parasol, or a canopy being held aloft,
then even while remaining there, one should predict that he will attain great sovereignty.
But he whose city is surrounded on all sides by intestines,
and who swallows the moon and the sun, should be predicted to possess great sovereignty.
If, at the end of a dream, one swallows a man or a portion of land,
or if one swallows this lake or the ocean, one shall attain great sovereignty.
If one obtains a bow, a weapon, a blade, red ornaments, a banner,
or armor in a dream, one should predict the acquisition of wealth.

If one sees in a dream a precipice, a mountain, a palm tree, a bull, an elephant, a horse, an arched gateway, a city, a door, or the moon and sun along with the stars falling down, one should predict calamity for kings.
The rising of the moon and the sun seen in a dream is praised;
however, seeing their setting, one should predict calamity for the king.
If a man climbs a tree in a cremation ground, a sacrificial post,
an anthill, or a heap of ashes in a dream, one should predict misfortune for him.
If a woman dressed in black clothes desires a man in a dream while wearing a garland of oleander flowers, that is the end of his life.
If one enters darkness in a dream, or likewise [enters] the abode of Śambhu or the immortals;
or if one falls from a tree in a dream, one should predict death for that person.
If one sees trees, wood,
or even grass withering in a dream, or if one's head or body [is severed], one should predict his death.
Wherever the god rains, or wherever a thunderbolt falls,
or wherever the earth trembles— in such a dream, one should predict calamity.
If, in a dream, one sees the moon and the sun broken or split apart,
or fallen or falling, his sight shall perish.
Seeing a woman clad in saffron robes, shaven-headed, wearing soiled garments, or dressed in blue and red clothes,
one encounters distress.
Having obtained iron, copper, bronze, silver, or collyrium in a dream, a person suffers the loss of wealth. (4.33cd)
If she awakens while singing, laughing, or dancing,
or while musical instruments are being played, one should indicate that there will be exhaustion in that situation.
If one sinks into mud, mire, or sand,
or if while staying there one awakens, one encounters disease.
Or one might play at dice with eight-sided pieces or other such games for victory or defeat;
or one might play with unfavorable marks, or having seen [such things] in a dream, discord is certain.
Whether it be a seat, a bed, a vehicle, a garment, an ornament, or a house— when these are lost, ruined, or decayed,
one experiences great distress.
A man who drinks surā, maireya, sugar-based liquors, fermented spirits,
or honey-wine in a dream experiences exhaustion.
When one does not see one's own reflection in clear water or in a mirror, the aggregate of the elements (skandha-nyāsa) will certainly arise for that person; of this there is no doubt.
If the god rains incessantly, or if he rains water,
dust, or even glowing embers, one should predict death in that case.
One should recognize that in such a region there will be slaughter of people and great terror;
one should predict an invasion by a foreign army from the appearance of ropes or nets in a dream.
If, in a dream, a city is surrounded on all sides by water,
or by a net, or by something else, there will be the emergence of a hostile army.
A man whose limbs are smeared with oil and mud, who possesses a red throat and a [red] cord, sings and laughs; one should predict that he will receive a blow.
If a woman dressed in black— whether wet or soiled—
embraces a man in a dream, one should predict his imprisonment.
If a black snake climbs upon a man in a dream,
or even if it should coil its body around his limbs, one should predict that he will suffer imprisonment.
If a man is surrounded by creepers, clusters of stumps, or mechanical devices at the end of his dream, one should predict his imprisonment.
If all mechanical devices or snares and traps should break at the end of one's dream, that person is liberated from bondage.
He who, at the end of a dream, beholds uneven terrain, depressions, mountains, and cities, is swiftly liberated from suffering.
Whether it be a *pūtana*, a *piśāca*, a wanton woman, or one who is filthy— having seen such forms in a dream, discord is certain.
If one sees in a dream a man or a woman who is well-bathed, well-attired, fragrant, and dressed in white garments, there will be great happiness.
If grass, a tree, or even wood growing there is seen,
whether in the house or in the field, there will soon be a loss of wealth.
Whether sitting upon an auspicious seat or lying upon a well-prepared bed,
a man obtains a woman, or a woman obtains a man.
If a man sees a white garment, anointed with white perfumes,
at the end of his dream, one should predict for him the acquisition of a woman.
But he who sees food and likewise ornaments bound with fetters,
that man obtains a wife, or that woman obtains a husband.
Having obtained a girdle, an ear-ornament, a garland, or the jewelry of women,
a man shall find a wife, and a woman shall find a husband.
That woman who greets an elephant, a bull, a serpent, the moon, the sun with its stars, or her husband, shall soon obtain her husband.
If any one of these enters the womb of a woman,
she will, in due time, give birth to a glorious son with all his limbs fully developed.
And the fruits were all complete, and the forests were green.
At the end of her dream, a woman obtains [a boon] and gives birth to a glorious son.
If a woman obtains in a dream an utpala, a kumuda, a padma, or a puṇḍarīka lotus together with its bud, she shall give birth to a glorious son.
If a woman, in a dream, receives a gift or sees the end of a thread with a ball of clay attached therein, she too shall give birth to a son; however,
if she sees a vessel or a staff, she gives birth to a daughter.
Furthermore, if one sees even one's own young wife withering away from the summer heat,
or likewise sees her dried up in a dream, there will be death within one's own faction.
If one's arms, eyes, or even fingers increase in size,
one's kinsmen will prosper and the death of enemies will occur.
If one's arms are bound, or if one's vision becomes confused,
or if one's arm should fall off, there will be death within one's own faction.
Whether it be a god or a departed spirit (preta), if he gives a garment or fruits to a woman in a dream, a son shall be born to her.
Whether he is drawn away, weeping, naked, or moreover, soiled, emaciated,
or [exhibiting] anger—
one should indicate [the omen].
If one obtains in a dream a hide, a mechanical device, a calculation, a peg, or even a piece of inspissated milk, one should know for certain that the acquisition of clothing will surely occur.
Whether it be a non-human being, a king, a god, a deceased person, or a brahmin who speaks to you in a dream, the matter shall come to pass exactly as they say.
That which was previously contemplated, that which one recollects upon seeing it, and that which one sees extensively; [all these are objects of consciousness].
Just as one who has set out on a path awakens from a dream,
so too does he encounter a treacherous road or a dangerous precipice.
Having extinguished a blazing, heated fire, one is praised;
the building of houses is commended, but their demolition is not praised.
A cloudless sky is praised; one with clouds is not commended.
Clear water is auspicious; turbid water is not praised.
Traveling on a journey is auspicious; turning back anywhere is not.
Seeing gold is auspicious; possessing it is not praised.
The sight of meat is auspicious, but its consumption is not praised; the sight of liquor is commended, but its drinking is not praised.
Green earth is praised; discolored earth is not commended. Ascending a vehicle is praised; falling from it is not commended.
In dreams, weeping is auspicious, while laughing is not praised;
seeing things hidden is auspicious, but seeing them naked is never praised.
The sight of a garland is auspicious, but wearing one is not praised;
likewise, a limb that has been cut is good, but one that has been sprinkled with water is not praised.
A gentle wind is praised, but an excessively strong wind is not praised.
One who is ill or dirty is commended [for bathing], but one who is already adorned is not praised [for doing so]. Ascending a mountain is commended, but descending from it there is not.
Smoke-colored clouds, the sound of kettledrums and conchs, wind, and rain from the clouds on all sides;
whatever among all stable things may become unstable, and whatever internal disorders caused by humors (doṣas) there may be—[these portend calamity].
Just as in former times the royal sages and all the hosts of gods were desired in their various forms,
so too is the cutting of a Brahmin’s body;
all these things are indeed auspicious.

Whatever may be auspiciously indicated by the preliminary signs, these [remedies] bring such bad dreams to rest. The gift of cows and the honoring of the twice-born—by this, the evil dream shall be completely overcome.
A person who has attained devotion to whichever deity should strive to worship that deity and others as well;
however, having seen a dream during the first part of the night, they say its fruition occurs at the end of a year.
That which occurs in the second [month] is six-monthly; that which occurs in the third is every six fortnights;
and that which occurs at the end of one and a half months bears fruit at dawn on the fourth night.
The gift of a vessel of sesame seeds to an excellent brahmin, rites for pacification, the performance of auspicious ceremonies,
worship of one's gurus, and well-prepared food— these destroy the effects of bad dreams.

But for one whose enemy might become submissive, or whom he desires to bring under his control—
if such a person sees a quarrel in a dream, affection will soon arise.
He who, during the first watch of the night, has seen that which brings both pleasure and pain,
will likewise return after a long time upon his journey.
In the middle [period] it does not come to pass at all; in the last [period] it comes to pass slowly.
However, seeing a swift Vaivārṇa, one should predict the acquisition of a woman.
Having seen the fish moving in the water, the wise man should know this:

If one should seize a *dhṛṣaṇa* in Campā, or seize it within dreams,
once awakened one should know that one's complexion will become such [as described].
Indeed, all drinks are sweet and pleasant;
however, he who drinks them at the end of sleep shall be endowed with gains.
In this dream, one is surrounded and devoured by dogs and jackals;
yet upon waking, one should know that it is indeed an enemy who is being overwhelmed.
If crows and vultures run about and fly overhead,
one should know that he is held captive and an enemy will kill him.
If the dogs of another's house urinate at one's door, one who has awakened should know: "My wife desires a paramour."
If one foot is on the ground and the second is placed upon the head,
one who is awake should know that the acquisition of a kingdom will occur.
If he should see the ocean or desire to drink its water,
once he has awakened, he should know that the acquisition of a kingdom will come to pass.
If one dreams of climbing a tree, a mountain, an elephant, or likewise a horse,
and then awakens, one should know that the acquisition of a kingdom will come to pass.
But he who, within a dream, sees his ancestors as they appear here in this world,
as well as his mother and father, they shall live for a long time.
But he who, within a dream, sees his hair and beard shorn,
should understand upon waking that the accomplishment of his purpose will come to pass.
If one sees one's own face in water, or sees it fleeing into the midst of fire,
upon waking one should know that there will be an increase in the family.
Running, leaping, and wandering through villages—
the awakened one should recognize these as his own self being cut down.
Furthermore, he who sees even a gathering of thieves at the end of a dream should recognize,
upon waking, that his own self has been cut down.
If one sees oneself seized by a black serpent at the end of a dream,
upon waking one should know that there will be affliction from an enemy.
If one should see bracelets, earrings, swan-shaped armlets, and circular pendants— indeed, any such ornament— it shall be a member of one's circle of kinsmen.
On a wall or the rampart of a house, they run here against one another; when there is a union with wealth,
the Khajas fly about for a moment.
But he who, within a dream, sees himself scorched by fire,
should recognize upon waking that fever will soon arise.
Seeing the king enraged and himself defiled,
one who has awakened should know that his household will perish.
If one repeatedly sees a heavy load of wood and grass upon one's own head, it indicates that a serious illness will arise.
But he who travels toward this direction in a vehicle yoked with monkeys should recognize,
once awakened, that this is indeed the final night.
Having grasped both the moon and the sun, he strokes them with his hand.
One who has awakened should understand that this is indeed the arrival of the noble Dharma.
He who, at the end of a dream, sees jasmine, vārṣika, kumuda, and blue lotuses, as well as an encounter with those worthy of offerings (dakṣiṇīya), [will attain success].
Upon seeing a brahmin, a śramaṇa, a kṣapaṇa, or a leader of the gods, one who has awakened should understand: "The yakṣas are indeed compassionate toward me."
Having been smeared with blood and having bathed in one's own blood,
when one awakens, one should recognize it as the attainment of sovereign power.
Whoever should see mung beans, black gram, barley, grain,
or the sight of fire within a dream, one should predict an abundance of food there.
Furthermore, he who sees gold, silver, or likewise a necklace of pearls within a dream, one should predict that there is a treasure-trove there.
Having seen much imprisonment, as well as cutting and crushing,
one who has awakened should know that the accomplishment of his purpose will come to pass.
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is another chapter on dreams.
Now, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter called 'The Examination of Months';
listen to that."

(E)35 u6 Examination of the Months (p.164) u6.1. If there should be thunder in the month of Phālguna, it portends the death of men.
The new moon appears with a reddish luster;
it portends the failure of all crops.
However, if the clouds thunder first, there will be an abundance of great harvests.
There will be no later crop;
it incites quarrels.
(Udānavarga 6.2) If the clouds thunder in the month of Caitra, then they incite the production of all crops.
If there is an eclipse of the moon, a great confluence of calamities will occur;
villages and fields will become desolate.
If frost covers the earth, it portends an abundance of food.
If the deity thunders in the month of Vaiśākha, it portends an abundance of food.
If there is a lunar eclipse during the first or last watch of the night, it portends security.
If a meteor falls, then in whichever country it strikes, the destruction of a leading person occurs in that region.
If there is an earthquake, it portends an abundance of food.
If the god thunders in the month of Jyeṣṭha, it portends disease.
If there is a solar eclipse, it portends the destruction of human beings.
If some sign of the moon or the sun is perceived in the eastern or western horn [of the lunar crescent], it portends security.
If a lunar eclipse occurs at midnight, it portends mutual slaughter among men.
And if there is a thunderous roar above, it portends affliction for the official.
And regarding the arrival of enemy armies:
if there is a solar eclipse in the month of Āṣāḍha that possesses a beautiful luster, it indicates an abundance of food.
If there is an eclipse of the moon, it portends disease;
if lightning flashes forth, it portends auspiciousness;
if mist covers the earth, [it portends the same].
If there is a solar eclipse in the month of Śrāvaṇa, the kingdom will undergo a change.
If there is a lunar eclipse, it portends famine in the first month;
due to wild beasts, there will be the destruction of excellent crops.
If stars fall upon a particular place, they portend war in that location;
if there is an excessive earthquake, it portends disease;
and if there is a thunderous roar, it portends the destruction of the one who is the master of the house where it occurs.
And during this month, one must not put on new upper garments;
no marriage ceremony, whether for a son or a daughter, should be performed;
[if done], it becomes unsuccessful.
If the god thunders in the month of Aśvayuja, it portends the destruction of human beings;
if there is a solar eclipse, it portends the destruction of great men;
if a sign of the moon is seen in the first watch of the night, it portends an abundance of food.
If an earthquake occurs that causes agitation, it indicates:
"A foreign king will destroy the country, and there the people will slay one another. Thus it indicates.
If, in the month of Kārttika, the god rains, it will incite great turmoil;
living creatures will devour the grain. And if the wind blows with alternating intervals, people there will be distressed by the water.
It portends the destruction of a great-souled person.
If a portent occurs during the first watch of the night, there will be heavy rain and the death of a great man.
If there is a thunderclap, it portends disease. (U6.9) If the god thunders in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, there will be the destruction of the crops,
and another person shall become the master there.
If a thunderous sound occurs in the sky, it portends disease for the people living in the eastern region. If an earthquake occurs, the leading person of that country will be released from execution.
If in the month of Pauṣa the clouds thunder during the first watch of the night, there will be the destruction of the country.
In the second [watch], it portends the bondage of the Great-Souled Person (mahātmā puruṣa).
And if, during the first watch, there is an eclipse of the moon and it appears red in color, it portends the arrival of water and portends a Great-Souled Man.
If a solar eclipse occurs, there will be war among pure men;
if falling stars are seen there, it portends turmoil in that region;
and if a thunderous roar arises in the sky, it portends the death of men.

If there is a thunderclap in the second month, humans will be slain by thieves. If a meteor is cast down in this very month and the moon is not seen, it portends the destruction of the crops. If there is an earthquake, the death of a great man occurs.
In this very month, a temple site should be established;
trees should be planted;
and the foundation for a pillar should be consecrated.
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter called 'The Examination of Months.
Now then, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter called 'The Knowledge of the Khañjarīṭaka Bird';
let it be heard."
"What then?
Let the Blessed One relate the knowledge of Triśaṅku and the Khañjarīṭaka."
Indeed, on Mount Gandhamādana, the Khañjarīṭaka-śāstra is seen by the mountain-dwellers; O gentle one, there is great danger for the mountain-dweller.
Whatever signs the wagtail (*khañjarīṭaka*) may display while moving about,
a twice-born man who has seen them shall attain five additional steps.
In that regard, all [the monks] should proceed wherever and with whomever it may be;
on grassy ground there shall be abundance of clothing, and on cow-dung [ground] there shall be continuity [of robes].
In Kañcāra there is an abundance of clothing; in Kardama, an abundance of food;
in Kṛkara, a scarcity of clothing; and in Purīṣa, the sight and hearing of feces.
In ashes, there is fruitless dispute; in sand, agitation. At the gateway of a deity, there is honor; in lotuses, great wealth.
In fruits, results are said to be according to their nature; in flowers, there is union with beloved ones.
There is fear regarding the ramparts and turrets, and the sight of enemies on the mountain ridges;
disease moves through the wings, and one should predict death for those who have fallen.
Fragrant oil, spirits, and the sight of a treasure during sexual union;
a drink is found at the top of a tree, and likewise in the houses of those who are playful.
If there is a rumor of the destruction of the country, there will be imprisonment for one who has entered into conflict;
but seeing that the nectar remains,
there is no doubt that there is rice here.
On the back of cows, success is certain; on the back of horses, victory is certain;
on the backs of sheep and goats, it is praised for all purposes.
On the back of a camel there is certain suffering; on the back of a dog, there is flight.
And on the back of a donkey here, death occurs—of this there is no doubt.
One should know that death occurs at a kīla (stake) or at the top of a sacrificial post (yūpa), of this there is no doubt;
likewise, if one is seen dead in the place of a water-jar (kumbha) or in a cremation ground (śmaśāna).
If one sees a wagtail flying in the sky,
one should predict that it will be fruitless;
however, seeing a wagtail perched together on its roost, one should be joyful.
One should assign [the results] for human beings according to their respective positions and according to their respective colors.
If the lines are uneven and have very narrow margins, there will be strife; if they are even and the field is uniform, one should predict people of equal status.
However, if the lines flow like a mountain river, one should predict exile.
There is no excessive anxiety regarding pieces of wood, nor is there loss of wealth regarding bones.
One should know that the bird, having five syllables in its name, flies toward whichever direction it approaches; one should understand one's own movement to be exactly like that of the bird.
Whether it be insects or even moths, whatever fear is seen here,
when [the signs] are abundant, one should indicate the bones of a man.
He who beholds the Khañjana bird near water, on the head of an elephant, at sunrise, in the presence of a Brāhmaṇa, in a prominent light, or on the head of a serpent, is fortunate.
The wise King Triśaṅku, the lord of the Mātaṅgas, declared the truth regarding the *Kañjana* treatise:
"In soil that is moist or dry, uneven or level, one should give instruction according to the faults and qualities as they have been described.
Having examined it there, the learned man should predict the auspicious or inauspicious results."
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter called 'The Knowledge of the Khañjarīṭaka Bird.
Now then, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter called 'The Cry of the Jackal';
let it be heard."
"What then? Let the Blessed One Triśaṅku speak.
"Homage to all the Noble Ones! 8.1.
Homage to all speakers of truth!
By means of the ascetic power and vigor of them all, I shall explain this chapter named "The Cry of Śiva.
Thus spoke the Blessed One Triśaṅku. 8.2.

He spoke this to Śāṇḍilya: "Listen to me regarding the nature and the manner in which those jackals howl. If a jackal stands facing the east and howls three times in the eastern direction, it announces prosperity."
If it cries out four times here, it announces auspiciousness;
if it cries out five times, it announces rain;
if it cries out six times, it announces fear of a foreign army.
If it cries seven times, it announces imprisonment;
if it cries eight times, it announces a reunion with loved ones.
"If it cries repeatedly, it announces the fear of a foreign army," so said the Blessed One Triśaṅku.
(U8.3) If, standing facing south in the southern quarter, it cries three times, making the sound "atṛ atṛ," it announces death in that place.
If it cries four times while standing facing the south, it announces a pleasant reunion from the southern direction itself and announces the acquisition of wealth;
if it should cry five times, it announces wealth.
If it cries out six times, it announces success;
if it cries out seven times, it announces dispute and quarrel;
if it cries out eight times, it announces fear.
He reports;
or he cries out repeatedly, reporting in a state of agitation.
Having approached, the Blessed One Triśaṅku says:
If, in the west, a jackal stands facing west and howls three times, it announces death;
if it howls four times, it announces imprisonment;
if it howls five times, it announces rain.
If it cries out six times, it announces food and drink;
if it cries out seven times, it announces sexual union;
if it cries out eight times, it announces the accomplishment of one's purpose.
"If it cries repeatedly, it portends a great rain-cloud," so said the Blessed One Triśaṅku.
(U8.5) If, standing facing north in the northern direction, it cries three times for a man who has set out on a journey, his travel will be fruitless.
If it cries out four times, it announces danger from the king;
if five times, it announces a dispute;
if six times, it announces prosperity.
If it cries seven times, it announces rain for seven years;
if it cries eight times, it announces punishment from the royal court;
if it cries incessantly, it announces [the same].
"It announces the fear of yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and kumbhāṇḍas," so said the Blessed One Triśaṅku.
"Listen to my instruction regarding that [fear] in every direction and intermediate direction, on mountain slopes and mountain peaks."
"She shall be satisfied, even when afflicted by thirst, and likewise for the attainment of knowledge" (U8.7ab).
"The wise man should predict the acquisition of knowledge or the acquisition of wealth" (U8.7cd),
if she is seen crying at a sacred ford, a temple, or at the root of a tree.
One should indicate success in all matters.
Even when there is fear of a jackal, [the sight of] a female jackal on one's left is auspicious;
therefore, being vigilant and mindful, one should always worship the female jackal.
One should perform service with offerings of incense and flowers;
thus being worshipped, she will bestow all accomplishments.
Thus, "all his goals are accomplished, just as the word of Triśaṅku [declared]. If the Krauṣṭrika cries out, it announces the acquisition of wealth;
if it cries facing downward, there is a treasure-trove there.
It indicates:
if it cries facing upwards, it indicates rain there;
if it cries while standing on a forked path and facing the east, it indicates the acquisition of wealth.
If it cries facing south, it announces a meeting with a beloved;
if it cries facing west at a forked path, it announces quarrel, dispute, conflict, and death;
if it cries at the edge of a well, it announces wealth there.
If it cries upon a grassy meadow, it announces the accomplishment of one's purpose;
if it cries with excessive softness, it announces illness in that place.
If a crow cries out while carrying a branch, it announces both profit and loss:
three times it indicates profit; four times, loss; five times, a meeting with loved ones; six times, food; seven times, danger; and eight times, conflict and dispute.
Thus spoke the Blessed One Trisaṅku.
"Furthermore, I shall speak again; listen to me in due order.
Whether it be when one is eating various foods or when one is standing on a path, I shall explain everything—listen to me.
When a jackal howls as a man is setting out, or stands facing the east, it announces swift departure and the accomplishment of his purpose."
Now, if it cries facing south, it announces the accomplishment of one's purpose;
if it cries facing west, it announces fear;
and then, if it faces north—
If it cries out, it announces the acquisition of wealth.
If it cries out as he has set forth, standing in front of him, it announces an affliction.
If it cries out on the right, provided he is facing toward the southern direction...
And it announces the accomplishment of one's karma.

If it cries out from the west, it indicates that there is harm from a thief; it announces suffering and mental distress for him. Furthermore, if it cries out from the right side while one is traveling on a road, it announces a great illness, misfortune, and that thieves will plunder one; this is for one who is ill.
If it howls facing the south,
"He cannot be cured, for he has been urged on by the messenger of Death.
If it howls while standing facing the north, it announces the recovery of the sick person and the acquisition of wealth.
If it cries out from the top of its head, it announces distress.
If it stands facing west and calls out to one another, it announces the decree of Yama.
If it cries while eating various kinds of food, [it portends misfortune].
"She who announces agitation," so said the Blessed One Triśaṅku.
"If a jackal howls in front of a man who has set out on a journey... (U8.10).
That which indicates the path of safety ahead and announces the accomplishment of one's purpose—

when this person traveling on the road is met by a jackal coming from the left and going toward the right, one should know that it signals the path of safety and announces the accomplishment of one's purpose.
If, as a man is traveling on a road, an auspicious jackal comes from the left and howls in front of him, it indicates that the path is dangerous;
a wise man should turn back.
Or, having gone toward the right direction, if it turns back from the left, one should not proceed by that path, according to the words of Triśaṅku.
If a jackal goes before one and sits down in front, one should recognize the path as being fearful;
the wise man should turn back. If a jackal comes from the front and turns toward the left, there is danger here; by that also, the wise man should recognize fear.
When the army has been summoned, if an auspicious jackal howls, it announces a return;
if [the army] should go forth, there will be defeat.
The army should not go.
When an army is marching, if a jackal comes from the front, it announces victory for the army and announces the defeat of the enemy force.
When a caravan is traveling, if a jackal goes before them, it indicates a safe path.
Likewise, it brings about the accomplishment of one's purpose.
When a man is traveling on a path, if the jackal howls to his left, it indicates the way:
"One must go by that path, according to the word of Triśaṅku."
"Likewise, at a shrine site belonging to a village or even a city,
if a jackal howls to the east or to the north, it announces safety there;
but if it howls to the south or to the west, it announces danger there."
They do not praise [omens] from the left, nor likewise those in the intermediate directions;
nor do they praise those that are excessively long or excessively harsh when occurring at the end of a month.
Now I shall describe the danger regarding the lower [direction], according to the words of Triśaṅku.
Having recognized a woman with a sweet voice as auspicious when the proper time and occasion have arrived,
the wise should consider both security and the accomplishment of their goals.
Diseases and calamities, however,
come to an end, just as by the words of Triśaṅku.
One should observe the omens of the howling of jackals in the cardinal and intermediate directions as a ritual practice.
That day which belongs to Śivā should be recognized as such.
On that day, offerings of flowers, perfumes, garlands, and oblations should be presented.
One must always maintain reverence for the deity.
One must be devoted to the divine teacher;
service should be rendered to the goddess;
she will accomplish all goals.
He reports all his affairs;
whatever task he is about to undertake, he reports all of that.
Incense made from resin and *guggulu* should be offered to the Goddess,
and an offering of flowers should be presented at the appropriate time;
thus spoke the Blessed Triśaṅku.
8.17. Here, in this place where the cries of jackals are heard, I shall declare the vidyā so that it will become true.

"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter named 'The Cries of the Omen-Birds.
Now then, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter named 'The Lines on the Hand';
let that be heard."
Then what shall the Blessed One Triśaṅku say? [Regarding] the lines on the hand:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which resides upon the hands of men."
The characteristics of pleasure and pain, as well as life and death.
Relying upon the base of the thumb, an upward line extends;
one born there experiences supreme happiness, while the second [line] exists within the knowledge [of the lineage].
That third line where the forefinger proceeds—
therein, according to the treatise, the reasons are stated to be briefly of four kinds.
If there are nodes at times other than the [proper] nodes, or if there is an affliction of the lunar mansions,
he who has emerged from the two [wombs] with a purified self shall indeed live for a hundred years.

One should give birth when thirty years have passed with a third part [added], or when fifty years have passed with half [added]; when seventy years have passed with three parts added, one should live for a full hundred years.
Thus, the intermediate region is revealed as being visible from the earth;
it should be understood by men according to its purpose through the designations of the lunar mansions.
Whichever number of lines there are on the path of the thumb's belly, one should know that he will have that many offspring; of this there is no doubt.
One should know that a person will have a long life if there is a long line;
however, one should know that a person will have a short life if there is a short line.
If a barley grain is found at the base of the thumb during the night, one should predict birth;
however, if it is found on the thumb during the day, birth is certainly predicted.
Wherever the unmanifest barley-grain (yavaka) is located, there one should designate the ascendant (lagna);
the ascendant is to be known as masculine, and one should designate it as day and night.
One should designate birth as occurring during the day; at night, it should be designated as female.
Night is declared to be the twilight, along with the other divisions—of this there is no doubt.
One should state that their rising from the male designation occurs at the end of the day and night.
If there is a barley-grain at the base of the thumb and a crack, happiness is ordained;
one should know that from a horse there will be auspiciousness here when there is a barley-grain at the thumb.
A garland of barley and a fish, as well as the thumb and barley-grain [marks], indicate pleasure during sexual union;
one should predict happiness for her in childhood, youth, middle age, and old age respectively.
Those upon whose palms are seen barley, water, or likewise a svastika—
those men are indeed fortunate.

In the first quarter of Pisces, there will be grain for enjoyment; in the first quarter of Aries, wealth from meat and the like; and in the first quarter of Pisces, one should know there is enjoyment and good fortune—of this there is no doubt.

One should recognize a lord of the earth by banners, flags, spears, and likewise by javelins; or by goads held in the palms of the hands. Furthermore, one should designate as a mere king (rājamātra) one who is born of a royal lineage.
Five branches are seen in Śākha, and likewise four in Hasta;
such a person shall be a Kṣatriya, an enjoyer of pleasures, and honored even by kings.
Then a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya becomes eloquent and possesses wealth and grain, without a doubt;
and a Śūdra who is devoted to the sacred festivals and steadfast shall become a possessor of great fortune.
He should always be honored by all and speak kindly to everyone;
yet one who lacks virtue or whose virtue is hollowed out is not truly great, even if he possesses much.
Moreover, if that line is dark-colored or broken, one is a partaker of suffering. He on whose [palm] are seen lines that are thick, full, and well-formed,
shall be of great enjoyment, a great scholar, and he shall live for a hundred years.
One upon whose palms the hoofprint of a goat, a royal parasol, and a conch and discus appear preceded [by these marks],
one should know him to be a lord of the earth.
The vulva portends fortune; the king [is indicated] by banners, flags, elephants, horses, garlands, and elephant-goads.
The fish portends drink; barley, wealth; and the sacrificial altar, sacrifice; while the cow-pen portends cattle.
If the little finger exceeds the joint of the ring finger, he lives for a hundred years;
if it is equal [to that joint], he lives for eighty years, as one might indicate by seven full rivers.
Having observed the lines arising from the complexion of the body— whether they possess their proper crests or are devoid of color—
one who knows [the signs] recognizes those of low, superior, or middling status as they move amidst poverty.
Having rubbed his hands with unguents, fragrant powders, and respectful scented dusts,
and having washed them until the streaks from rubbing against the inner garment have disappeared, he should examine his hand with a one-pointed mind.
Wearing bracelets, they attend upon the Lord of Men; moreover, three lines follow along the wrist.
Furthermore, that Great-Souled One has declared that between births, there will be the acquisition of garments and vast wealth and glory.
One whose hand is constantly raised gives perpetually; one with long and thick hands becomes wealthy for a long time;
one whose hand is covered with visible veins falls into ruin; and one whose hand is hidden by flesh acquires wealth.

The virtuous have palms as beautiful as the surface of a mirror, while the rogues have them crooked and wrinkled. One whose palms are here long joined together, resembling blood and deeply red, shall become a lord.

One whose mind is firm and radiant, whose hands are like blazing, reddish-gold lotuses upon stone, becomes possessed of great wealth; with hidden palms, he lives long in this world, enjoying drinks and pleasures.

O fair one, here likewise, he who has long and warm hands is certainly fortunate, whereas he whose hands are cold is a eunuch. Indeed, O slender-limbed one, he whose lines on the palm are well-formed possesses great wealth and is endowed with strength.
The line on the hand that brings wealth in this world is one that is well-formed from birth, very long like water,
follows the shape of water, is golden in color, and possesses both depressions and elevations.

One whose palms are very red obtains abundant wealth, provided their fingers are closely set; however, even if one possesses great riches, a person with broken lines on the palms that are faded and indistinct will surely squander it helplessly.
A man whose lines on the palms lack the color of ghee becomes wealthy and endowed with strength;
likewise, his wife will be virtuous, adorned with ornaments, beautiful, and faithful to him alone.
Having acquired sacred learning, he becomes possessed of great wealth; though at times deprived of riches, he possesses broad lines on the palms of his hands.
With straight lines on the palms that are as stainless as a blue serpent, he is a lord and a fortunate man.
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter on the lines on the palm of the hand.
Now, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter called 'The Cawing of Crows'; let it be heard.
What more [is there to say]?"
May the Blessed One relate the story of Triśaṅku.
Homage to the Arhats!
Having paid homage to them...
U10. The Cawing of Crows: U10.1. I shall here proclaim this treatise concerning the auspicious and inauspicious [omens] of crows, as well as victory and defeat, and likewise gain and loss.
I shall now explain, according to the prescribed rule, the accomplishment of the crows' speech regarding pleasure and pain, the pleasant and the unpleasant, as well as life and death.
The most excellent gods proclaim: "Homage, homage to the crows!
These crows, who feed upon offerings, have come to the world of men."
When a crow is ahead of one who has set out on a journey,
perched upon a milk-tree (kṣīravṛkṣa) and uttering its cry, it indicates the attainment of one's purpose.
With a voice full of satisfaction, he took refuge among the fruit-bearing trees;
having accomplished his purpose, he announced his return once more.
When the leaves of the trees have grown large and it blows a sweet fragrance,
one should predict that the food will be served without soup, yet mixed with molasses and cow's milk products.
If, however, it is seen licking its own body with its snout and feet, one should know that there is food there consisting of milk-rice mixed with ghee; of this there is no doubt.
If it rubs its beak against something rough and strokes its head while perched upon a fruit-bearing tree, there will certainly be a meal of meat.
Perched upon a fruit-bearing tree, he observes and speaks;
he announces the meat killed by a hunter as food.
If a crow perched upon a tree utters a terrible cry regarding a task, one should know that there will be quarrel and the fear of battle; of this there is no doubt.
If one sits upon a withered tree and speaks in a feeble and dejected manner,
or after having engaged in a great quarrel, no purpose whatsoever will be accomplished therein.
Having sat beneath a milk-exuding tree (kṣīravṛkṣa), one should utter words that are emaciated and dejected;
by proceeding gradually at the distance of a yoke’s length, the purpose there will not be accomplished.
If, sitting upon a withered tree, a female crow shrieks lustfully, at that very moment one should announce it; there will be danger from thieves.
If, sitting upon a withered tree, it cries out like a desirous crow,
one should indicate that it will show its back [in flight] and point to suffering from hunger.
If a bird, shaking its wings and looking about, cries out upon the road, one should not proceed there; the path is beset by thieves.
If a crow drags along either a rope or even a wooden plank, one should not proceed there; it is better not to go, for the path is beset by thieves.
If a crow alights upon cow dung, or on dry wood, or even upon ash, there will be quarrels, harsh words, and disease; nor shall one's purpose be accomplished there.
If the bird shows grass or wood,
and moreover has its claws dry before it, there will be danger from thieves in that place.
Sitting upon the caravan leader, one should speak in a weak and dejected manner;
one should fall down in the midst of the caravan, for there is no doubt that this is a band of thieves.
When birds cry out in various ways while moving to the right or in a state of fear, or when they perch upon a withered tree, one should know that there is great danger.
If a bird speaks while frightened, terrified, and overwhelmed,
and while striking at all the directions, then danger has arrived there.
One should follow after him as he goes; standing before him, one should speak. One should not proceed there oneself; rather, one should clear the path for him.
If one utters something emaciated or dejected in the center of the site or at its foundation,
one should recognize that there will be disease there, either in the dwelling itself or for the owners of the house.
If a crow caws confidently at the sound of a cart,
one should know that someone has arrived from afar and predict his success.
If a crow caws while perched upon a gargara, a small jar, or even on a cooking pot or a large earthen vessel, a journey is certain and well-known to take place.
If a crow caws while one is seated on a seat, lying down, or even standing, it foretells a certain departure; if one is away from home, it indicates a reunion with them.
If a crow sits upon a place sacred to Brahmā or caws while remaining steady,
one should know that there will be the acquisition of wealth and the gain of riches.
If, having sat in the place of Brahmā, it cries out weakly and piteously, a thief will take away goods from the place of junction; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding deities among deities and the groves belonging to a god,
one should predict the attainment of wealth for whoever he addresses with these words.
One should predict the acquisition of gold for that person from whom one takes it away.
A bowl, a small vessel, or even an excellent earthenware jar—
whichever of these one should take away, for that person one should predict the acquisition of wealth.
When a crow stands auspiciously in a flock at a height of a yoke’s length,
or where crows carry a piece of wood onto a house,
one should understand from this that there will be great danger arising from a beggar.
Where crows display blue, yellow, and red colors, as well as signs of withdrawal,
one should diagnose disease in that place.
If a crow caws at the edge of a village, it certainly foretells danger; or if they caw individually, one should know that there is great fear therein.
If a crow should take a bone and fly away toward the north,
and then sit upon a fruit-bearing tree, it indicates a meal of meat.
If a crow sits upon one's head and pulls at the ear,
one should predict death for that person within seven nights.
If it cries in a water-jar, in water itself, or in moist places,
and gazes upward with its face turned up, one should predict rain for the world.
If it cries at sacred fords or among trees with a highly gratified voice,
and likewise speaks with its face turned upward, one should predict a wind and rain.
If a crow cries out "kilakila" against its body in a moist place,
or beats its breast, one should immediately predict rain.
If it cries with a contented voice, affectionately and sweetly,
and utters a portion of syllables accompanied by a liquid sound, there will be food.
If a crow caws at the top of a gate or on a turret,
or repeatedly rubs its beak there, one should predict a battle in that place.
If there are circles or whirlpools outside the city,
one should predict fierce enmity and terrible conflict in that very place.
Whether in a village or even in a city, wherever they perform the mandala,
the owls cry out with their faces turned upward, and a state of despondency arises.
When a female crow caws to the east of a village,
forests and cities overflow with little water.
If a female crow caws in front or on the right side,
it rains in the first month, but thereafter the god does not rain;
black grains flourish, while beans perish.
When a female crow lays her eggs upon the crown of a tree to the south,
there will be an abundance of frogs, insects, dice, and thieves.
But when the female crow lays her eggs on the northwestern side,
there will be a middling year, and the crops will be of moderate quality.
If a female crow caws on the northwestern side,
lightning will strike there, and there will be danger for wild animals and birds.
When a female crow caws upon the topmost branch of a tree in the north,
one should know that grain which was sown previously is now coming forth.
When a female crow caws upon the top of a tree, one should know that there will be little rain; one should plant seeds on dry land.
But when a female crow makes her nest in the middle of a tree, it rains with moderate rain, and a moderate harvest is produced.
When a female crow lays her eggs at the root of a tree trunk, there shall be a terrible drought; one should predict famine in that region.
When a female crow brings forth four or five young at once,
there will be abundance of food and an increase in fruit there.

What more [is there to say]?"
Let the Blessed One explain Triśaṅku. Regarding the characteristics of the gates:
it is taught that the eastern gate is auspicious, pertaining to Mahendra and the divine.
In the southern direction, however, are Pūṣan and the Pitṛs (ancestors).
One should indicate Sugrīva and Puṣpadanta to the west here;
one should know Bhallātaka and Rājayakṣman to the north as auspicious.
Furthermore, there is indeed the friend who harms and the friend who is supremely friendly.
The wise and high-minded Viśvakarman spoke according to the rules:
"I shall declare, in due order, the merits and defects of building sites."
It should be level, quadrangular, and the soil should be extensive;
for a Brahmin, a site abounding in milk-yielding trees is considered auspicious and highly praised.
A site that is shaped like a chariot wheel because of its eastern extension,
where the soil is red, is highly praised for kings.
A triangular site that is strewn with *kuśa* grass, level, and sweet; one that is well-exercised and possesses water—such a site has wealth and medicinal herbs as its property.
That which has the appearance of glowing coals, the shape of a cow's mouth, or the form of a cart is declared to be uninhabitable, and it brings about the destruction of one's sons.

Furthermore, one should avoid from afar that which has been touched by collyrium or the armpits, as well as that which has been washed away by rainwater, and likewise water offered with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).
The [fire-pan] of a Brāhmaṇa is square, that of a Kṣatriya is circular;
for a Vaiśya it is ten [aṅgulas] and for a Śūdra twelve; therein lies the rule for their measurement.
In the north-eastern quarter of the site, one should cause a cow-pen to be constructed;
likewise, the fire-hall should be situated in the south-eastern direction.
To the south, one should establish the rain-shed, the granary, and the armory;
and to the west and north of these, one should establish the storehouse for the merchant's wares.
In the north, however, one should construct the unsurpassed place for excrement;
likewise, all [other structures] should be in the northeast, and the palace should face the east.
By reversing the prescribed rule, there would be enmity and slaughter therein;
the length of all the constructed gates is considered to be double [the width].
One may construct temples for the gods as one desires, including their gateways;
however, women seen at the ends of the arms of those gateways bring about misfortune.
If there should be the seizing of tribute at the gate of a hostile local king, or a kingdom in the city of Mahendra, or solar radiance like that of the sun; u11.16cd.
In the Satya region, there is mildness; in the Mṛga region, heroism; in the Antarīkṣa region, the loss of wealth;
in the Vāyavya region, many diseases; and in the Bhaga region, the reversal of fortune.
In Puṣya, one is always fortunate; in Vitatha, however, one becomes unfortunate.
In Śoka, there will be a transformation of the elements (disease); in Soṣa, there is dejection for him.
If the planet is in Ballāta, there is residence in a house; if in Rājayaṣma, there is obstruction. If it is in Hradu, there is the settling of dust; but if in Āditya, strife is certain.
If there is great fear of *nāgas* from the *nāga*-king, there will be long life for him;
however, one should predict that there will be danger from fire at whatever gate he possesses.
One should know that there is the destruction of that very wealth and of the family;
one should recognize Yama as death for the most excellent and noble lineage. When Bhṛṅgirāja is present, the wise man [should know] the Gandharva as being the fragrance of garlands.
If [the moon] is in Bhṛṅga, there is anger and strife; in Pitṛ, there is an abundance of enjoyments;
in Dauvārika, very little wealth; and in Sugrīva, one is honored by the king.
In Puṣpadanta there is the acquisition of wealth; in Varuṇa, there is the sight of water;
in Asura there is terrible death; and in Roga, there is the presence of many ailments.
I shall now describe the offerings and oblations according to each household;
having honored them with various regional perfumes, one should present the oblation.
In the *Kalatra* mansion, the causes and seeds are located; in the *Madhyama*, however, only what has been acquired.
In *Mahendra*, there are scattered flowers; and in *Pāvaka*, milk and curd.
When the sun is in Āditya, one should offer food and millet;
when it is in Antarīkṣa, divine water and aquatic flowers.
The first lunar day (pratipad) is to be known as Nandā, and the sixth and thirteenth days as Jayā.
On those respective days, a wise and discerning person should certainly perform [the ritual].
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter called 'The Characteristics of the Gates.
Now then, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall explain the chapter called 'The Twelve Houses';
let it be heard."
