Let the Blessed One relate the account of Triśaṅku, who possessed twelve *ṛśikas*. (p. 183)
12.1ab. Hereafter, I shall explain the section on mind and consciousness (cittavijñāna), 12.1cd.
just as it has been illustrated for people by means of examples alone.
I shall now fully explain that supreme consciousness of the mind;
indeed, those twelve minds are the ones that circulate in the world.
I shall explain them to you; therefore, listen to me according to the truth.
A wise man should indeed construct twelve mandalas.
The first should be named Aries (Meṣa), and the second is known as Taurus (Vṛṣa).
The third is called Gemini, and the fourth is Cancer.
The fifth is Leo, and the sixth is known as Virgo;
Libra should be known as the seventh, and Scorpio as the eighth.
Dhanu (Sagittarius) is to be known as the ninth; Makara is recorded as the tenth.
Kumbha is to be known as the eleventh, and Mīna is said to be the twelfth.
The first house (horā) is the body of the one born; in the second, wealth is considered;
in the third, likewise the brother; and in the fourth, one's own kinsmen.
In the fifth [house], a son is considered; in the sixth mandala, enmity;
in the seventh, union with a wife; and in the eighth, death is traditionally taught.
In the ninth house, dharma is considered; in the tenth, the fruit born of dharma;
in the eleventh, the acquisition of wealth; and in the twelfth, the occurrence of futility.
These twelve states of mind have been perceived by the great seers exactly as they are;
and they are to be understood by embodied beings as being the very self of all living beings.
O Agastya, someone asks: which [part] should one first touch of the mandala? One who touches the head, and a sound is also perceived.
If one should say that he himself is diseased, or that there are fiery portents of destruction,
then that [dream] should be considered as intended for his own sake.
He would intensely consume gold, silver, copper, and even iron;
and that all-pervading fire certainly consumes everything.
Having observed such a fiery portent, one should indicate its nature;
whatever the sound may be, by that very sound the thought [of the dreamer] is to be discerned.
If some man should come and touch the second mandala,
or should stroke his neck, his throat, and again his chin;
If a sound is heard and cows are likewise seen,
having observed such an omen as this, one should indicate the sound of a cow there;
or else, whatever the sound may be, by that the object of his thought is indicated.
If some man should come and touch the third mandala, he should cleanse his face; one should indicate that his mind is that of a woman.
Now, if there should be a sound there, let such things as these be heard:
"born," "procreated," "produced," and likewise, "will be born."
Having seen such an omen, one should predict the nature of his fetus;
or rather, whatever the sound may be, by that [sound] one should discern what he has thought.
If some man comes and touches the fourth circle,
or if he touches the tortoise, one should predict a quarrel;
and if there is a quarrel, there will undoubtedly be legal proceedings with his own kinsmen.
The sounds "ākaṭṭā" and "kaṭṭeti" arise incessantly;
having seen such an omen as this, one should predict a quarrel there.
If some man comes and touches the fifth mandala,
or touches the heart, then offspring is considered there.
One who has died while gone to another village should be known as a "banished" (pravāsaka) corpse;
whatever weapons or property he possessed that remained in the family of Brāhmaṇas [are to be dealt with accordingly].

Now, if there should be a sound there, which the great seers have observed—such as the cry "Son! Son! or a sound that has already passed away—having seen such an omen, one should predict death in that place.
If some man comes and touches the sixth mandala,
and also touches the sides, then the "thought of the limbs" (gātracintā) is considered to have been indicated.
But a battle that is most terrible occurs, and even an enemy is slain;
or else, whatever sounds are heard there, they are undoubtedly [omens of victory].
But this [bird] is indeed exuding fluid, killed, and likewise struck down;
having seen such an omen as this, one should predict a conflict with enemies.
Or else, whatever the sound may be, by that the [enemy's] intention is revealed.
A certain man, having arrived, should touch the seventh mandala;
he should rub his hand with his hand and likewise rub the channel (nāḍī).
One should understand that thoughts concerning a dwelling pertain to another village;
however, these are the sounds that must be heard by one desiring land.
Whether it be stationary, settled, moving, completed, or already in one's hand— having seen such an omen, one should predict the dwelling accordingly;
or whatever sound has been heard, by that one's thoughts are determined.
A certain man, having arrived, should touch the eighth circle; he should then rub both the belly and the hip.
Its end is seen, and its death is also seen;
if there were to be death, it would be like the union with another's beloved.
In these cases, the following sounds should be heard: "He will surely die.
Having seen such an omen, one should predict his impending calamity.
A certain man came and touched the ninth mandala;
he further touched my thigh, and the contemplation of the Dharma was contemplated.
In that place, sounds are indeed to be heard; of this there is no doubt.
"Perform the sacrifice! O officiating priest! And likewise, O patron!"—having heard such sounds as these, one should direct one's thoughts toward the sacrifice.
If some man should come and touch the tenth circle,
having reflected upon the consideration of karma, it is undoubtedly domestic work.
If he touches his knees, one should indicate that he is contemplating an action;
in that case, these sounds will surely be heard, and there is no doubt about it.
Having observed such an omen as this— the work on the ground, the field, and likewise the work within the field— one should prescribe a deliberation regarding the ritual action.
If some man comes and touches the eleventh [digit],
and then touches the shanks again, one should predict the acquisition of wealth.
In this regard, these sounds are to be heard here without a doubt:
[the sounds of] cowries, gold, garments, grain, and likewise jewels and earrings.
Having heard such a sound, one should indicate gold for him;
or else, one should predict a result corresponding to the nature of the sound.
A certain man might come and touch the twelfth mandala;
he touches my feet while asking whether my mind is free from any harmful intent.
But those who have mastered the knowledge of signs should listen to the sounds that arise from the hope for the object contemplated, as well as those that are adventitious.
If the sound is despondent and voiceless, one should indicate that he is without hope;
or else, whatever the nature of the sound, such is what he has contemplated.

13. Characteristics of a Maiden.
13.1: By means of which [marks] reality is understood, and by which auspiciousness is established—those characteristics of women that are censured and those that are praised, I shall now declare.
One should examine the father, the mother, the maternal uncle, and likewise the brother— image by image— just according to the words of Triśaṅku.
When the muhūrta is auspicious, the lunar day (tithi) is complete, and the asterism (nakṣatra) is honored,
one who knows the scriptures should consult with the learned and examine the girl.
One should examine the hands and feet, as well as the nails and the fingers;
likewise, the lines on the palms, the shanks, the hips, the navel, and the thighs.
The lips, the tongue, and the teeth; likewise the cheeks, the nose, the eyes, the eyebrows, the forehead, the ears, and the hair as well.
An expert in the treatises should examine the hairline, the voice, the complexion, the gait, the intellect, and the character of maidens; therein,
the discerning man should first investigate these himself.
A woman with a voice like a bronze bell, the complexion of a cloud, and sweet eyes shall give birth to eight sons and be surrounded by male and female servants.
She whose four [teeth] do not recede, all of which are indeed turned to the right,
and whose limbs and body parts are well-proportioned, gives birth to eight sons.
A woman whose belly resembles that of a frog attains sovereignty;
she shall give birth to blessed sons and enjoy their affection.
She on whose palm the tortoise, the svastika, the banner, the goad,
the earring, and the garland are clearly and well-defined shall give birth to one son, and one should designate him as a king.
She whose hand grasps a storehouse or a chamber with an arched gateway shall become a queen,
even if she is born in the family of a slave.
She who has thirty-two teeth, all as white as cow’s milk,
with even peaks and a glossy luster, gives birth to a king.
One who has a glossy gaze like that of a kāraṇḍava bird, deer-like eyes, and delicate skin;
whose lips and tongue are red, and whose face is beautiful—such a woman attends upon a king.
She who has a slender and prominent nose, a face free from redness, a slightly reddish belly, beautiful eyebrows, and lovely hair-ends— that girl shall indeed have many offspring.
Her fingers are closely joined and lovely, her nails resemble lotuses, and her feet are straight and red; that maiden prospers in happiness.
She whose two curls are symmetrical and glossy, and both of whose sides are well-proportioned,
shall become the wife of a king.
One should proceed keeping [the bride] to the right and look at her while keeping her to the right; one should bring home a maiden who practices such circumambulation for the sake of a wife.
When her thighs, shanks, and sides are well-proportioned, and her stride is firm;
when her eyes have red corners and are large—such a girl prospers in happiness.
A woman who has deer-like eyes, deer-like calves, a deer-like neck, and a deer-like belly— indeed, a woman whose name corresponds to these qualities— who attends upon the king.
She whose hair is beautifully arranged at the crown and whose face is perfectly round,
and whose navel curls to the right— that maiden increases the prosperity of her family.
Neither too long nor too short, with well-set feet and delicate skin,
and with hair-ends that are pleasant to the touch— one does not transcend good fortune.
A wise man should choose for the sake of his household such a woman as has lovely lips, red lips, and speaks pleasantly— a woman who brings happiness to the home.
She whose palms have the luster of blue lotuses and gold, and whose fingers are long,
shall become the mistress of many thousands.
Having obtained a daughter endowed with auspicious marks, a man prospers, being possessed of wealth, grain, long life, fame, and splendor.
I have already described the auspicious women who possess the marks of good fortune;
now I shall explain, according to their enumeration, the characteristics that are inauspicious.
One who looks upward, one who looks downward, one who looks sideways,
one whose gaze is wandering, and one with wide eyes— these should be avoided by the wise.
She whose hair is split at the tips, rough, and hanging down in loose strands; u13.27ab.
She has variegated garlands and variegated limbs, and she moves according to her own will.
One who is lustful, tawny-eyed, fair-complexioned, or excessively dark; one who is too tall or too short—these should be avoided by the wise.
She whose forehead, belly, and buttocks—these three—hang down, kills three men: her husband's younger brother, her father-in-law, and her husband.
If there is a line of hair on the side [of the abdomen] and the hips are sunken,
one attains a long life, yet remains miserable for a long time.
A woman whose shanks resemble those of a crow, who has blood-red eyes and a harsh voice,
is devoid of happiness and hope, abandoned by her kin, and ruined.
She whose belly is excessively large and hangs down like a drooping nose is a woman who is utterly lacking self-control, yet possesses many sons and is deeply afflicted by suffering.

But she who is well-behaved in all her conduct, whose limbs are delicate, who has attained composure, and who is endowed with all equal virtues— she should be known as a woman who acts according to her will.
She whose shanks are covered with hair and whose face is perfectly round—
such a woman desires either a son, a brother, or even a lover.
She whose two forearms and wrists are covered with rows of body hair,
and who has hair upon her upper lip, will devour her husband.
If a woman has gaps between her fingers, gaps between her toes, and gaps between her teeth,
the wealth acquired by her husband does not find pleasure in her home.
As she walks, however, the joints of her limbs crack;
she should be known as one who experiences great suffering and never attains happiness.
She whose little toe does not touch the ground will abandon her husband from her youth and pursue her own pleasure.
If the ring finger of her foot does not touch the ground, she will not find pleasure in youth; she lives as a harlot.
If the second toe of a maiden's foot extends beyond her big toe,
that girl will take a lover, especially once she has reached the prime of youth.
She whose navel has a whorl at the back and is deeply recessed does not remain in maidenhood; she obtains a second husband.
Deformed, with a webbed hand, and having rough cheeks and hair—
even if born in a royal family, she falls into servitude.
But she whose cheek develops a dimple while laughing—
even if she goes to perform the fire-ritual— will quickly bring about misfortune.
A woman with beautiful eyebrows who has symmetrical and even cheeks,
yet whose lips are drooping, does not delight in one man for long.
With a hanging belly, a thick head, red eyes, and a tawny face, she devours eight heroes; she remains for a long time with the ninth.
Neither a name of a goddess, nor a river, nor a deity, nor one identical with a tree or a shrub— these should be avoided by the wise.
A woman whose name is that of a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), or one whose name corresponds to her lineage (*gotra*),
even if she is well-concealed and protected, may still commit a sin in her mind.
A man should always avoid these women whom I have described,
but he should always seek out such as those previously praised.
With a lotus, a goad, a svastika, a vardhamāna, a wheel, a banner, and a flask in his hands.
And those maidens who possess the excellent marks of the conch and the parasol become auspicious for the attainment of prosperity.
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter concerning the characteristics of maidens.

let it be heard."

Chapter 14: On Garments (p.
192). U14.1ab: Under Kṛttikā, fire burns; under Rohiṇī, there is the gain of wealth.
U14.1cd: Mṛgaśiras brings gadflies and stinging insects; Ārdrā is destructive to life.
Under Punarvasu one shall be prosperous; under Puṣya, one shall possess fine garments;
under Āśleṣā, there shall be loss; and under Maghā, one should go to the cremation ground.
Under the Phālgunī stars one acquires knowledge; under the Uttaraphalgunīs, one possesses fine garments; under Hastā, one performs manual crafts; and under Citrā, travel is certain.
Under Svāti, one obtains beautiful clothing; under Viśākhā, that which is pleasing to behold; under Anurādhā, many garments; and under Jyeṣṭhā, the destruction of clothing.
If one wears a garment under Mūla, it will become soiled; under Āṣāḍhā, disease arises.
Under Uttarā, one shall enjoy refined food; under Śravaṇā, there is pain in the eyes.
One should know that Dhaniṣṭhā brings an abundance of grain; Śatabhiṣaj brings fear;
Pūrvabhādrapadā brings water; and Uttarabhādrapadā leads to the gain of a son.
Revatī leads to the acquisition of wealth; Aśvinī bestows the gain of garments;
and Bharaṇī is filled with fear and is accessible to thieves.
"O Puṣkarasārin, this is the chapter on garments.
Now, O Puṣkarasārin, I shall proclaim the chapter on the *luṅga* plant;
let it be heard."
What then?
Let the Blessed One relate the story of Triśaṅku.
Chapter 15: On Divination (p.
193). 15.1ab: Where did these seeds of grain, such as barley and the like, originate?
By those [elements] this entire universe, both the stationary and the moving, is sustained.
How should one sow the seed, and how should one employ the plough? Under which conjunctions of lunar mansions and under which conjunctions of lunar days should these be done?
U15.3ab: Should one sow [the seeds] in the autumn or in the summer, and in which month should one sow them? U15.3cd: How many signs are praised, and which ones should one avoid?
U15.3ef: To whom should one cause incense to be given, and with what mantra should one cause it to be given?
If the *luṅgā* plant grows with its coils turning clockwise,
then that *nāgamukhī* *luṅgā*, even when its face is variegated, burns [the enemy].
Or even if it has the point of a darbha needle, what could be the cause therein?
How many are remembered as signs of prosperity, and how many are known as signs of famine?
How many castes have been fully described, and how many castes have been pointed out?
If Vāsava sends rain upon one whose seeds have been lost or destroyed, or if there should be a violent thunderclap, or even if the earth should quake; U15.6cd.
"What is the grain, what is the fruit, and what should one observe as the cause therein?
I wish to hear all of this in brief, according to its true nature."
Having heard the words of the brahmin Puṣkarasārin, Triśaṅku, the lord of the Mātaṅgas,
spoke these words: "Long ago, when the gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
and kinnaras churned the ocean, the nectar was seen arising from it."
While the nectar was being consumed, the twice-born one requested a share;
thereupon, the gods granted him ten drops of the nectar as his portion.
From that, these seeds were produced upon the earth, bringing happiness to the world:
barley, rice, sesame, wheat, mung beans, and black gram.
One should know that *śyāmaka* is the seventh [crop], and sugarcane is recorded as the eighth;
the remaining many varieties of grain have arisen from their combination.
In all the *harītakī* fruits and whatever other species of beings there were,
a ninth drop fell everywhere upon their bodies as nectar; likewise, a single drop was cast down upon all the roots.
In the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should sow rice and other grains; likewise, all the autumnal crops and so forth should be sown in the month of Bhādrapada.
In the month of Kārttika or Mārgaśīrṣa, one should sow grains in the field on the fifth,
the seventh of the bright fortnight, the sixth, or on the eleventh days.
On the thirteenth, the second, and likewise on the ninth days,
one should especially sow all seeds in low-lying places.

They say that the first lunar day, Nandā, is auspicious for all undertakings;

The second lunar day is declared to be Bhadrā; it is auspicious for activities involving ornaments. The third is explained as Jayā; it is highly praised for activities aimed at victory.
The fourth lunar day is declared to be *riktā* (empty); it is beneficial for the destruction of villages and armies.
The fifth lunar day should be known as *pūrṇā* (full); it is recommended for medical treatment, travel, and journeys, as well as for giving gifts, study, and the arts, and for physical exercise.

The sixth [lunar mansion], known as Jyeṣṭhā, is censured for journeys, but it is praised for entering a house, acquiring a field, marriage, or the rites of giving away a daughter; likewise, Maitra [Anurādhā] is so used.
The seventh [lunar day] is known as Bhadrā; it is most excellent for the path of virtuous deeds, for the royal insignia of kings, for the making of umbrellas, and for the construction of couches.
